teile.einleitung: Self-induction means that a coil produces a voltage in itself when the current changes. This voltage always works against the change, similar to the inertia of a heavy cart. That is why the current rises with a delay when you switch on, and a spark can form when you switch off.
wichtigste: In self-induction a coil induces a voltage in itself when the current changes.
The self-induced voltage is U = L times change in current divided by time.
The inductance L is measured in henries.
When you switch on, the current in a circuit with a coil rises with a delay.
After one time constant τ = L/R, the current reaches about 63 per cent of its final value.
A coil stores energy in its magnetic field, namely half of L times I squared.
The ignition coil of a petrol engine uses self-induction for the ignition spark.

abschnitte.text: When current flows through a **coil**, a magnetic field forms around it. If the current changes, the magnetic field changes too. But according to the law of induction, a changing magnetic field produces a voltage, and it does so in the same coil. This voltage is called the **self-induced voltage**. According to **Lenz's law**, it is always directed so that it works against the change in current.

You calculate the self-induced voltage with U = L · ΔI/Δt. Here L is the **inductance** of the coil, measured in henries. An example: if the current in a coil with L = 0.5 H falls evenly by 4 A in 0.02 seconds, a voltage of 0.5 · 4 / 0.02 = 100 volts is produced. The more turns and the better the iron core, the greater the inductance.

If you switch on a circuit with a coil, the current does not rise at once, but with a delay. How fast is described by the **time constant** τ = L/R. With L = 2 H and R = 100 Ω it is 0.02 seconds, that is 20 milliseconds. After one time constant the current has reached about 63 per cent of its final value; after about five time constants it has practically arrived. When you switch off, on the other hand, the current collapses suddenly, and a very high voltage can be produced.

A coil carrying current stores **energy** in its magnetic field. You calculate it with E = ½ · L · I². So a coil with L = 0.2 H and a current of 3 A stores 0.5 · 0.2 · 9 = 0.9 joules. When you switch off, this energy is released again, for example as a spark at the switch. That is why sensitive circuits are protected with a **flyback diode**.

The **ignition coil** of a petrol engine uses self-induction: if its current is suddenly interrupted, a high voltage is produced, which creates a spark at the spark plug. Electric fence energisers for pastures in Switzerland also produce short voltage pulses in this way. Coils in power supplies smooth the current, because they resist rapid changes. In older fluorescent lamps a choke coil helped with starting.

The American **Joseph Henry** discovered self-induction around 1832. At almost the same time the Englishman Michael Faraday was also studying electromagnetic induction. The unit of inductance is named after Henry. In 1834 the Baltic German physicist Heinrich Lenz formulated the rule about the direction of the induced voltage.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wound-up wire that produces a magnetic field when current flows.
A quantity that shows how strongly a coil resists changes in current.
The unit of inductance, H for short.
The time after which the current in a coil circuit reaches about 63 per cent of its final value.
The induced voltage always works against its cause.

gewusst: If you pull out the plug of a device with a motor, you sometimes see a small spark: that is self-induction.
An ignition coil briefly turns the 12 volts of a car battery into many thousands of volts.
Self-induction works similarly to inertia: the current in a coil wants to stay the way it is.

teile.einleitung: Tug of war is a game of strength in which two teams pull in opposite directions at the two ends of a rope. The winner is the team that pulls the rope to a mark on its own side. It is not only a fun game at a school fête, but also a competitive sport that has a lot to do with physics.
wichtigste: In tug of war two teams pull a rope in opposite directions.
A team wins when it pulls the rope to a mark on its side.
If both teams pull exactly as hard, the rope does not move.
A mark in the middle of the rope shows which way the rope is moving.
In a proper competition a team has 8 people.
From 1900 to 1920 tug of war was a sport at the Olympic Games.
As well as strength, the right body position and pulling at the same time are decisive.

abschnitte.text: Two teams line up at the two ends of a long, thick **rope**. In the middle of the rope there is a **mark**, and lines are drawn on the ground. At a starting signal both teams pull in opposite directions. The winner is the team that pulls the middle mark over a certain line onto its own side. The game is very popular on school trips, at gymnastics festivals and at children's birthday parties.

In tug of war two **forces** act in opposite directions. If they are exactly the same size, they cancel each other out and the rope does not move; this is called a **balance of forces**. Only when one side pulls harder is there an overall force that moves the rope towards it. Friction between the shoes and the ground is also decisive. Whoever grips the ground better can put more force into the rope without slipping.

Good tug of war pullers lean far **backwards** and dig their feet firmly into the ground. That way they work with their whole body weight and not just their arms. The legs have the strongest muscles and push the body backwards. It is especially important that everyone pulls **at the same time**; often one person sets the rhythm. If everyone pulls at the same moment, their forces add up; otherwise a lot of force is lost.

abschnitte.titel: Tug of war as a sport
abschnitte.text: From 1900 to 1920 tug of war was part of the **Olympic Games**. Today there are world and European championships, organised by the international tug of war federation. A competition team has 8 people, and there are **weight classes** so that teams can be compared fairly. The pullers wear special shoes and sometimes strain against each other for minutes. In Switzerland, too, there are clubs that do tug of war as a competitive sport.

Tug of war is very old and was known in many parts of the world, for example in China, Korea, India and Europe. It was often part of festivals and customs. In some areas whole villages or parts of towns pulled against each other on huge ropes. Because you only need a rope, you can play it almost anywhere. It encourages team spirit, because nobody can win alone.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that can move, slow down or change the shape of a body.
When equal, opposite forces cancel each other out.
The force that stops your shoes from slipping on the ground.
A grouping by body weight so that competitions are fair.

gewusst: At the 1908 Olympic Games in London, police officers from Great Britain won the tug of war.
In tug of war the tension is the same all along the rope, no matter where you pull.
A lighter team with good technique that pulls at the same time can beat a heavier team.

teile.einleitung: Thermodynamics is the study of heat and of how heat can be turned into other forms of energy. It explains how steam engines, car engines, fridges and power stations work. Its laws are among the most important laws in the whole of physics.
wichtigste: Thermodynamics studies heat, temperature and energy conversions.
The first law says: the energy of a closed system is conserved.
The second law says: the entropy of a closed system never decreases.
Heat always flows by itself from the warmer to the colder body.
Absolute zero is at 0 kelvin, that is minus 273.15 °C.
No heat engine can turn heat completely into work.
Heat is transferred by conduction, convection and radiation; radiation also works in a vacuum.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Greek and means something like “heat movement”. Thermodynamics describes how **heat**, work and energy are connected. It came about in the 19th century, when people wanted to improve steam engines. Important scientists were Sadi Carnot, Rudolf Clausius, James Joule and Lord Kelvin.

The first law is the **law of conservation of energy**: energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only converted. So in a closed system the total energy always stays the same. That is why a machine that runs for ever without any energy being added, a so-called perpetual motion machine, is impossible. When heating water, you can calculate the heat needed: to warm 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C takes about 669 kJ.

The second law says that the **entropy** of a closed system never decreases. Put simply, you can think of entropy as a measure of disorder. From this it follows that heat only flows by itself from warm to cold. A hot cup of tea therefore cools down, but it never gets hot again by itself.

Engines and power stations turn heat into movement. In 1824 the French engineer Sadi Carnot showed that part of the heat is always lost in the process. The greatest possible **efficiency** depends only on the hot and the cold temperature. If a machine works between 600 K and 300 K, it can turn at most 50 per cent of the heat into work.

Heat can be transferred in three ways. In **conduction** particles pass the energy on, for example in a metal spoon. In convection a flowing gas or liquid carries the heat. **Radiation** needs no substance at all and also works in a vacuum; this is how the Sun's heat reaches us.

The third law says that **absolute zero** can never quite be reached. It lies at 0 kelvin, that is minus 273.15 °C. Fridges and heat pumps use the laws of thermodynamics to pump heat from cold to warm with the help of electricity. This does not contradict the second law, because energy is added from outside.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic law of thermodynamics that always applies.
A measure of how spread out or disordered the energy in a system is.
The share of the energy put in that is really converted usefully.
An imagined machine that runs for ever without energy being added, which is impossible.
A space with almost no particles in it.

gewusst: There is even a “zeroth” law; it was formulated after the others but is seen as more basic.
A car engine turns only about a third of the energy in the petrol into movement; the rest becomes heat.
The unit of energy, the joule, is named after the English scientist James Prescott Joule.

teile.einleitung: Superconductivity is an amazing state of some materials: below a certain, usually very low temperature, they conduct electric current with no resistance at all. Current can flow in them without any energy being lost. An important part of this story was written in Switzerland.
wichtigste: A superconductor conducts current without any electrical resistance.
A material only becomes superconducting below its critical temperature.
A superconductor pushes magnetic fields out of its inside; this is called the Meissner-Ochsenfeld effect.
Superconductivity was discovered in 1911 by the Dutchman Heike Kamerlingh Onnes.
In 1986 Johannes Georg Bednorz and Karl Alexander Müller discovered high-temperature superconductivity at the IBM laboratory in Rüschlikon.
According to BCS theory, two electrons at a time form a Cooper pair.
Superconducting magnets are found in MRI scanners and in the LHC particle accelerator at CERN.

abschnitte.text: In an ordinary copper cable the electrons keep bumping into things, which turns part of the energy into heat. This loss is called **electrical resistance**. In a superconductor the resistance disappears completely as soon as it is colder than its **critical temperature**. If you start a current in a superconducting ring, it keeps flowing with no measurable weakening, even after years. For most classic superconductors the critical temperature is only a few degrees above absolute zero, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius.

The Dutch physicist **Heike Kamerlingh Onnes** was the first to turn helium into a liquid. This let him cool substances down to about 4 kelvin. In 1911 he noticed that the resistance of mercury suddenly dropped to zero at about 4.2 kelvin. For his research at low temperatures he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1913.

In 1933 Walther Meissner and Robert Ochsenfeld found out that a superconductor pushes an outside magnetic field out of its inside. This **Meissner-Ochsenfeld effect** leads to a spectacular experiment: a small magnet floats freely above a cooled superconductor. Superconductivity was only explained in 1957 by the **BCS theory** of Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer. According to it, pairs of two electrons form, the Cooper pairs, which move through the material undisturbed.

In 1986 Johannes Georg Bednorz and Karl Alexander Müller at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon on Lake Zurich discovered a new kind of superconductor made of **ceramic**. These substances became superconducting at much higher temperatures than any known before. As early as 1987 the two received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this. Soon materials with critical temperatures above 77 kelvin, that is minus 196 degrees Celsius, were found. These can be cooled with cheap liquid nitrogen instead of expensive liquid helium.

Most superconducting magnets are made of wires of the alloy **niobium-titanium**. Such magnets produce strong fields for MRI scanners, which doctors use to look inside the body. At CERN near Geneva, more than a thousand superconducting magnets keep the particles on their path in the Large Hadron Collider; for this they are cooled to 1.9 kelvin. In Japan, maglev trains float above the track with the help of superconducting magnets.

Scientists all over the world are looking for a superconductor that works at normal room temperature. With it electricity could be carried over long distances with almost no losses. So far, all known superconductors need strong cooling at normal air pressure. Breakthroughs that are reported again and again have so far not been confirmed.

begriffe.erklaerung: Temperature below which a material becomes superconducting.
Two electrons that join together in a superconductor.
Unit of temperature that starts at 0 at absolute zero.
A superconductor pushes magnetic fields out of its inside.
Metal mixture from which most superconducting wires are made.

gewusst: Only about a year passed between the discovery in Rüschlikon in 1986 and the Nobel Prize in 1987, one of the fastest Nobel Prizes ever.
A cooled superconductor can make a magnet float freely in the air.
At 1.9 kelvin, the LHC magnets are colder than space between the galaxies.

teile.einleitung: Sublimation is the direct change of a substance from a solid to a gas, without becoming liquid in between. That sounds unusual, but it happens in everyday life more often than you think, for example with snow in dry mountain air. Dry ice, iodine and comets are also famous examples.
wichtigste: In sublimation a solid turns directly into a gas.
The liquid state is skipped.
For a substance to sublimate, it needs energy in the form of heat.
With dry, cold air and sunshine, snow can turn directly into water vapour even below 0 °C.
Iodine slowly turns into violet vapour even at room temperature.
In freeze-drying, the ice is removed from frozen food at very low pressure.
The opposite process, from gas directly to solid, is called deposition.

abschnitte.text: Substances exist in three **states of matter**: solid, liquid and gas. Normally a solid first melts and then evaporates. In **sublimation** it skips the liquid state and becomes a gas directly. For this the substance needs energy in the form of **heat**, so that its particles can break free from the solid structure.

With very dry, cold air and sunshine, **snow** can disappear even below 0 °C without melting. It turns directly into water vapour. You can see this in winter in the mountains or when the Föhn wind blows. Washing that hangs outside in frost also slowly dries in this way.

**Dry ice** is frozen carbon dioxide and sublimates at about minus 78 degrees Celsius. This produces white clouds of mist, which are used on stage for special effects. The substance **iodine** forms dark crystals that slowly give off violet vapour even at room temperature. Mothballs made of naphthalene also get smaller over time, because they turn directly into gas.

In **freeze-drying**, food is first deep-frozen and then put into a room with very low pressure. There the ice sublimates and the water is removed without the food being cooked. This is how instant coffee, freeze-dried fruit and food for mountaineers and astronauts are made. Badly wrapped food in the freezer, on the other hand, gets **freezer burn**, because ice at the surface sublimates and the food dries out.

**Comets** are lumps of ice, dust and rock that circle the Sun. When a comet comes closer to the Sun, it warms up, and frozen substances turn directly into gas. They drag dust along with them, and a glowing cloud and a long **tail** form. That is why comets look so magnificent above all when they are near the Sun.

When a gas turns directly into a solid, this is called **deposition**. A beautiful example is **hoar frost**, which forms as fine ice crystals on branches and grasses on cold nights. Frost patterns on window panes and snowflakes in the clouds also form in this way. The heat that was needed for sublimation is released again.

begriffe.erklaerung: The form a substance takes: solid, liquid or gas.
Direct change from solid to gas.
Direct change from gas to solid.
Process in which the water is removed from frozen food at very low pressure.

gewusst: Dry ice got its name because it leaves no puddle when it disappears.
On Mars, part of the frozen carbon dioxide at the polar caps turns directly into gas every year.
Ice cubes in the freezer get smaller over time, because ice sublimates.

teile.einleitung: In music a note is a sound with a clear, steady pitch that you can sing or play on an instrument. Notes make up melodies, chords and whole pieces of music. They are written down in musical notation and given names such as C, D or E.
wichtigste: Unlike a noise, a musical note has a clear pitch.
In German there are 7 natural notes: C, D, E, F, G, A and H.
In German notation A is followed by H.
A series of notes that gets higher step by step is called a scale.
The distance from one C to the next higher C is called an octave.
You write a note down with a note symbol.
You can sing a scale with the syllables Do, Re, Mi.
Someone who makes up pieces of music and writes them down is a composer.

abschnitte.text: A musical note is produced when something vibrates very regularly, for example a guitar string or the air in a flute. We hear this regular **vibration** as a clear pitch that you can sing back. A **noise** such as rustling, knocking or hissing, on the other hand, has no clear pitch, because it is made of many disorderly vibrations. How high a note is depends on how often it vibrates per second. A note also has a volume, a length and a tone colour.

In German-speaking countries the seven **natural notes** are called C, D, E, F, G, A and H. After that the series starts again with C, only higher. In English, by the way, the H is called B. On the piano the natural notes are the white keys. The black keys lie in between; in German their notes are called, for example, Cis or Es, which in English are C sharp and E flat, and you get them by raising or lowering a natural note.

A **scale** is a series of notes that gets higher step by step, like a ladder. The best known is the C major scale from C up to the next C. The distance between two notes with the same name is called an **octave**, from the Latin word for eight, because the eighth note of the scale has the same name again. A note one octave higher vibrates exactly twice as fast. When singing, people often use the syllables Do, Re, Mi, Fa, So, La, Ti. They go back to the monk Guido of Arezzo, who used similar syllables almost 1000 years ago, at that time with Ut instead of Do.

So that music is not forgotten, notes are written down in **musical notation**. The notes sit on five lines, the stave. The higher the note is placed, the higher the sound. The shape of the note shows how long it lasts, for example a semibreve, minim or crotchet. In this way musicians all over the world can play a piece that a **composer** has written down.

So that all instruments fit together, they are tuned to a shared note. This **concert pitch** is the A above middle C, which usually vibrates 440 times a second, that is at 440 hertz. Before a concert the oboe often plays this A in the orchestra, and all the others tune their instruments to it. A small metal tuning fork also gives this note exactly.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the seven basic notes, in German C, D, E, F, G, A and H.
Distance between a note and the next note with the same name.
Series of notes that rises step by step.
Shared note A to which instruments are tuned.
Unit that shows how often something vibrates per second.

gewusst: Only in German-speaking countries and some neighbouring countries is there a note called H; in English notation it is called B.
A piano keyboard usually has 88 keys.
A tuning fork vibrates so regularly that it can be used to tune instruments very precisely.

teile.einleitung: An electricity meter is a measuring device that counts how much electrical energy is used in a flat or a house. It shows the consumption in kilowatt-hours. The electricity company uses its readings to work out how much you have to pay for the electricity.
wichtigste: An electricity meter measures how much electricity is used.
It shows the consumption in kilowatt-hours.
It usually hangs in the cellar or the stairwell.
You read it to know how much you have to pay.
In old meters a disc turned when electricity was flowing.
A modern smart meter sends the readings by itself.
When many appliances run at the same time, the meter counts especially fast.

abschnitte.text: An **electricity meter** measures the electrical energy that flows through the wires into the house. It counts continuously and shows a number in **kilowatt-hours** that keeps getting bigger. Each flat usually has its own meter. The meters often hang together in the cellar or the stairwell, at the so-called service connection.

abschnitte.titel: The old meter with a disc
abschnitte.text: For a long time there was almost only the **Ferraris meter**, named after the Italian physicist Galileo Ferraris. In it a horizontal aluminium disc turns as soon as electricity flows. The more electricity is used, the faster it turns. A counter with number rollers counts the turns and so shows the consumption.

Today the old meters are being replaced by electronic meters. A **smart meter** measures consumption digitally and sends the readings to the electricity company by itself. Nobody has to come round to read it any more. In Switzerland most meters are to be replaced by smart meters by the end of 2027.

To work out the consumption, you read the meter at the beginning and at the end of a period. The difference gives the kilowatt-hours used. You multiply these by the **electricity price**, about 25 to 30 centimes per kWh, and that gives you the electricity bill. Some meters distinguish between the **peak rate** during the day and a cheaper off-peak rate at night.

The meter counts especially fast when many appliances are running at the same time or a powerful appliance is switched on. A cooker, a tumble dryer or a kettle drive it hard. At night, when only the fridge and a few appliances on standby are running, it counts slowly. With an experiment you can see how the consumption changes when you switch an appliance on and off.

You can help to make the electricity meter count more slowly. Switching off the light when nobody is in the room saves electricity. Switching appliances off completely instead of leaving them on **standby** also helps. With a smart meter you can often even follow the consumption in an app and see when the most electricity is used.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number that the electricity meter is showing at the moment.
Unit of energy in which electricity use is measured.
Electronic meter that sends its readings by itself.
The price you pay per kilowatt-hour.

gewusst: Old meters often state how many turns of the disc equal one kilowatt-hour.
If a house has a solar system, the meter can also measure how much electricity flows back into the grid.
Electricity meters are officially checked so that nobody has to pay too much.

teile.einleitung: The SI redefinition of 2019 was a major reform of the world's units of measurement. Since then, all base units such as the kilogram, metre or second have been defined by fixed constants of nature. This means the kilogram no longer depends on a lump of metal in a safe.
wichtigste: Since 2019, 7 constants of nature with exactly fixed values have formed the basis of the SI.
Since then the kilogram has been defined by the Planck constant.
Before that, the international prototype kilogram made of platinum-iridium was the standard.
The prototype was given up because its mass changed slightly compared with its copies.
Since 2019 the ampere has been defined by the elementary charge.
The mole used to be defined by the number of atoms in 12 g of carbon-12.
With the Kibble balance a mass can be linked directly to the Planck constant.

abschnitte.text: The **SI**, the International System of Units, sets the units of measurement used almost everywhere in the world. It has seven base units: second, metre, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. So that measurements can be compared worldwide, these units must be defined very precisely. This is overseen by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres near Paris.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the prototype kilogram
abschnitte.text: From 1889 the kilogram was defined by a small cylinder made of **platinum-iridium**, the international prototype kilogram. It was kept well protected in a safe near Paris. But comparisons with its copies showed that over the decades the masses drifted apart by tiny amounts. A standard that changes is a problem for science.

abschnitte.titel: Constants of nature as the basis
abschnitte.text: In November 2018 experts from many countries decided on the redefinition in Versailles, and it came into force on 20 May 2019. Since then seven **constants of nature** have had an exactly fixed value, including the speed of light, the **Planck constant** and the elementary charge. The kilogram now depends on the Planck constant, the ampere on the elementary charge and the mole on a fixed number of particles. The candela is defined by the luminous efficacy of exactly 683 lumens per watt.

With the **Kibble balance**, a mass can be linked directly to the Planck constant through electrical measurements. It compares the weight of a body with an electromagnetic force. It is named after the British physicist Bryan Kibble. The Federal Institute of Metrology **METAS** in Bern-Wabern has also worked on such a balance.

In everyday life you notice nothing of the redefinition: a kilo of apples weighs as much as before. The values were chosen so that the old and new units fit together seamlessly. The advantage is that the units can now be reproduced anywhere and at any time. You no longer need to compare with a single object in France.

begriffe.erklaerung: International System of Units with seven base units.
Quantity in nature that has the same value everywhere and always.
Tiny constant of nature from quantum physics that defines the kilogram today.
Metal cylinder that defined exactly one kilogram until 2019.
Science of precise measurement.

gewusst: The prototype kilogram was a cylinder only about 39 mm high and 39 mm across.
20 May is World Metrology Day, the day the redefinition came into force.
The metre has been defined by the speed of light since 1983.

teile.einleitung: The sievert, Sv for short, is the unit used to measure how strongly radioactive and other ionising radiation affects the body. It is named after the Swedish physicist Rolf Sievert. Because a whole sievert is a lot, in everyday life people usually calculate in millisieverts (mSv).
wichtigste: The equivalent dose or the effective dose is given in sieverts.
The unit is named after the Swedish physicist Rolf Sievert.
The unit gray, on the other hand, gives the energy absorbed per kilogram.
Alpha radiation has a radiation weighting factor of 20, so it is especially harmful.
In Switzerland a person receives about 6 mSv per year on average.
The biggest contribution comes from the gas radon in buildings.
For the population, a limit of 1 mSv per year applies to artificial sources, not counting medicine.

abschnitte.text: Ionising radiation, for example from radioactive substances or X-ray machines, can damage cells in the body. The **sievert** tells you how great this effect on people is. In calculations, one sievert equals one joule of energy per kilogram of body tissue, weighted by the type of radiation. Because one sievert is already a lot, millisieverts, that is thousandths, are mostly used.

The **gray** (Gy) only measures how much energy the tissue absorbs, the so-called absorbed dose. But different types of radiation do different amounts of harm. So you multiply by a **weighting factor**: for gamma and beta radiation it is 1, for alpha radiation 20. If a tissue absorbs 2 mGy of alpha radiation, the equivalent dose is therefore 40 mSv.

People in Switzerland receive about 6 mSv per year on average. Most of it comes from the radioactive noble gas **radon**, which can get from the ground into cellars and houses, especially in the Alps and the Jura. Next come medical examinations such as X-rays or CT scans. Further parts come from space, from the ground and from food.

So that nobody receives too much radiation, there are **limits**. For the population, radiation from artificial sources, not counting medicine, may be at most 1 mSv per year. People who work with radiation as part of their job, for example in hospitals or nuclear power stations, may receive at most 20 mSv per year. For this they wear a small measuring device, a **dosimeter**, on their body.

Rolf Sievert (1896 to 1966) was a Swedish medical physicist. He researched how radiation can be used safely in medicine and built instruments for measuring radiation doses. He helped to set up international rules for **radiation protection**. The unit sievert was introduced in his honour in 1979.

begriffe.erklaerung: Very high-energy radiation that can change atoms and damage cells.
The radiation dose that takes into account how harmful the type of radiation is.
Unit for the energy that one kilogram of tissue absorbs from radiation.
An invisible, radioactive gas that comes from the ground.
A measuring device that shows how much radiation someone has received.

gewusst: A chest X-ray usually gives less than 0.1 mSv, much less than the natural radiation of a whole year.
In Switzerland you can have the amount of radon in your own home measured.
On a long-haul flight you receive a little more radiation, because more cosmic radiation arrives at high altitude.

teile.einleitung: In physics a collision is a short, violent impact between two bodies, for example two billiard balls. In a very short time, motion is passed from one body to the other. Collisions happen in sport, in traffic and in the playground, and in Switzerland pushing and throwing heavy stones is even an old custom.
wichtigste: A collision is a short impact in which motion is passed on.
A billiard ball at rest starts rolling when another one knocks into it.
An object that is knocked moves in the direction of the push.
In table football you give the ball a push.
In stone throwing, a Swiss custom, you push a heavy stone as far as possible.
Bike helmets and airbags absorb hard impacts and protect people.
In a collision the total momentum, that is mass times velocity, is conserved.

abschnitte.text: When one body crashes into another, the two press hard against each other for a brief moment. In this way **motion is passed on**: a billiard ball at rest starts rolling when another one hits it. A marble rolls in the direction in which you flick it with your finger. In skittles, the impact of the rolling ball knocks the pins over.

Physicists describe collisions with **momentum**, which is mass times velocity. In a collision the total momentum of all the bodies involved stays the same; this is called the **conservation of momentum**. If a billiard ball hits an equally heavy ball at rest exactly head-on, the first one stops and the second rolls on at the same speed. At the same speed, a heavy lorry has much more momentum than a bicycle.

In an **elastic collision** the bodies bounce apart again, like billiard balls or a bouncy ball. In an **inelastic collision** they change shape and sometimes even stick together, like two balls of modelling clay. Kinetic energy is turned into heat and deformation in the process. A well-known toy on this topic is Newton's cradle, in which a ball is passed along a row of hanging balls.

A hard impact is dangerous because very large forces act in a very short time. Protective equipment makes this time longer and so makes the force smaller. A **bike helmet** protects the head with soft foam that squashes on impact. In a car the **airbag**, seat belt and crumple zone absorb the impact for the people inside. In a dodgem you only feel a jolt, because the rubber edges cushion the bump.

abschnitte.titel: Pushing as a sport and a custom
abschnitte.text: In the **shot put** in athletics you push a metal ball as far as possible; for men it weighs 7.26 kg, for women 4 kg. In Switzerland there is the old custom of **stone throwing**. The most famous stone is the Unspunnen stone, which weighs about 83.5 kg and is thrown at the Unspunnen Festival in Interlaken. Stone throwing is also part of the Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival.

begriffe.erklaerung: A short, violent impact between two bodies.
Mass times velocity, a measure of how much force a moving body carries.
A collision in which the bodies bounce apart again.
Part of a car that changes shape in an accident and absorbs the impact.

gewusst: In Newton's cradle the movement seems to travel magically through the balls at rest.
The Unspunnen stone has already been stolen twice, the first time in 1984.
When it is kicked, a football is properly squashed for a tiny moment before it flies off.

teile.einleitung: Armbands are inflatable swimming aids that small children wear on their upper arms. They help them stay up in the water and get used to the water. But they are not safe protection against drowning.
wichtigste: You wear armbands on your upper arms.
They are usually filled with air.
Before putting them on, you check that they are well inflated.
If an armband has a hole, the air escapes and it no longer holds you up.
A child with armbands must never go into deep water alone; an adult has to keep watch.
A foam float also helps when learning to swim.
The goal is to be able to swim without armbands.

abschnitte.text: Armbands are small plastic air cushions that you slide over your upper arms. Many have two separate **air chambers**, so that not all the air escapes if one chamber has a hole. They are one of the **swimming aids**, like swimming belts or floats. They were invented in 1956 by Bernhard Markwitz in Hamburg.

Air is much lighter than water. The armbands push water aside but weigh almost nothing, which creates extra **buoyancy**. Together with the body's own buoyancy, this keeps the shoulders and head above water. If the air escapes, this buoyancy is suddenly missing.

Armbands can slip off the arm or lose air, so they never replace **supervision**. An adult must always be within reach and must not get distracted. Drowning often happens quietly and quickly, without shouting or waving. With its water safety rules, the Swiss Life Saving Society SLRG reminds people never to let children out of their sight in the water.

Armbands help small children to enjoy the water. Over time, in swimming lessons, they learn to glide, to dive under and to keep themselves above water. A foam **float** is a useful training aid for kicking. In Switzerland there is the **Water Safety Check**, in which children show that they can save themselves after falling into the water.

Before every swim you check that both chambers are firmly filled and the valves are closed. The armbands must fit the child's size and sit tightly on the upper arm. They are not suitable in rivers and lakes with currents or waves. There, a proper life jacket is much safer.

begriffe.erklaerung: Aid that helps you stay up in the water.
Force of the water that pushes a body upwards.
Closed part of an inflatable object that contains air.
An adult keeps watch and can help immediately.

gewusst: Armbands are not life-saving equipment, which is why they clearly state that they do not protect against drowning.
In English they are often also called water wings.
Every year the SLRG trains many lifeguards in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland's electricity mix shows which energy sources the electricity produced and used in Switzerland comes from. The largest part is supplied by hydropower from the Alps, followed by nuclear energy. Solar energy has been growing especially fast in recent years.
wichtigste: In Switzerland hydropower supplies about 60 per cent of the electricity produced in the country (as of 2024).
In 2024 nuclear energy supplied the second largest share of electricity production.
Photovoltaics, that is solar power, has grown most strongly in recent years.
In winter Switzerland typically depends on electricity imports.
In 2025 there were 4 nuclear power units in operation in Switzerland.
The Swiss power grid runs at a frequency of 50 Hz.
Since the Energy Act of 2017, no general licences for new nuclear power stations may be granted.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is a water tower: many rivers rise in the Alps, and the water falls from high mountains into the valleys. That is why about 60 per cent of the electricity produced in the country comes from **hydropower** (as of 2024). A **run-of-river power station** stands on a river and uses the flowing water without a large reservoir. A **storage power station** collects water in a reservoir, for example behind the Grande Dixence dam in Valais, and can then supply electricity when it is needed.

Nuclear energy supplies the second largest share: in 2024 just under a third of Swiss electricity. In 2025 four units were in operation: **Beznau** 1 and 2 in Aargau, Gösgen in the canton of Solothurn and Leibstadt in Aargau. The Mühleberg nuclear power station near Bern was shut down at the end of 2019. Under the **Energy Act**, which the people approved in 2017, no general licences for new nuclear power stations are granted any more.

**Photovoltaics** is the source of electricity that has grown most strongly in recent years; more and more roofs carry solar panels. There is also electricity from biomass, waste incineration plants and a few wind turbines, for example in the Jura. So far, however, wind power plays only a small part in Switzerland. Together with hydropower, most Swiss electricity comes from sources that give off hardly any CO₂.

In summer snow and glaciers melt, the rivers carry a lot of water and the sun shines for a long time. Then Switzerland often produces more electricity than it needs and sells it abroad. In **winter** it is the other way round: more electricity is needed for light and heating, but less is produced. That is why Switzerland typically depends on **imports** in winter, and reservoirs and pumped storage plants such as Nant de Drance in Valais become especially important.

The Swiss power grid is closely linked with the neighbouring countries and, like the European grid, runs at **50 Hz**. At the **Star of Laufenburg** grid hub in Aargau, the power grids of Switzerland, Germany and France were connected for the first time in 1958. This was an important step towards the interconnected European grid. Today the national grid company Swissgrid runs the Swiss extra-high-voltage grid.

The **production mix** shows how electricity is produced in Switzerland. The **supply mix** on the electricity bill, on the other hand, shows which sources the electricity that a supplier sells to its customers comes from. These can be very different, because suppliers also buy electricity or trade certificates of origin. Today many households can choose whether they want to get, for example, pure hydro or solar electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: The make-up of electricity from different energy sources.
A power station on a river that uses the flowing water.
A power station with a reservoir that keeps water for later.
Technology that uses solar cells to make electricity from sunlight.
Information on the electricity bill about where the supplied electricity comes from.

gewusst: The Grande Dixence dam in Valais is 285 metres high and is one of the highest in the world.
A pumped storage plant pumps water up when there is too much electricity and lets it flow back down when electricity is short.
The cantons of Valais and the Grisons together produce almost half of Switzerland's hydroelectric power.

teile.einleitung: A soap bubble is a wafer-thin skin of soapy water that traps air. In the air it takes the shape of a ball and shimmers in all the colours of the rainbow. Soap bubbles can teach you a lot about surface tension and light.
wichtigste: In the air a soap bubble is shaped like a ball.
It shines in many colours, because light is reflected by the thin skin.
It bursts after a short time, because its skin becomes too thin.
Pure water does not make good soap bubbles; only the soap makes the skin stretchy.
Glycerine in the soapy water makes soap bubbles last longer.
If a soap bubble touches a dry hand, it usually bursts.
With two sticks and a loop of string you can make giant soap bubbles.

abschnitte.text: A soap bubble consists of a thin layer of water that is covered on the outside and inside by a layer of **soap particles**. The skin is usually only a few thousandths of a millimetre thick, much thinner than a hair. The air inside is slightly compressed. The soap lowers the **surface tension** and makes the skin stretchy and stable.

The skin of the bubble pulls together as tightly as it can. A **sphere** is the shape that has the smallest surface for the same contents. That is why freely floating soap bubbles always become round. When several bubbles meet, they form shared walls that meet at certain angles.

Light is reflected on the outside and on the inside of the thin skin. The two reflected light waves overlap; this is called **interference**. Depending on the thickness of the skin, some colours are strengthened and others cancelled out. Because the skin is slightly different in thickness everywhere and is constantly moving, the colours wander across the bubble.

Gravity slowly pulls the water in the skin downwards, and at the same time water **evaporates**. As a result the skin becomes thinner and thinner in some places until it tears. Shortly before bursting, the top of the bubble often becomes colourless or dark. Glycerine slows down evaporation, whereas a dry hand or a speck of dust makes the bubble burst immediately.

For giant bubbles you need two sticks and a **loop of string**, which you dip into a large bowl of soap solution. If you pull the sticks apart and walk slowly backwards, a long, floating bubble forms. Good soapy water contains water, washing-up liquid and a little glycerine. It works best when the air is damp and there is little wind, because outdoors a soap bubble drifts away with the wind.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force that makes the surface of a liquid behave like a stretched skin.
Overlapping of light waves, which can strengthen or cancel out colours.
Thick, sweetish liquid that makes soap bubbles last longer.
Slow change of water into water vapour without boiling.

gewusst: In great cold, soap bubbles can freeze and then look like glass balls with frost patterns.
You can touch a soap bubble with a wet hand without it bursting.
With a drinking straw you can blow a small bubble into a large one.

teile.einleitung: The drag coefficient, known in German as the cw value, is a number that shows how streamlined a body is. The smaller the value, the more easily a car, a cyclist or an aeroplane glides through the air. It is important for saving fuel and effort.
wichtigste: The drag coefficient describes how strongly the shape of a body affects air resistance.
Air resistance is calculated with F = ½ · ρ · v² · cw · A.
For a car, the frontal area is used as the reference area.
The product of the drag coefficient and the frontal area is called the drag area.
At double the speed, the air resistance becomes four times and the power needed eight times as great.
A streamlined body shaped like a drop has an especially small drag coefficient.
With blunt bodies such as lorries, pressure drag is the main part.

abschnitte.text: When a body moves through air or water, **drag** slows it down. How great this is depends on the speed, the size and the shape of the body. The **drag coefficient** describes only the influence of the shape and has no unit. In German it is called the cw value; the w stands for Widerstand, meaning resistance. It is usually measured in a **wind tunnel**.

Air resistance is F = ½ · ρ · v² · cw · A. Here ρ is the density of the air, about 1.2 kg per cubic metre, v is the speed and A is the **frontal area**. A car with cw = 0.3 and a frontal area of 2.2 m² feels about 356 newtons of air resistance at 30 m/s, that is 108 km/h. The product of cw times A is called the **drag area**.

Because the speed is squared in the formula, air resistance grows very quickly. If a car speeds up from 72 km/h to 108 km/h, that is to 1.5 times the speed, the resistance rises by a factor of 2.25. At double the speed it becomes four times as great. The **power** needed even grows with the third power and becomes eight times greater, which is why fast driving uses much more energy.

A **streamlined body** shaped like a drop has a very small drag coefficient, because the air flows gently around it. Modern cars have values of about 0.25 to 0.35, especially streamlined electric cars even less. A flat plate across the wind has a value of about 1.1 to 1.2. Behind blunt bodies such as lorries, suction with eddies forms, which is why **pressure drag** is the main part there.

Racing cyclists crouch low over the handlebars to make their frontal area smaller. In the **slipstream** of another rider the oncoming air is slower, so they save a lot of effort. Ski racers go into a crouch, which is also called the egg position. Bobsleigh teams, for example from Switzerland, also test their sleds and suits in the wind tunnel.

Many fast animals have a streamlined shape, such as dolphins, penguins, trout and falcons. Engineers learn from such shapes when they design cars, trains or aeroplanes. That is why high-speed trains have long, pointed noses. Lowering the drag coefficient saves fuel, electricity and therefore money.

begriffe.erklaerung: Number without a unit that shows how streamlined a shape is.
The area you see from the front, like a silhouette.
Facility in which air is blown against a model to measure the resistance.
Area behind a body where there is less wind.

gewusst: A parachute has a very large air resistance on purpose, so that you land slowly.
At motorway speed a car uses most of its driving power just against air resistance.
An open car window or a roof box noticeably increases air resistance.

teile.einleitung: A storage power station is a hydroelectric power station that collects water in a reservoir and only produces electricity when it is needed. In Switzerland, with its high mountains, such power stations play a very large part. A special kind is the pumped storage power station, which works like a giant battery.
wichtigste: A storage power station supplies electricity on demand.
The water is collected in a reservoir in the mountains.
It flows down through penstocks to the turbines.
The reservoirs of the Alps fill up mainly in summer with meltwater.
A pumped storage power station needs at least two water basins.
A pumped storage power station uses more electricity than it supplies and is therefore a store.
The Nant de Drance pumped storage power station is in the canton of Valais.
Enough residual water must remain in the stream below a water intake.

abschnitte.text: A storage power station holds back water behind a **dam** in a **reservoir**. When needed, the gates are opened and the water rushes down to the valley through steep **penstocks**. At the bottom it drives turbines and generators. The big advantage: electricity can be produced exactly when many people need it, for example on winter evenings.

A **pumped storage power station** has an upper and a lower basin. When there is too much electricity in the grid, it pumps water upwards. When electricity is scarce, the water is let flow down again and electricity is produced. About a fifth of the energy is lost in the process, so it is not a real producer, but an **energy store**.

At 285 metres, the **Grande Dixence** dam in Valais is the highest gravity dam in the world. The **Nant de Drance** pumped storage power station in Valais lies deep inside the mountain between two reservoirs and went into full operation in 2022. In the canton of Glarus the large Linth-Limmern pumped storage plant is at work. Altogether, hydropower supplies more than half of Switzerland's electricity.

In summer snow and glaciers melt and the reservoirs fill up. In autumn they are usually at their fullest. In winter, when rivers carry little water and a lot of electricity is needed, the stored water is released. In this way storage power stations carry **summer energy** into the winter.

If water is taken from a stream for a power station, the stream below can almost dry out. That is why Swiss law requires a minimum amount of **residual water**. It makes sure that fish, insects and plants in the stream survive. The sudden rise and fall of rivers when a power station is running, called **hydropeaking**, is also meant to be reduced today.

begriffe.erklaerung: An artificial lake behind a dam in which water is collected.
A thick, steep pipe that carries water from the reservoir to the turbines.
A wheel with blades that is turned by the water and drives a generator.
The water that must remain in the stream below a water intake.

gewusst: The Grande Dixence dam is almost as high as the Eiffel Tower in Paris.
The machines of Nant de Drance stand in a cavern deep in the rock that is almost as long as two football pitches.
Pumped storage power stations can switch from pumping to producing electricity within a few minutes.

teile.einleitung: An electric circuit is a closed path along which electric current can flow from a voltage source through an appliance and back again. Only when the circuit is closed does a lamp shine or a motor run. Circuits are found in every device, from a torch to a computer.
wichtigste: A circuit needs a voltage source, wires and an appliance.
Current only flows when the circuit is closed.
A switch opens or closes the circuit.
In a series circuit all the lamps go out if one burns out.
In homes lamps are connected in parallel so that each one works on its own.
Ohm's law is U = R · I.
A short circuit is a direct connection between the poles without an appliance.

abschnitte.text: A simple **circuit** needs at least a voltage source such as a battery, wires and an appliance such as a lamp. The wires connect the positive terminal through the lamp to the negative terminal. Only when the circuit is **closed** without any gap does current flow and the lamp shine. If it is broken anywhere, the lamp stays dark.

Metals such as copper conduct electricity well; they are called **conductors**. Plastic, glass or dry wood hardly conduct it at all; they are called **insulators**. With a circuit with a small bulb you can test whether an object conducts electricity. If the bulb lights up when you hold the object in the gap, it is a conductor.

In a **series circuit** the lamps are one after the other in a single loop. If one burns out, the circuit is broken and all the lamps go out, as with some old fairy lights. In a **parallel circuit** each lamp has its own branch. This is how the lamps in a flat are wired, so that each one can be switched on and off on its own.

**Voltage** U is measured in volts, **current** I in amperes and resistance R in ohms. Ohm's law links the three quantities: U = R · I. If a current of 0.05 amperes flows through a resistance of 100 ohms, the voltage is 5 volts. The law is named after the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm, who discovered it in 1826.

If the two poles are connected directly without an appliance, a **short circuit** occurs. Then a very large current flows, the wires get hot and a fire can start. In this case a fuse breaks the circuit. You can experiment safely with batteries, but the 230-volt socket is life-threatening.

begriffe.erklaerung: A battery or power supply that drives the current.
A device that uses electrical energy, for example a lamp.
A substance through which current can flow well.
How strongly a component slows down the flow of current, measured in ohms.

gewusst: Your body also contains circuits, because nerves carry signals with tiny electric currents.
Sockets in Switzerland have their own shape, Type J, which often does not fit abroad.
The electrical signal spreads through a cable very fast, even though the electrons themselves move only very slowly.

teile.einleitung: The swim bladder is a gas-filled organ in the body of many fish. It works like a built-in life jacket that lets a fish hover at a certain depth in the water without effort. In doing so, the fish uses the physical principle of buoyancy.
wichtigste: The swim bladder is a gas-filled organ in the belly of many bony fish.
With it a fish can hover at a certain depth without using energy.
In evolutionary history the swim bladder is related to the lungs of land vertebrates.
Carp and other fish with a connection to the gut fill it by gulping air at the surface.
Sharks have no swim bladder and stop themselves from sinking with a large, oil-rich liver.
Carp-like fish also use the swim bladder to hear better.
If a fish is pulled up very quickly from great depth, the swim bladder expands a lot.

abschnitte.text: The **swim bladder** is a thin-walled sac in a fish's belly that is filled with gas. It usually lies above the gut and below the backbone. Many **bony fish** have one, such as carp, trout, pike or the European perch, which in Switzerland is called Egli. In the evolution of animals the swim bladder is related to the **lungs** of land vertebrates. Both developed from a pouch of the front part of the gut.

Fish flesh and bones are a little heavier than water, so a fish without any help would slowly sink. The gas in the swim bladder makes the fish lighter overall, until it is exactly as heavy as the water it pushes aside. Then weight and **buoyancy** balance each other, and the fish hovers without effort. More gas makes it rise, less gas makes it sink. In this way the fish saves a lot of energy, because it does not have to work its fins all the time.

In some fish, for example **carp** and trout, the swim bladder is connected to the gut by a duct. They gulp air at the surface and use it to fill their bladder. In other fish, such as the perch, the bladder is closed. These fish release gas from the blood into the bladder through a **gas gland** and take it back into the blood at another place. This is slower, so they can only change their depth gradually.

In the deep, water pressure is greater than at the surface. If a fish is pulled up very quickly from great depth, the pressure suddenly drops, and the gas in the swim bladder **expands** strongly. The bladder can then squeeze organs or even be pushed out of the mouth. It is the same principle as a balloon that gets bigger higher up. Anglers in deep lakes and at sea know this problem well.

**Sharks** and rays have no swim bladder. Instead, sharks have a very large, oil-rich liver, because oil is lighter than water. They also create lift with their pectoral fins as they swim, similar to the wings of an aeroplane. Adult **flatfish** such as the plaice have no swim bladder either, because they live on the seabed and do not need to hover at all. Many deep-sea fish also manage without one.

In **carp-like fish** the swim bladder is connected to the inner ear by a chain of tiny bones. This connection is called the **Weberian apparatus**. Sound waves make the gas-filled bladder vibrate, and the tiny bones pass the vibrations on to the ear. So carp and their relatives hear much better than many other fish. Some fish can even make sounds with muscles on the swim bladder, such as growling or drumming noises.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas-filled organ that lets fish hover in the water.
The force with which water pushes a body upwards.
Fish with a skeleton made of bone, unlike sharks with a skeleton of cartilage.
An organ that releases gas from the blood into the swim bladder.
Tiny bones that connect the swim bladder to the ear in carp-like fish.

gewusst: In the past, the swim bladders of certain fish were used to make a glue and a clearing agent for wine and beer called isinglass.
The idea of the swim bladder is similar to the diving tanks of a submarine, which are filled with water or air.
Lungfish have a real lung instead of a swim bladder and can breathe air with it.

teile.einleitung: The law of inertia is the first of Newton's three laws of motion. It says: a body stays at rest or keeps moving steadily in a straight line as long as no force acts on it. So every body is “inert” and wants to keep its state of motion.
wichtigste: The law of inertia is Newton's first law.
Without a resultant force, a body stays at rest or keeps moving steadily in a straight line.
Steady motion means the same speed in the same direction.
Isaac Newton published his laws of motion in 1687 in the work “Principia”.
A ball on the lawn rolls to a stop because friction and air resistance slow it down.
An ice hockey puck slides a long way because there is only little friction on the ice.
A space probe keeps flying in space without an engine, because there is almost no friction to slow it down.
If a body moves in a circle, a force must be acting on it.

abschnitte.text: A body on which no **resultant force** acts does not change its state of motion. If it is lying still, it stays where it is. If it is moving, it keeps flying with **steady motion**, that is, at the same speed in the same direction. This property is called **inertia**. The greater the mass of a body, the more inert it is and the more force it takes to move it or stop it.

abschnitte.titel: Why does the ball roll to a stop?
abschnitte.text: In everyday life it seems as if every movement stops by itself. But a ball on the lawn only rolls to a stop because **friction** and air resistance slow it down. On smooth ice the friction is very small, which is why an ice hockey puck slides a long way after a shot. In space there is almost no friction to slow things down, so a space probe keeps flying for years without an engine. In this way the probe Voyager 1, which was launched in 1977, is still moving further and further away from the Sun today.

For a long time people believed, like the Greek philosopher Aristotle, that a body only stays in motion if it is constantly pushed. In the 17th century the Italian scientist **Galileo Galilei** realised through experiments with rolling balls that this is not true. The Englishman **Isaac Newton** summed up this discovery as the first of his three laws of motion. He published them in 1687 in his famous work “Principia”.

A change of direction is also a change of motion. So if a body moves in a circle at constant speed, a force must be acting on it towards the centre all the time. On a chair swing ride, the chains keep the seats on their circular path. If a string on which you are swinging a ball round in a circle breaks, the ball flies off in a straight line, in the direction it was moving at the moment the string broke.

If a bus brakes suddenly, your body wants to keep moving forwards, and you tip forwards. That is why **seat belts** in the car are so important: they hold the body back in an accident. In the well-known tablecloth trick, you pull a tablecloth away in a flash, and the heavy crockery stays almost where it is thanks to its inertia. When you shake ketchup out of a bottle, you are also using inertia.

begriffe.erklaerung: The property of a body to keep its state of motion.
The force that is left when you add up all the forces.
Force that slows down movements between two surfaces.
How much matter a body has, measured in kilograms.

gewusst: The space probe Voyager 1 has been flying through space without propulsion for almost 50 years.
Newton's “Principia” is regarded as one of the most important books in the history of science.
A seat belt protects you by working against the inertia of your body.

teile.einleitung: A boiling water reactor is a type of nuclear reactor in which the water is brought to the boil directly in the reactor core. The steam produced drives a turbine that generates electricity. This type of reactor was also used in the Swiss nuclear power station at Mühleberg and in the reactors of the Fukushima disaster.
wichtigste: In a boiling water reactor the water evaporates directly in the reactor core.
The operating pressure is about 70 bar, that is about seventy times the air pressure.
There is only a single water and steam circuit between the reactor and the turbine.
The control rods are moved into the core from below.
If more steam bubbles form in the core, the reactivity drops, which slows the reactor down by itself.
The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern worked with a boiling water reactor.
The units of Fukushima Daiichi in Japan that were damaged in 2011 were also boiling water reactors.

abschnitte.text: A boiling water reactor is a **nuclear reactor** that gets heat from splitting uranium. This heat brings water to the boil, as in a giant saucepan. The steam flows to a **turbine** and turns it, and the turbine drives a generator. Boiling water reactors were developed from the 1950s onwards, mainly in the USA.

In a boiling water reactor the steam flows directly from the reactor to the turbine. After that it is turned back into water in the **condenser** with cooling water from a river or a cooling tower. This water is pumped back into the reactor. A pressurised water reactor, on the other hand, has two separate circuits, so that the water from the core never reaches the turbine.

In the reactor pressure vessel there is a pressure of about **70 bar**. At this pressure water does not boil until about 286 degrees Celsius. Above the core are steam separators and steam dryers, which remove drops of water from the steam. Because so much equipment is fitted at the top, the **control rods** are moved into the core from below.

The water in the core slows the neutrons down so that the chain reaction keeps going. If more steam bubbles form, there is less water and the **reactivity** drops. In this way the reactor partly throttles itself when there is too much heat. Because the steam passes through the core, it contains the short-lived nuclide **nitrogen-16**, which is why the turbine is shielded during operation. After shutdown, nitrogen-16 decays within seconds.

From 1972 the **Mühleberg** nuclear power station on the River Aare near Bern supplied electricity with a boiling water reactor. At the end of 2019 it was shut down for good and has been dismantled since then. The **Leibstadt** nuclear power station in the canton of Aargau also has a boiling water reactor. The Beznau and Gösgen power stations, on the other hand, work with pressurised water reactors.

In March 2011 a severe earthquake with a **tsunami** hit the Japanese coast. At the Fukushima Daiichi power station the power supply for the cooling failed. In several boiling water reactors the fuel elements overheated and partly melted. Afterwards Switzerland decided not to build any new nuclear power stations.

begriffe.erklaerung: The innermost part of the reactor with the fuel elements, where nuclear fission takes place.
A rod that swallows neutrons and so slows down or stops the chain reaction.
A measure of whether the chain reaction is getting stronger, staying the same or getting weaker.
A part in which steam is cooled down and turns back into water.

gewusst: The nitrogen-16 in the steam has a half-life of only about seven seconds.
In a boiling water reactor the water is used at the same time for cooling, for slowing down the neutrons and as driving steam.
Dismantling the Mühleberg nuclear power station is expected to take many years before the site can be used freely again.

teile.einleitung: A life jacket is a vest that keeps a person at the surface in the water. You wear one when boating, canoeing or sailing. It can save lives if someone unexpectedly falls into the water.
wichtigste: A life jacket makes sure that you stay up in the water.
Many life jackets are filled with light foam.
They are often bright orange or yellow so that you can be seen easily.
You put it on before you get into the boat.
A life jacket must be properly fastened and fit well.
A collar behind the head keeps the head above water.
On boat trips with children an adult is also needed to supervise.

abschnitte.text: Life jackets usually contain foam with many small, closed air bubbles. This foam is very light and creates a lot of **buoyancy** in the water. In the past cork was used for this. There are also **automatic jackets**, which inflate themselves with gas from a small cartridge when they come into contact with water.

How strongly a jacket holds you up is given in newtons. Light **buoyancy aids** of about 50 N are meant for good swimmers close to the shore, for example when canoeing. **Life jackets** with 100 N or more even turn an unconscious person onto their back. That way the mouth and nose stay above water, even if the person can no longer move.

When canoeing, sailing, stand-up paddleboarding and river rafting, a jacket is part of the equipment. Children should always wear a jacket on boats, even if they can swim well. You put it on while still on the shore, because after falling into the water it is too late. In Switzerland the rules for navigation say that on many boats there must be a suitable **life jacket** for every person.

A jacket must suit your body weight, which is written on the label. All buckles and zips are closed and the straps pulled tight. If someone pulls on the shoulders, the jacket must not slip over your head. Jackets for children often have a **crotch strap** and a collar that supports the head.

The colours orange, yellow and red stand out clearly against blue or green water. Many jackets also have **reflective strips**, which shine in the light of a torch. Often a whistle is attached too, which you can use to draw attention to yourself. This helps rescuers find a person in the water more quickly.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force that pushes a body upwards in the water.
Jacket with a lot of buoyancy that even turns unconscious people onto their back.
Light vest for good swimmers close to the shore.
Strip that strongly reflects light and is therefore easy to see.

gewusst: Cold water in Swiss lakes can quickly exhaust even good swimmers, which is why a life jacket is so important.
When dry, automatic jackets are as flat as a collar.
On large passenger ships there are life jackets ready for everyone on board.

teile.einleitung: A dam is a huge concrete structure that blocks a river and holds back the water to form a reservoir. In Switzerland many dams stand high up in the Alps. They store water from which electricity is produced in hydroelectric power stations.
wichtigste: A dam holds back the water of a reservoir.
Large dams today are usually built of concrete.
A bank of earth and stones that holds back water is called an embankment dam.
An arch dam is curved when seen from above and passes the water pressure into the rocks.
Water pressure increases with depth, which is why dams are thickest at the bottom.
Most of the large dams in Switzerland are in the Alps.
People bungee jump from the Verzasca Dam in Ticino.

abschnitte.text: A dam blocks off a valley and holds back the water of a river to form a **reservoir**. It is usually made of **concrete**; older walls are also made of masonry. If the barrier is a bank of earth, gravel and stones instead, it is called an **embankment dam**. Inside the wall there are inspection galleries, measuring instruments and outlets through which water can be released.

The deeper the water, the greater its **pressure**: for every ten metres of depth it rises by about the weight of one kilogram on every square centimetre. That is why a dam is much thicker at the bottom than at the top. A **gravity dam** holds back the water simply through its enormous weight. An **arch dam** is curved when seen from above and passes the pressure sideways into the rock walls, like the arch of a bridge. It therefore needs much less concrete.

The water in the reservoir is led down through tunnels and penstocks to a power station. There it drives **turbines**, which produce electricity through generators. Because the water can be stored, electricity can be produced exactly when a lot is needed. In Switzerland more than half of the electricity comes from hydropower.

At 285 metres, the **Grande Dixence** in Valais is the highest gravity dam in the world; it was completed in 1961. The Mauvoisin arch dam is also in Valais. The **Verzasca Dam** in Ticino holds back the Lago di Vogorno and is about 220 metres high. It became famous through a bungee jump in a James Bond film, and today many brave people jump into the depths on a rope there.

Reservoirs do not only supply electricity; they can also hold back **floods** and store water for irrigation. At the same time they change landscapes and habitats: valleys are flooded, and fish can no longer move about freely. Below the wall the river often carries much less water. That is why Swiss law requires a minimum amount of water that must remain in the river.

Dams are constantly monitored, in Switzerland under the supervision of the federal government. Measuring instruments check whether the wall is moving or whether water is seeping through. In an arch dam the crest leans by a few centimetres depending on the water level, which is perfectly normal. For emergencies there are plans and alarm systems for the villages in the valley.

begriffe.erklaerung: An artificial lake that forms behind a dam.
A curved dam that passes the water pressure into the rock walls.
A very heavy wall that holds back the water through its weight.
A wheel with blades that is turned by flowing water.
Energy from flowing or falling water.

gewusst: With the concrete of the Grande Dixence you could build a low, narrow wall once round the whole Earth.
For many reservoirs whole villages used to be moved, for example when the Sihlsee was built.
Reservoirs in the Alps often receive meltwater from glaciers, which is why they are turquoise.

teile.einleitung: The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid begins to boil and turns into vapour. At sea level water boils at 100 °C, but on high mountains it boils sooner. Every substance has its own boiling point, and it depends on the air pressure.
wichtigste: At the boiling point, large vapour bubbles form inside the liquid.
At standard pressure water boils at 100 °C, on Mount Everest at only about 70 °C.
If you turn the hotplate up, the temperature of boiling water stays the same.
If you dissolve a lot of salt in water, the boiling point rises slightly.
Ethanol boils at about 78 °C, mercury at about 357 °C.
Liquid nitrogen boils at about minus 196 °C.
Helium has the lowest boiling point of all the elements.

abschnitte.text: When you heat water, its particles move faster and faster. At the **boiling point** they have enough energy to form vapour bubbles even inside the liquid. These rise and burst at the surface. Unlike **evaporation**, which happens at the surface even at low temperatures, during boiling the liquid turns into vapour everywhere.

As long as water is boiling, its temperature does not rise any further. The extra heat from the hotplate is needed to turn the water into vapour; it is called the **heat of vaporisation**. If you turn the hotplate up, the water only boils more fiercely and evaporates faster. That is why you can save energy by turning the hotplate down once the water has come to the boil.

The boiling point depends on the **air pressure**. The lower the air pressure, the more easily vapour bubbles can form, and the lower the boiling point. On the Jungfraujoch, at about 3500 m, water boils just below 90 °C, and on Mount Everest at about 70 °C. In a **pressure cooker**, on the other hand, the pressure is higher, the water gets hotter than 100 °C and the food cooks faster.

Every pure substance has its own boiling point, by which it can be recognised. Ethanol, the alcohol, boils at only about 78 °C, mercury not until about 357 °C. Liquid nitrogen boils at about minus 196 °C and therefore boils at once at room temperature. At about minus 269 °C, helium has the lowest boiling point of all the elements.

If you dissolve salt in water, the boiling point rises slightly; this is called **boiling point elevation**. With a teaspoon of salt in the pasta water, however, the difference can hardly be measured. Different boiling points are used in **distillation** to separate mixtures of substances. For example, crude oil is split into petrol, diesel and other parts in this way.

begriffe.erklaerung: Temperature at which a liquid boils and turns into vapour.
Energy needed to turn a liquid into vapour.
Pan with a tight lid in which water gets hotter than 100 °C under higher pressure.
Separating liquids by evaporating them and cooling them down again.

gewusst: On Mount Everest, cooking pasta takes much longer because the water does not get as hot.
The Celsius scale was originally set so that water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.
In space, water would boil even at room temperature because there is no pressure.

teile.einleitung: Sinking means that an object goes down in a liquid until it lies on the bottom. Whether something sinks or floats does not only depend on its weight, but on its material and its shape. With a few simple experiments in the bath you can find this out yourself.
wichtigste: An object sinks if it is heavier than the water it pushes aside.
A metal spoon sinks in water.
A potato usually sinks, an apple floats.
A ball of modelling clay sinks; shaped into a flat little boat, the same clay floats.
A glass sinks when it fills up completely with water.
A ship sinks when a lot of water runs in through a hole.
Things that have sunk end up on the bottom of the lake or the seabed.

abschnitte.text: Every object in water pushes water aside; we say it **displaces** it. The water then pushes upwards from below with a force called **buoyancy**. If the object is heavier than the water pushed aside, gravity wins and it sinks. If it is lighter, it floats on top.

What is important is **density**, that is, how much a piece of material weighs compared with its size. Metal, stone and glass have a greater density than water and therefore sink. Wood, cork and most plastics have a lower density and float. A potato is a little denser than water and sinks; an apple contains a lot of air and floats.

A ball of modelling clay goes under at once. If you shape the same clay into a flat **little boat** with a high edge, it floats. This is because the little boat pushes aside much more water, as there is air inside it. Huge steel ships float in exactly the same way.

If water runs into a ship through a hole, the air inside is pushed out and the ship becomes heavier. At some point it is heavier than the water it pushes aside, and it sinks. A famous example is the **Titanic**, which went down in 1912 after colliding with an iceberg. That is why large ships have walls in the hull that limit the water coming in to individual compartments.

Sometimes something is meant to sink: a heavy metal **anchor** falls to the bottom and holds the ship in place. A submarine fills tanks with water to dive and blows the water out again with compressed air to surface. Divers wear lead weights so that they do not drift at the surface. On the **lake bed** of Swiss lakes there are even old shipwrecks and remains of pile dwellings.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the water pushes an object upwards.
How heavy a substance is in relation to its size.
To push water aside because an object needs the space.
The bottom of a lake, where things that have sunk stay lying.

gewusst: An egg sinks in tap water, but floats in very salty water.
The Greek scholar Archimedes discovered the law of buoyancy more than 2000 years ago.
In the Dead Sea the water is so salty that people can hardly sink in it.

teile.einleitung: The Dead Sea is a huge salt lake in the Middle East. Its water is so salty that you can lie in it as if on an airbed. For physics it is a perfect example of buoyancy.
wichtigste: The Dead Sea is a salt lake between Israel, the West Bank and Jordan.
Its water contains about 30 per cent salt, almost ten times more than ordinary sea water.
The shore lies more than 400 metres below sea level, making it the lowest point on land on Earth.
The most important river flowing into it is the Jordan.
The lake has no outflow; the water evaporates in the heat and the salt stays behind.
The water has a density of about 1.24 grams per cubic centimetre.
Because the water is so dense, a person does not sink in it.

abschnitte.text: The Dead Sea lies in the **Jordan Rift Valley**, a long rift in the Earth's crust. On the west shore are Israel and the West Bank, on the east shore **Jordan**. The shore is more than 400 metres below sea level. All around there is desert, steep cliffs and hardly any rain.

The **Jordan** and a few streams bring water with dissolved salts into the lake. But there is no **outflow**. In the great heat the water evaporates, while the salt stays behind. In this way the salt content has risen over thousands of years to about 30 per cent.

Salt water is heavier than fresh water; we say it has a greater **density**. One litre of water from the Dead Sea weighs about 1.24 kilograms instead of 1 kilogram. The denser a liquid is, the more strongly it pushes a body upwards; this is called **buoyancy**. A body with a volume of 60 litres that is completely under water there experiences a buoyancy of 744 newtons. That is why bathers float at the surface almost by themselves.

Fish and plants cannot live in the Dead Sea, which is where its name comes from. Only some tiny **microorganisms**, such as special bacteria and archaea, can bear the high salt content. Where fresh water flows in, on the other hand, there are green oases on the shore such as En Gedi.
