On the shore stands the ancient rock fortress of **Masada**, which is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. From 1947, ancient scrolls were found in caves near Qumran; they are famous as the Dead Sea Scrolls. Since ancient times people have been getting salt and other minerals here.

The water level has been falling for decades, by about one metre a year. One reason is that a lot of water from the Jordan is taken off for fields and drinking water. In addition, mineral factories let water evaporate. As a result, dangerous **sinkholes**, sudden holes in the ground, are forming on the shore.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which a liquid pushes a body upwards.
How much mass there is in a certain volume.
A lake without an outflow in which a lot of salt has built up.
When water slowly turns into invisible water vapour.

gewusst: In the Dead Sea you can lie on your back and read a newspaper without paddling.
If you get water from the Dead Sea in your eyes, it stings badly.
On the shore, salt crystals grow out of the water like small white sculptures.

teile.einleitung: The second is the basic unit of time. It is roughly as long as it takes to say “twenty-one” slowly. Today it is measured with atomic clocks more precisely than any other physical quantity.
wichtigste: The second is the basic unit of time in the International System of Units.
Its symbol is a small s.
60 seconds make a minute, 3600 seconds an hour.
A day has 86,400 seconds.
Saying “twenty-one” slowly takes about one second.
In sport, times are measured with a stopwatch or electronically to the hundredth of a second.
Today the second is defined with atomic clocks.

abschnitte.text: The **second** is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units, SI for short. A second is shorter than a minute, because a minute consists of 60 seconds. The name comes from Latin and means the second division: the hour was first divided into minutes and then a second time into seconds. If you count slowly from 1 to 10, about 10 seconds pass. A heartbeat at rest lasts about one second.

abschnitte.titel: From the Sun to the atomic clock
abschnitte.text: In the past the second was taken from the day: it was the 86,400th part of an average solar day. But the Earth does not turn completely evenly; it is even slowing down very slightly. So in 1967 it was decided that the second would be defined with the help of **caesium** atoms. One second is the time in which a certain radiation of these atoms oscillates exactly 9,192,631,770 times. **Atomic clocks** measure this so precisely that in millions of years they are hardly a second wrong.

In sport, fractions of a second are often decisive. In the past timekeepers pressed a **stopwatch** by hand; today light barriers start and stop the time automatically. The 100 metres world record is held by Usain Bolt from Jamaica: in 2009 in Berlin he ran it in 9.58 seconds. In ski races in Switzerland the best skiers are often only a few hundredths of a second apart. For decades Swiss companies have been in charge of **timekeeping** at Olympic Games and world championships.

Switzerland is famous for its **watch industry**, especially in the Jura and in Geneva. Mechanical watches count seconds with a swinging balance wheel, quartz watches with a tiny vibrating quartz crystal. Official Swiss time is set with atomic clocks by the Federal Institute of Metrology METAS in Bern-Wabern. The station clocks of the SBB are famous for their red second hand with the round disc at the end. It goes round a little faster and then waits briefly at the top until the signal for the new minute comes.

For very short times, parts of a second are used. A **millisecond** is a thousandth, a microsecond a millionth of a second. A computer carries out billions of calculation steps in one second. In one second light travels almost 300,000 kilometres. Light takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to get from the Sun to the Earth.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed quantity used for measuring, for example the metre or the second.
An extremely precise clock that counts the oscillations of atoms.
A watch that you can start and stop to measure a length of time.
The thousandth part of a second.

gewusst: Sometimes a leap second is added on New Year's Eve or at the end of June so that clocks match the Earth's rotation.
The red second hand of the SBB station clock waits briefly at the top at twelve every minute.
A hummingbird beats its wings dozens of times in one second.

teile.einleitung: Seismic waves are waves of vibration that spread through the Earth and over its surface during an earthquake. They make the ground shake and can damage buildings. At the same time they are an important tool for researchers to look inside the Earth.
wichtigste: Seismic waves are mainly caused by earthquakes, but also by explosions or volcanic eruptions.
P waves are the fastest and are the first to arrive at a measuring station.
S waves are transverse waves and cannot travel through liquids.
Surface waves usually cause the greatest damage to buildings.
Earthquake waves are recorded with a seismometer.
From the time difference between the P wave and the S wave you can calculate how far away an earthquake is.
In Switzerland the Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich monitors earthquakes.

abschnitte.text: In an **earthquake**, masses of rock deep underground suddenly shift against each other. This releases enormous energy, which spreads out as waves in all directions. These **seismic waves** travel through the inside of the Earth and along its surface. The place inside the Earth where the earthquake starts is called the hypocentre, and the point above it on the surface is the **epicentre**. Blasting, volcanic eruptions or collapsing cavities can also set off seismic waves.

The fastest waves are the **P waves**; the P stands for primary. They are longitudinal waves: the rock is squeezed and stretched in the direction of travel, similar to sound. In the Earth's crust they reach about 6 km/s. Then come the **S waves**; the S stands for secondary. They are transverse waves: the rock vibrates at right angles to the direction of travel, and in the crust they travel at about 3.5 km/s.

When the waves reach the Earth's surface, **surface waves** form, which spread along the surface. The most important are called Love waves and Rayleigh waves, named after two British scientists. Love waves shake the ground sideways; Rayleigh waves make it roll like waves on a lake. They are slower than P and S waves, but often have the biggest movements. That is why they usually cause the greatest damage to buildings.

Earthquake waves are recorded with a **seismometer**; the recording is called a seismogram. Because P waves are faster than S waves, they arrive earlier, and the gap grows with the distance. If a station measures 10 s between the P and S wave, then with 6 km/s and 3.5 km/s the earthquake is about 84 km away. From the measurements of at least three stations, the location of the earthquake can be found exactly. In Switzerland the **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich runs a dense network of measuring stations.

Nobody can drill down to the Earth's core, but seismic waves reveal how the Earth is built inside. In 1909 the Croatian scientist **Andrija Mohorovičić** discovered the boundary between the Earth's crust and mantle, which today is called the Moho after him. On the side of the Earth opposite the earthquake there is a **shadow zone** where no S waves arrive. From this it was concluded that the outer core is liquid, because S waves do not travel through liquids. In 1936 the Danish scientist Inge Lehmann realised that the inner core is solid.

In Switzerland, too, the earth shakes regularly, but mostly so weakly that you cannot feel it. The strongest earthquake in Switzerland on historical record is the **Basel earthquake** of 1356. It destroyed large parts of the city, and a fire afterwards caused further damage. Today the areas most at risk of earthquakes are Valais, the Basel region, the Grisons and Central Switzerland. That is why there are building regulations so that buildings can withstand shaking.

begriffe.erklaerung: An instrument that records shaking of the ground.
The point on the Earth's surface directly above the origin of an earthquake.
The fastest earthquake wave, a longitudinal wave.
A slower earthquake wave in which the rock vibrates sideways.
The boundary between the Earth's crust and mantle.

gewusst: Seismometers are so sensitive that they also register lorries, trains or football fans cheering after a goal.
The waves of a strong earthquake travel right through the Earth and are measured on the other side of the world.
Hundreds of earthquakes are recorded in Switzerland every year, but only a few of them can be felt.

teile.einleitung: The special theory of relativity is a physical theory that Albert Einstein published in Bern in 1905. It says that the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers and that time and space are therefore relative. Its consequences sound crazy, but have been confirmed by many experiments.
wichtigste: Einstein published the special theory of relativity in 1905.
The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers.
Nothing can move faster than light.
Moving clocks run more slowly; this is called time dilation.
Moving objects appear shorter in the direction of motion; this is called length contraction.
The formula E = mc² shows that mass and energy are equivalent.

abschnitte.text: In 1905 **Albert Einstein** was working as a technical expert at the patent office in Bern. In his free time he thought about light and motion. In the same year his paper On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies appeared, which founded the special theory of relativity. It is called special because it only applies to observers moving steadily without gravity.

First, the laws of nature are the same for all observers who are moving steadily. Second, the **speed of light** in a vacuum is always the same, about 300,000 kilometres per second. This is true even if you fly after the light or towards it. For this to be true, time and space must change depending on motion.

The faster something moves, the more slowly time passes there; this is called **time dilation**. If a spaceship flies at 80 per cent of the speed of light, only 6 years pass on board while 10 years pass on Earth. In everyday life we notice nothing of this, because we are far too slow. But the effect has been measured with very precise **atomic clocks** in aeroplanes.

Lengths are not the same for everyone either. A fast-moving object appears shortened in its direction of motion; this is **length contraction**. In addition, no object with mass can reach the speed of light. The closer it gets, the more energy it needs to go even faster.

The most famous consequence of the theory is the formula **E = mc²**. It says that mass is a form of energy, where c stands for the speed of light. Even a tiny amount of mass equals a huge amount of energy. The energy of the Sun and of nuclear power stations is based on this, and at **CERN** in Geneva the theory is used every day.

begriffe.erklaerung: The speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres per second.
Moving clocks run more slowly than clocks at rest.
Moving objects appear shorter in the direction of motion.
A frame of reference that is at rest or moving steadily in a straight line.

gewusst: Muons from cosmic rays only reach the ground thanks to time dilation; otherwise they would decay before they got there.
Einstein was only 26 years old when the theory was published.
In Bern the Einstein House in the Kramgasse recalls his time in the city.

teile.einleitung: Mirror writing is writing that is written back to front, the way normal writing looks in a mirror. The easiest way to read it is to hold it up to a mirror. The famous artist Leonardo da Vinci wrote many of his notes in this way.
wichtigste: Mirror writing is writing written back to front.
The easiest way to read mirror writing is with a mirror.
Leonardo da Vinci wrote many notes in mirror writing.
The capital letter A looks exactly the same in a mirror.
The name OTTO in capital letters also looks the same in mirror writing.
When learning to write, children often mix up “d” and “b”, because one is the mirror image of the other.
The number 8 looks exactly the same in a mirror.

abschnitte.text: In **mirror writing** you write from right to left, and every letter is back to front. The result looks like normal writing seen in a **mirror**. If you hold mirror writing up to a mirror, you can read it quite normally again. This is because a mirror swaps left and right, but not top and bottom. That is why writing in a mirror is not upside down.

The Italian artist and inventor **Leonardo da Vinci** lived from 1452 to 1519. He filled thousands of pages with drawings and notes on machines, plants, water and the flight of birds. He wrote most of these notes in mirror writing. Leonardo was **left-handed**, and by writing from right to left he did not smudge the fresh ink. Whether he also wanted to hide his ideas in this way is not known for certain.

Some letters look exactly the same in a mirror, because they are **symmetrical**. Among the capital letters these include, for example, A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X and Y. The number 8 also stays the same in a mirror. A word that reads the same forwards and backwards is called a **palindrome**. The name OTTO is a palindrome made of symmetrical letters, so it looks exactly the same in mirror writing.

abschnitte.titel: Mirror writing when learning to write
abschnitte.text: Many children write individual letters or numbers back to front when they are learning. Most often **b and d** are mixed up, because one is the mirror image of the other. It also often happens with 3 or S. This is perfectly normal, because otherwise our brain recognises objects regardless of whether they face left or right. With a little practice the brain learns that with letters the **direction** matters.

On the front of many **ambulances** the word AMBULANCE is written in mirror writing. This lets drivers in front of it read the word correctly in their **rear-view mirror** and make way. On rubber stamps, too, the writing has to be back to front so that the print comes out the right way round. In the past, printers also put their lead letters together back to front. If you want to try it out, have a go at writing your own name in mirror writing.

begriffe.erklaerung: The image of an object in a mirror, in which left and right are swapped.
When both halves of a shape look exactly the same, as with a butterfly.
A word that reads the same forwards and backwards, for example OTTO or Anna.
A person who mainly writes and works with their left hand.

gewusst: Some people can write with both hands at the same time, normally with one and in mirror writing with the other.
A mirror does not really swap left and right, but front and back, which is why the writing looks back to front.
The capital letter H also looks the same in a mirror and even stays the same upside down.

teile.einleitung: A solar light is a lamp that gets its energy from sunlight. During the day it collects electricity with a small solar cell, and at night it shines without any cable or socket. You often see them in gardens, on balconies and along paths.
wichtigste: A solar light gets its energy from sunlight.
The dark plate on top of the lamp is the solar cell.
The energy for the night is stored in a rechargeable battery.
The lamp switches on by itself when it gets dark.
It is best to put it in a sunny spot.
After a dull winter day it only shines for a short time, because it could only collect a little energy.
If the solar cell is dirty, wiping it clean helps.

abschnitte.text: A solar light is a small, self-contained lamp with a built-in power station. It needs no power cable, so you can stick it into the ground anywhere in the garden. They come as path lights, fairy lights, lanterns or house number lamps. Larger solar lights even light up bus stops or paths in parks.

On top is a **solar cell**, a dark plate usually made of silicon. Inside is a **rechargeable battery**, which stores the electricity. The light source is almost always a **light-emitting diode** (LED), because it shines brightly with little electricity. A small electronic circuit controls when it charges and when it shines.

During the day the solar cell turns light into electricity and charges the battery. The electronics notice how bright it is; often the solar cell itself is used as the light sensor. When it gets dark, the cell no longer supplies electricity and the lamp switches on automatically. In the morning it switches off again by itself and charging starts all over again.

In summer the sun shines for a long time and strongly, the battery fills up and the lamp shines all night. In winter the days are short and often dull, so the cell collects only a little energy. The lamp then sometimes shines for only one or two hours. The cold also weakens many **batteries**, so that they give off less energy.

Put a solar light in a spot that gets many hours of **direct sunlight**, not under a tree. Wipe dust, leaves and bird droppings off the solar cell regularly. After a few years the battery gets weaker; often you can simply replace it. Old batteries do not belong in the household rubbish, but back at the **collection point** in the shop.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plate that turns light into electricity.
A battery that can be recharged and stores electricity for later.
Light-emitting diode, a very economical small light source.
A switch that turns a light on automatically when it gets dark.

gewusst: Many pocket calculators also work with a small solar cell and need no battery.
In areas without a power grid, solar lamps help many children to do their homework in the evening.
A solar light can charge a little in the shade too, but much less than in the sun.

teile.einleitung: The gradient tells you how steep a road, a path or a slope is. If you cycle uphill, you feel it in your legs straight away, and downhill you go faster and faster without pedalling. In Switzerland, with its Alps and passes, you come across gradients almost everywhere.
wichtigste: The gradient says how many metres you go up or down for every 100 metres of horizontal distance.
A road that leads over a high mountain is called a pass, for example at the Gotthard.
Going uphill takes strength, because you have to lift your weight against gravity.
Downhill the bike speeds up by itself, so you have to brake in good time.
Uphill it is easiest to pedal slowly and steadily in a low gear.
If a hill is too steep, you can get off and push the bike.
An e-bike helps uphill with an electric motor.

abschnitte.text: The **gradient** is usually measured in per cent. A gradient of 10 per cent means that you go up 10 metres for every 100 metres of horizontal distance. If the road goes down, we speak of a **downward slope**. In mathematics the gradient of a straight line is the ratio of the difference in height to the horizontal distance.

Uphill, **gravity** pulls the bike and the rider backwards. The steeper the road and the heavier the bike and luggage, the more strength you need. So if you have a light bike, you get up more easily. With the **gears** you choose a low gear; then you pedal more often, but with less force.

Downhill the bike speeds up even without pedalling, because gravity pulls it down. That is why it is important to **brake** early and evenly, ideally with both brakes. Before bends you slow down while still on the straight. A helmet is especially important on such rides.

A road over a high mountain is called a **pass**. Well-known passes are the Gotthard Pass, the Grimsel Pass, the Furka Pass and the Susten Pass. The old Gotthard road on the Ticino side is called the **Tremola** and winds up the slope in many tight bends. Such bends are called hairpins; they make the road longer, but less steep.

Railways also have to climb gradients. Normal railways can only manage a few per cent, because otherwise the wheels slip on the rails. With up to 48 per cent, the **Pilatus Railway** in Central Switzerland is considered the steepest rack railway in the world. With a gradient of up to 110 per cent, the **Stoos funicular** in the canton of Schwyz is one of the steepest funiculars in the world.

Road signs with a percentage warn of steep roads. Ramps for wheelchairs may only rise gently so that they are easy to use. Hiking trails, ski pistes and roofs also have a gradient. With an app or a map with contour lines you can find out how steep a path is.

begriffe.erklaerung: Measure of how steeply a route goes uphill, often given in per cent.
How steeply a route goes downhill.
Road or path over a mountain crossing.
Tight bend of a mountain road that zigzags up the slope.

gewusst: A gradient of 100 per cent equals an angle of 45 degrees.
The Stoos funicular is so steep that its round carriages turn so that passengers always stand upright.
In bike races such as the Tour de Suisse, the professionals ride over high Alpine passes.

teile.einleitung: A voltage divider is a simple electric circuit made of two resistors connected one after the other. It divides a voltage into two smaller parts. Voltage dividers are found in almost every electronic device, from volume controls to dusk switches.
wichtigste: A voltage divider consists of two resistors in series.
The total voltage is divided in the ratio of the resistances.
For the voltage across the second resistor: U₂ = U · R₂ / (R₁ + R₂).
The larger voltage drops across the larger resistor.
If you connect a load in parallel with R₂, the output voltage falls.
A potentiometer is an adjustable voltage divider with a sliding contact.
With a light-dependent resistor in a voltage divider you can build a dusk switch.

abschnitte.text: A voltage divider consists of two **resistors** R₁ and R₂ that are connected in **series** to a voltage source. The same current flows through both. The total voltage is therefore shared between the two resistors. At the point where they join, you can pick off a smaller part of the voltage.

The voltages are in the same ratio as the resistances: if R₂ is twice as large as R₁, R₂ gets twice as much voltage. The **voltage divider rule** is U₂ = U · R₂ / (R₁ + R₂). Example: R₁ = 1 kΩ and R₂ = 2 kΩ on 12 V give exactly 8 V across R₂ and 4 V across R₁. If R₁ is three times as large as R₂, R₂ gets only a quarter, so on 20 V that is 5 V.

As long as nothing is connected to the output, it is called an **unloaded** voltage divider. If you connect a device, the **load**, in parallel with R₂, the resistance of the lower part falls. This also makes the output voltage fall. Example: two resistors of 10 kΩ on 12 V give 6 V, but with a load of 10 kΩ across R₂ it is only 4 V.

A **potentiometer** is a resistor with a movable sliding contact. The slider divides the resistor into two parts, creating an adjustable voltage divider. When you turn the knob, the output voltage changes smoothly. In the past such rotary knobs were found in almost every radio as the volume control.

If you replace one resistor with a **sensor**, the voltage divider becomes a measuring probe. A **light-dependent resistor** (LDR) has a high resistance in the dark. If it forms the lower part of the divider, its voltage rises when it gets dark and can switch on a lamp. Electronic thermometers are built in the same way with temperature-dependent resistors.

begriffe.erklaerung: A component that slows down the flow of current, measured in ohms (Ω).
Components one after the other, so that the same current flows through all of them.
The device or component that draws current at the output of a circuit.
An adjustable resistor with a slider that serves as an adjustable voltage divider.
A resistor whose value changes with the brightness.

gewusst: Many joysticks of games consoles contain small potentiometers that measure the position of the lever.
A voltage divider always uses some energy, because current is constantly flowing through both resistors.
For large amounts of power, a transformer or a voltage regulator is therefore preferred.

teile.einleitung: Stabilisers are two small wheels that are screwed on to the left and right of the back wheel of a child's bike. They stop the bike from falling over while a child cannot yet balance. But you hardly learn to balance with them, which is why many children today prefer a balance bike.
wichtigste: Stabilisers sit on the left and right of the back wheel of a child's bike.
A child's bike usually has 2 stabilisers.
They are there so that the bike does not fall over.
With stabilisers you hardly learn to balance.
In fast bends a bike with stabilisers can tip outwards.
Many children today learn to balance on a balance bike.
The stabilisers are unscrewed when the child can balance.

abschnitte.text: **Stabilisers** are small wheels made of plastic or rubber on a metal holder. They are screwed on to the axle on the left and right of the back wheel. When the bike stands still, up to 4 wheels touch the ground: the front wheel, the back wheel and the two stabilisers. Usually the stabilisers are set a little higher, so that the bike can wobble slightly from side to side while riding.

abschnitte.titel: How do stabilisers hold the bike up?
abschnitte.text: A normal bike stands on only two points and would fall over straight away when standing still. The stabilisers make the **base** bigger, so that the **centre of gravity** of child and bike stays above this area. That is why the bike does not tip over. This gives small children a feeling of safety when they pedal for the first time.

When riding a normal bike, you lean into the bend, that is, inwards. With stabilisers you cannot do this, because the bike is held upright. In a fast bend the **centrifugal force** then pushes the bike outwards, and it can tip over the outer stabiliser. That is why you take bends slowly with stabilisers.

abschnitte.titel: The balance bike as an alternative
abschnitte.text: Today many children first learn on a **balance bike**, a bike without pedals that you push along with your feet. This lets them practise **balance** from the start, because they learn to balance and steer while rolling. When they later move on to a bike with pedals, they often do not need stabilisers at all. The idea comes from the running machine invented by the German Karl Drais in 1817.

Stabilisers are unscrewed when the child can balance. At first an adult often helps by running along lightly holding the saddle or the shoulder. A flat, safe place without traffic is best for practising. A **bike helmet** is part of every ride.

abschnitte.titel: Learning to ride a bike in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland many children learn to ride a bike at kindergarten age. Children are only allowed to cycle alone on roads from a certain age; smaller children need someone with them. Later at school there is often a **cycling test**, in which children show the most important traffic rules. Cycling is healthy, good for the environment and fun.

begriffe.erklaerung: When you are steady enough that you do not fall over.
Small bike without pedals that you push along with your feet.
Point where you can imagine the whole weight to be concentrated.
Force that pushes outwards in a bend.

gewusst: A moving bike stays upright mainly because you are constantly steering very slightly.
Karl Drais's first running machine had no pedals yet and was made of wood.
Adults can hardly remember how difficult balancing was at the beginning.

teile.einleitung: Swissgrid is Switzerland's national grid company and runs the transmission grid, the country's “electricity motorways”. Electricity flows through its high-voltage lines from the power stations to the regions and across the borders into neighbouring countries. Swissgrid makes sure that at every moment exactly as much electricity is produced as is used.
wichtigste: Swissgrid runs the Swiss transmission grid at voltages of 380 and 220 kilovolts.
In Switzerland Swissgrid's transmission grid is called grid level 1.
Swissgrid keeps the balance between electricity production and electricity use.
The Electricity Supply Act required an independent national grid company.
Swissgrid must be owned mostly, directly or indirectly, by cantons and municipalities.
The Federal Electricity Commission ElCom supervises the grid charges.
Swissgrid works with other European grid operators in the association ENTSO-E.

abschnitte.text: Swissgrid is a public limited company with its headquarters in **Aarau**. It was founded in 2006 and has owned the entire Swiss transmission grid since 2013. This grid includes about 6700 kilometres of lines and works with the highest voltages of 380 and 220 kilovolts. It can be compared with motorways on which large amounts of electricity travel long distances.

The Swiss power grid is divided into seven **grid levels**. Grid level 1 is Swissgrid's transmission grid; right at the bottom, at grid level 7, is the low-voltage network that leads to the sockets in houses. In between are substations that lower the voltage step by step. The lower levels are run by regional and local energy suppliers, for example city electricity companies.

Electricity can hardly be stored in the grid, so production and use must be equal at every second. One sign of this is the **grid frequency** of 50 hertz. If more is used than produced, it drops slightly, and Swissgrid calls up extra power station output, the so-called balancing energy. For this Swissgrid has control centres where experts monitor the grid around the clock. The **(n-1) criterion** is also important: the grid must be able to cope with the loss of any single element, such as a line, without an interruption in supply.

The basis for Swissgrid is the **Electricity Supply Act**, which required an independent national grid company. In the past the high-voltage lines belonged to various electricity companies. Today, according to the law, Swissgrid is mostly owned, directly or indirectly, by cantons and municipalities. The Federal Electricity Commission **ElCom** is an independent authority and supervises, among other things, the grid usage charges.

Building, maintaining and running the transmission grid costs a lot of money. It is mainly paid for through the **grid usage charges**, which appear on every electricity bill. In this way every household and every company pays a small share towards the electricity motorways. The money is also used to build new lines and renew old ones.

Switzerland lies in the middle of Europe and is connected by many lines to Germany, France, Italy and Austria. That is why a lot of electricity that is really being exchanged between other countries also flows through the Swiss grid. Swissgrid is a member of **ENTSO-E**, the association of European transmission system operators. Together the grid operators make sure that the large interconnected European grid stays stable.

begriffe.erklaerung: Extra-high-voltage grid that carries electricity over long distances.
How often the alternating current changes direction per second, 50 times in Europe.
Facility in which the voltage of the electricity is changed.
Extra electricity that secures the balance in the grid at short notice.
Independent authority that supervises Switzerland's electricity market.

gewusst: At every second Swissgrid has to make sure that exactly as much electricity flows into the grid as is taken out.
Swissgrid's high-voltage pylons also stand high in the Alps, where maintenance is difficult in snow and wind.
A power cut in one country can also affect other countries in the interconnected European grid.

teile.einleitung: In a solar eclipse the Moon moves between the Sun and the Earth and covers the Sun completely or partly. In a total solar eclipse it becomes almost as dark as at dusk in the middle of the day. It is one of the most impressive natural spectacles of all.
wichtigste: In a solar eclipse the Moon is exactly between the Sun and the Earth.
If the Moon covers the Sun only partly, it is called a partial solar eclipse.
A total solar eclipse can only be seen in a narrow strip on the Earth.
The complete darkness lasts a few minutes at most.
In a total eclipse you can see a bright ring of rays around the Sun, the corona.
It gets cooler and many birds fall silent as they do in the evening.
You may only watch a solar eclipse with special eclipse glasses.

abschnitte.text: A solar eclipse can only happen at **new moon**, when the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth. The Sun is about 400 times bigger than the Moon, but also about 400 times further away. That is why both look almost the same size in the sky and the Moon can cover the Sun exactly. Because the Moon's orbit is slightly tilted compared with the Earth's orbit, there is not an eclipse at every new moon.

In a **partial solar eclipse** it looks as if someone has taken a bite out of the Sun. In a **total solar eclipse** the Sun is completely covered. If the Moon happens to be a little further away from the Earth, a bright ring is left; this is an **annular solar eclipse**. On the Earth the Moon's umbra is only about as wide as a country, which is why totality can only be seen in a narrow strip.

When the Sun is completely covered, it suddenly becomes twilight and you can see bright stars and planets. Around the black disc of the Moon the **corona**, the outer layer of the Sun, shines as a silvery ring of rays. The temperature drops noticeably, birds fall silent and some animals behave as they do in the evening. After at most about seven and a half minutes, but usually much sooner, it is all over.

You must never look at the Sun without protection, not even when it is almost completely covered. The strong light can permanently damage the **retina** in the eye without it hurting. Only tested **eclipse glasses** with a special film are safe. Ordinary sunglasses, photo negatives or soot on glass do not protect enough.

On **12 August 2026** there was a total solar eclipse that could be seen in Spain, Iceland and Greenland. In Switzerland it was only visible as a partial eclipse. The next total solar eclipse over Switzerland will not be until 2081. Astronomers can calculate such events to the minute many centuries in advance.

begriffe.erklaerung: The outermost, very hot layer of gas around the Sun, which can only be seen in a total eclipse.
The phase of the Moon in which it is between the Sun and the Earth and stays dark.
The darkest part of the Moon's shadow, in which the Sun is completely covered.
The short time during which the Sun is completely covered.

gewusst: Every year the Moon moves a few centimetres further away from the Earth, so in the distant future there will be no more total solar eclipses.
During a solar eclipse in 1919, scientists proved that stars behind the Sun appear slightly shifted, as Albert Einstein had predicted.
The Moon's shadow races across the Earth's surface at well over 1000 kilometres per hour.

teile.einleitung: Pitch tells you whether a sound is high or low. A mouse squeaks high, a lorry rumbles low. In physics, pitch depends on how fast something vibrates.
wichtigste: Pitch shows how high or low a sound is.
The faster something vibrates, the higher the sound.
Small children usually have higher voices than adults.
The chirp of a bird or the squeak of a mouse is higher than the rumble of a lorry.
Among the string instruments, the double bass plays the lowest notes in the orchestra.
Soprano is the highest female voice in a choir.
A high note is placed higher up on the stave.
With a wailing siren the pitch changes.

abschnitte.text: Every sound is produced by a **vibration**, for example of a string, a drumskin or the vocal cords. This vibration makes the air tremble, and we hear that as sound. How often something swings back and forth per second is called its **frequency**. It is measured in **hertz**. The higher the frequency, the higher the sound.

Young people hear sounds from about 20 hertz to about 20,000 hertz. As people get older, they hear the very high sounds less and less well. Many animals hear far beyond this range. Bats and dolphins use very high sounds, **ultrasound**, to find their way, and dogs hear a dog whistle that we humans cannot hear. Elephants, on the other hand, also communicate with very low sounds, infrasound.

Small, short or thin things vibrate quickly and sound high; large, long or thick ones vibrate slowly and sound low. That is why a violin sounds high and the big **double bass** very low. On a guitar the note gets higher when you tighten a string or make it shorter with your finger. A small recorder sounds higher than a long organ pipe. The lowest instrument in the orchestra is usually the double bass or the contrabassoon.

The voice also has a pitch; it is produced by the **vocal cords** in the larynx. Small children have short vocal cords and therefore usually a higher voice than adults. In a choir four voice types are distinguished: soprano is the highest, alto the lower female and children's voice, tenor the higher and bass the lowest male voice. When you sing up a scale, the notes get higher step by step.

A siren wails alternately low and high, and its pitch changes. When an ambulance with its siren on drives past you, it sounds higher at first and then lower. This **Doppler effect** happens because the sound waves are squeezed together in front of the vehicle and stretched out behind it. In music, high notes are written higher up on the stave and low notes further down.

begriffe.erklaerung: How often something vibrates per second.
Unit of frequency; 1 hertz means one vibration per second.
Sounds so high that people cannot hear them.
Two bands in the larynx that vibrate when you speak and sing.
A sound is higher when the source comes closer and lower when it moves away.

gewusst: A mosquito beats its wings so fast that it makes a high humming sound.
A note one octave higher vibrates exactly twice as fast.
With ultrasound bats find insects even in complete darkness.

teile.einleitung: Solar thermal energy means catching the Sun's heat and using it. Unlike photovoltaics, it does not make electricity, but hot water or heat for heating. In Switzerland you can see solar collectors for this on many house roofs.
wichtigste: Solar thermal energy produces heat, whereas photovoltaics produces electricity.
The part that catches the Sun's heat is called a solar collector.
The absorbers are dark, because dark surfaces take in the most light.
Glycol is often added to the water so that it does not freeze in winter.
The heated water is stored in the hot water tank.
In Swiss detached houses, solar thermal energy is mostly used to heat water.
In solar tower power stations, many mirrors focus sunlight onto a tower.

abschnitte.text: The German word Solarthermie is made of “solar” for Sun and “Thermie” for heat; in English we say solar thermal energy. It uses the heat of the Sun's rays directly. Everyone knows the principle: a **garden hose** lying in the sun soon contains warm water. **Photovoltaics**, on the other hand, turns light into electricity.

A **solar collector** on the roof contains a dark plate, the **absorber**. Dark surfaces swallow the most light and so become hot. A liquid flows through thin pipes on the absorber, usually water with **glycol** as antifreeze. A sheet of glass on top keeps the heat in, like in a greenhouse.

As well as flat collectors there are **evacuated tube collectors**. In these the absorber lies in glass tubes from which the air has been pumped out. Because almost no heat is conducted away in a vacuum, very little is lost. Such collectors work quite well even in winter and in cool weather.

A pump carries the hot liquid from the roof down to the cellar. There it passes its heat through a coiled pipe to the water in the **hot water tank**. This means there is hot water for showering even when the sun is not shining. In Switzerland solar thermal energy is mainly used for this, sometimes also to support the heating.

In very sunny regions such as Spain, North Africa or California there are large **solar tower power stations**. Hundreds of movable mirrors direct sunlight onto the top of a tall tower. It gets so hot there that steam is produced to drive a turbine. Other power stations use long, curved **parabolic troughs**, which focus the light onto a pipe.

begriffe.erklaerung: The dark surface in the collector that swallows sunlight and gets hot.
An antifreeze that stops water from freezing in winter.
A space with almost no air, through which heat can hardly escape.
A well-insulated tank in which hot water is kept for later.

gewusst: The ancient Romans already built bath houses with large windows facing south to use the Sun's warmth.
On a summer day the liquid in a solar collector can get hotter than 100 degrees.
With a solar cooker made of mirrors you can even bring water to the boil in the sun.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Science Center Technorama in Winterthur is the largest science centre in Switzerland. Here you are allowed to touch and try out everything: lightning, magnets, mirrors, water and whirlpools. Instead of just looking, you learn science through your own experiments.
wichtigste: The Technorama is in Winterthur in the canton of Zurich.
It is a science centre, that is, a hands-on museum for science and technology.
There are more than 500 experiment stations to try out for yourself.
The exhibition opened in 1982.
Several hundred thousand visitors come every year.
Since 2020 there has also been an outdoor area with experiments on water and wind.
The Technorama also offers courses and laboratories for school classes.

abschnitte.text: The Technorama is in **Oberwinterthur**, a district of Winterthur in the canton of Zurich. The address is Technoramastrasse 1. You can get there by S-Bahn train to Oberwinterthur or by city bus to the Technorama stop. The exhibition area is about 6500 square metres, which is almost as big as a football pitch.

The **Technorama Foundation** was set up in 1969. At first the aim was a classic technology museum with old machines. In 1982 the exhibition opened in today's building. Later the Technorama turned into a **science centre**, in which trying things out yourself is the focus. Today it is one of the best-known destinations for families and schools in Switzerland.

The experiments are arranged by topic. In the **Mechanicum** area it is about forces and motion, and in “Electricity and Magnets” about electricity and magnetism. “Light and Vision” shows mirrors, colours and optical illusions, and in “Mathemagic” you can play with shapes and numbers. There is also a large collection of **toy trains**, which is regarded as cultural heritage of national importance.

In 2020 the outdoor area **Technorama Outdoors** opened. It has a large bridge, water features and experiments with wind. You can watch, for example, how water flows, forms whirlpools or how mist is created. In this way you can also experience physics in the fresh air.

At the Technorama there are hardly any signs with long texts, but instead many buttons, cranks and levers. The idea is that you first marvel, then ask questions and look for an explanation yourself. In the **laboratories** school classes can do chemistry and physics experiments with guidance. There are regular demonstrations, for example with high voltage and artificial **lightning**.

The Technorama is very popular. In 2024 about 373,000 people came, more visitors than ever before, and in 2025 there were about 369,000. Many visitors are families and school classes from all over Switzerland and from nearby countries. There are also changing special exhibitions, for example in 2025 about **acoustics** and sounds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A museum in which you discover science through your own experiments.
A test in which you try something out and observe it to understand it better.
An organisation with money and a fixed purpose, for example running a museum.
A picture or object with which our eyes and brain see something wrong.

gewusst: At the Technorama there is an unusual rule: touching is expressly encouraged.
The exhibition area of the Technorama is almost as big as a football pitch.
The Technorama also has a large collection of toy trains.

teile.einleitung: Gravity is the force with which the Earth pulls everything towards itself. It makes sure that a ball thrown up into the air comes back down and that we do not float off into space. It also keeps the Moon in its orbit around the Earth and the Earth in its orbit around the Sun.
wichtigste: All bodies with mass attract each other; this is called gravitation.
The Earth pulls everything towards its centre, which is why things fall downwards.
Isaac Newton described gravity in the 17th century, inspired, as a story goes, by a falling apple.
On the Moon gravity is about six times weaker than on Earth.
Air slows falling things down, which is why a sheet of paper falls more slowly than a stone.
Bathroom scales show how strongly the Earth pulls on you.
Gravity keeps planets and moons in their orbits.

abschnitte.text: Every body that has **mass** attracts other bodies. This attraction is called **gravitation** or gravity. The greater the mass, the stronger the attraction. The Earth is huge and therefore pulls strongly on all things on its surface: people, water, air and balls.

The English physicist **Isaac Newton** published his law of gravitation in 1687. A famous story says that a falling apple gave him the idea. He realised that the same force makes the apple fall to the ground and makes the Moon circle the Earth. Later Albert Einstein explained gravity even more precisely with his general theory of relativity.

Without air, all things would fall at the same speed, a feather just like a hammer. An astronaut showed this on the Moon in 1971 with a hammer and a feather. On Earth, **air resistance** strongly slows down light, wide things such as a sheet of paper. A **parachute** uses this: it slows the parachutist down in the air so that he lands gently.

The Moon has much less mass than the Earth; its gravity is only about one sixth as strong. So on the Moon you can jump much higher and further. The astronauts of the **Apollo missions** hopped across the Moon's surface like kangaroos. On Jupiter, on the other hand, the pull would be more than twice as strong as on Earth.

**Bathroom scales** measure how strongly the Earth pulls you downwards and use this to show how heavy you are. Physicists distinguish between mass in kilograms and **weight** as a force in newtons. Your mass is the same everywhere, but your weight on the Moon is much smaller. Gravity also causes the tides, because the Moon pulls on the sea water.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of attraction between all bodies with mass.
How much matter a body has, measured in kilograms.
The force with which a body is pulled by the Earth.
The slowing force of the air on moving bodies.

gewusst: Astronauts on the ISS space station float even though almost 90 per cent of the Earth's gravity still acts there, because they are constantly falling around the Earth.
A unit of force, the newton, is named after Isaac Newton.
Without gravity, the Earth's air would escape into space.

teile.einleitung: A solar cell is a flat electronic component that turns sunlight directly into electricity. Many solar cells together form a solar panel like the ones you see on house roofs. They supply electricity without noise, without exhaust fumes and without moving parts.
wichtigste: A solar cell turns sunlight directly into electricity.
Most solar cells are made of the semiconductor silicon.
The process is called photovoltaics.
Several solar cells are connected together to form solar panels.
Solar cells produce direct current; an inverter turns it into household electricity.
In Switzerland the number of solar systems on roofs is growing fast.

abschnitte.text: A **solar cell** is usually a thin, bluish or black shimmering wafer about 15 by 15 centimetres. When light falls on it, it supplies electricity. A single cell produces only a small voltage of about half a volt. That is why many cells are connected together to form a **solar panel**.

Solar cells are usually made of **silicon**, a semiconductor obtained from sand. The cell has two differently treated layers, and at the boundary between them there is an electric field. When light hits the cell, it knocks electrons out of their places. The electric field drives these electrons in one direction, and so **direct current** flows; this is called the photovoltaic effect.

The French physicist Alexandre Edmond **Becquerel** discovered the photovoltaic effect as early as 1839. In 1954 researchers at Bell Labs in the USA presented the first usable silicon solar cell. At first solar cells were used mainly in **satellites**, because there they supply electricity for years without fuel. Today they are much cheaper and found all over the world.

You can find small solar cells in pocket calculators, garden lights and parking meters. Large **photovoltaic systems** on roofs supply houses with electricity. An **inverter** turns the direct current into the alternating current that comes out of the socket. Extra electricity can be fed into the grid or stored in a battery.

Switzerland wants to become climate-neutral by 2050 and is relying heavily on solar power to do so. Every year many thousands of new systems are added on roofs, walls and noise barriers. At the **Muttsee dam** in the canton of Glarus there is a large alpine solar system that supplies a lot of electricity even in winter. In the mountains the sun often shines above the fog in winter, and the snow reflects extra light.

begriffe.erklaerung: The direct conversion of light into electricity.
A semiconductor element that most solar cells are made of.
A device that turns direct current into alternating current.
Many solar cells connected together in a frame.

gewusst: In 2015 and 2016 the solar aircraft Solar Impulse 2 of the Swiss Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg flew around the Earth on solar power alone.
Solar cells actually work a little better in the cold than in great heat.
The ISS space station gets its electricity from huge solar cell wings.

teile.einleitung: Silicon is a chemical element with the symbol Si and the atomic number 14. It is found in sand, stones and glass and is the most important material for computer chips and solar cells. Without silicon there would be no smartphones and no modern computers.
wichtigste: Silicon has the atomic number 14 and the chemical symbol Si.
After oxygen, silicon is the second most common element in the Earth's crust.
Silicon is mainly obtained from quartz, that is silicon dioxide.
Silicon is a semiconductor and therefore ideal for computer chips.
Large single crystals are pulled from a melt with the Czochralski process.
Silicon melts at about 1410 degrees Celsius.
Silicon Valley in California is named after this element.

abschnitte.text: After **oxygen**, silicon is the second most common element of the Earth's crust; about a quarter of its mass is made of it. In nature it is almost never found pure, but mostly as **quartz** or in silicate rocks such as granite and gneiss. The sand on the beach is also often made mostly of grains of quartz. In the Swiss Alps you can find beautiful rock crystals, which are also made of quartz.

Pure silicon is grey, has a metallic shine and is hard and brittle. Its atoms are arranged in a **diamond structure**, exactly like the carbon atoms in a diamond. It melts at about 1410 degrees Celsius and is lighter than aluminium. Chemically it is one of the **metalloids**, so it conducts electricity less well than metals but better than insulators.

Quartz is heated together with coal in an electric furnace, which produces raw silicon. For chips it has to be extremely pure: for every billion silicon atoms there may hardly be a single foreign atom. With the **Czochralski process** a large, round single crystal is pulled from the melt. This is cut into wafer-thin slices called **wafers**, which today are up to 300 millimetres across.

Silicon is a **semiconductor**: by adding tiny amounts of other substances, you can control exactly how well it conducts electricity. Transistors, the smallest switches in every computer chip, are based on this. Billions of such transistors can sit on a single chip. Most **solar cells** on house roofs are also made of silicon.

In 1824 the Swedish chemist **Jöns Jakob Berzelius** was the first to produce fairly pure silicon. The name comes from the Latin word “silex” for flint or pebble. That is why in German silicon compounds used to be called “Kiesel”, meaning pebble. From the 1950s onwards silicon became the most important material in electronics, and the area around San Francisco got the nickname **Silicon Valley**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that conducts electricity sometimes well and sometimes badly, depending on how it is treated.
A thin, round slice of silicon on which computer chips are made.
A very common mineral made of silicon and oxygen, for example as sand or rock crystal.
A crystal in which all the atoms are arranged without gaps in one single regular lattice.

gewusst: Silicon is not the same as silicone: silicone is a soft plastic that only contains silicon.
The English name “silicon” is often wrongly translated into German as “Silikon”, which means silicone.
Window glass is also made mostly of silicon dioxide.

teile.einleitung: Significant figures are the digits of a number that really say something about how precise a measurement is. Anyone who writes 3.060 metres is claiming to have measured much more precisely than someone who writes 3 metres. In physics and chemistry these rules help you to round results honestly and sensibly.
wichtigste: Significant figures show how precise a measured value is.
You count from the first digit that is not zero to the last digit given.
The number 3.060 has four significant figures, 2.5·10^3 has two.
When multiplying and dividing, the result has as many significant figures as the least precise value.
When adding and subtracting, you go by the smallest number of decimal places.
Scientific notation lets you show the precision clearly.
Counted numbers such as 12 pupils are exact and have any number of significant figures.

abschnitte.text: Every measurement is only possible up to a certain precision. A ruler with millimetre marks lets you give, say, 12.3 centimetres, but not 12.3456 centimetres. The digits you have really measured are called **significant figures**. The last of them is usually already a little uncertain. Anyone who writes down more digits is pretending to have a **precision** that does not exist.

You start at the first digit that is not zero. Zeros at the front never count, so 0.0045 has only two significant figures. Zeros between other digits and zeros at the end after the decimal point always count. That is why 3.060 has exactly four significant figures. In 2.5·10^3 only the digits before the power of ten count, which makes two.

When multiplying and dividing, the result gets as many significant figures as the value with the fewest. For 2.5 · 3.41 the calculator shows 8.525, but because 2.5 has only two significant figures, the result is **8.5**. For 7.20 ÷ 2.4 the calculator shows 3, but written correctly it is **3.0**, because 2.4 has two significant figures. The zero after the decimal point is important here and must not be left out.

When adding and subtracting, what counts is not the number of significant figures but the number of **decimal places**. The result must not be more precise than the value with the fewest decimal places. For 12.1 + 0.256 the calculator gives 12.356. Because 12.1 has only one decimal place, you round to **12.4**.

With numbers such as 1200 it is unclear whether the zeros were measured or are only filling the places. **Scientific notation** makes it clear. If you write 1.20·10^3, exactly three significant figures are meant; with 1.2·10^3 only two. This notation is also used for very large or very small numbers, for example in astronomy or chemistry.

Counted numbers such as 12 pupils or 3 apples are **exact**; they have any number of significant figures. Fixed conversions such as 100 centimetres per metre are also exact. In everyday life you come across significant figures on the kitchen scales or a fever thermometer that shows 37.4 degrees, for example. The important thing is to round only at the end of a calculation, otherwise rounding errors pile up.

begriffe.erklaerung: How precisely a measuring device or a measurement can determine a value.
Shortening a number to fewer digits and adjusting the last digit.
A number such as 10^3, that is 10 times 10 times 10.
Writing a number as a decimal times a power of ten, for example 1.20·10^3.

gewusst: A calculator often shows eight or more digits, even though the measured values are much less precise.
In exams a result with too many digits can be marked as imprecise, even though the calculation was correct.
The speed of light in a vacuum is fixed exactly by definition and therefore has no measurement uncertainty.

teile.einleitung: A vibration damper is a device that weakens unwanted vibrations. Such dampers are found in cars, skyscrapers, bridges and power lines. Without them, many vehicles and buildings would sway dangerously.
wichtigste: Vibration dampers usually turn kinetic energy into heat.
As well as springs, a car needs shock absorbers, otherwise it would keep bouncing for a long time after every bump.
A tuned mass damper is an extra mass that swings along with the same natural frequency but in the opposite phase.
The pendulum ball in the Taipei 101 skyscraper weighs about 660 tonnes.
With base isolation a building stands on elastic bearings that weaken earthquake movements.
Stockbridge dampers on high-voltage lines damp vibrations caused by wind.
Eddy current dampers brake without contact using induced currents and magnetic fields.

abschnitte.text: Each wheel of a car hangs on a spring that absorbs bumps from the road. Without damping, the car would bob up and down like a trampoline after every bump. A hydraulic **shock absorber** forces oil through narrow openings and so slows the movement down. The kinetic energy is turned into **heat** in the process.

Very tall buildings sway in strong winds. That is why a huge steel ball of about 660 tonnes hangs in the Taipei 101 skyscraper in Taiwan as a **tuned mass damper**. It has the same natural frequency as the building and always swings in the opposite phase, that is, in the other direction. In this way it takes a large part of the movement away from the tower.

With **base isolation** a building does not stand directly on its foundations, but on elastic bearings made of rubber and steel. When the ground shakes jerkily in an earthquake, the bearings pass on the movement only in a weakened form. This technique is used especially often in countries such as Japan. In Switzerland too, where the earthquake risk is greatest in Valais and around Basel, there are buildings with such bearings.

Wind can make high-voltage lines swing, which damages the cables over time. Dumbbell-shaped **Stockbridge dampers**, named after their inventor George Stockbridge, swallow these vibrations. On tall steel chimneys you often see spiral-shaped strips. They stop air eddies from breaking away regularly and setting the chimney swinging.

When a piece of metal moves through a magnetic field, **eddy currents** form in it. These produce their own magnetic field, which brakes the movement. This kind of damping works completely without contact and hardly wears out. It is used in measuring instruments, scales and even in free-fall towers at theme parks.

begriffe.erklaerung: Part of a car that slows down the bouncing of the springs.
Extra mass that swings against the vibration of a building.
Swinging exactly in the opposite direction.
Earthquake protection using elastic bearings under a building.
Electric current that forms in moving metal in a magnetic field.

gewusst: When it opened in 2000, the Millennium Bridge in London swayed so much that it was closed and fitted with dampers.
The huge ball in Taipei 101 is a tourist attraction and even has its own mascots.
Washing machines also have shock absorbers so that they do not wander across the room during the spin cycle.

teile.einleitung: A tennis ball is a small rubber ball covered with felt that is used in tennis. Inside it there is air under pressure, which makes it bounce so well. It can teach you a lot about physics: about pressure, temperature and energy.
wichtigste: A tennis ball weighs about 58 grams.
On the outside a tennis ball is covered with felt.
Inside there is air under pressure.
Tennis balls are usually bright yellow so that they are easy to see.
New balls are sold in airtight tins so that they keep their pressure.
An old ball and a ball on a cold day bounce less high.
The tight strings of the racket act like a small trampoline.

abschnitte.text: A tennis ball consists of a hollow **rubber** core, which is glued together from two half shells. Over it goes a covering of **felt**, sewn together from two pieces shaped like a figure eight. This creates the typical curved seam. According to the rules of the world governing body, a ball weighs between 56 and just under 60 grams, so about 58 grams, and is about 6.7 centimetres across.

Inside most tennis balls the air is squeezed together more than outside. This **excess pressure** makes the ball firm and lets it bounce well. Over time air slowly escapes through the rubber, and the ball bounces less high. That is why new balls are sold in airtight tins, which are also under pressure. When you open one, you hear a loud hiss.

When the ball hits the ground, it is briefly squashed and the air inside is compressed. Then it expands again and shoots upwards; **kinetic energy** is stored and released again in the process. Part of the energy is lost as heat, which is why the ball never bounces quite as high as it fell. On a cold day the rubber is less elastic and the air pressure in the ball is lower, so it bounces less high. The tight **strings** of the racket also spring the ball back, like a small trampoline.

In the past tennis balls were white or black. When tennis was shown more and more on colour television, bright yellow balls were introduced in the 1970s, because they were easier to see on the screen. The Wimbledon tournament in London went on playing with white balls until 1986. Today almost all tennis balls are a bright **yellow-green**, which players, umpires and spectators can see well.

Tennis is very popular in Switzerland, and there are hundreds of tennis clubs. Tennis became famous here above all through **Roger Federer**, who won 20 Grand Slam singles titles, including Wimbledon eight times. Martina Hingis, Stan Wawrinka and Belinda Bencic also had great successes. At big tournaments the balls are often exchanged for new ones after only a few games.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thick, soft fabric made of pressed fibres.
When the pressure inside is greater than outside.
The ability of a material to go back to its shape after being squashed.
The four most important tennis tournaments in the world.

gewusst: Tens of thousands of tennis balls are used at big tournaments.
Used tennis balls are sometimes put under chair legs so that the chairs slide quietly over the floor.
When professionals serve, a tennis ball is accelerated to over 200 kilometres per hour.

teile.einleitung: A hairpin road, or serpentine road, is a road or path that zigzags up a steep slope in tight bends. Instead of climbing straight up, you take a longer route and get a gentler gradient in return. Famous examples are the Tremola on the Gotthard Pass and the road up the Stelvio Pass.
wichtigste: A serpentine road leads up a steep slope in tight bends.
The longer route reduces the gradient, so vehicles and people get up more easily.
A very tight bend in which the direction of travel almost reverses is called a hairpin bend.
The cobbled Tremola road on the Gotthard Pass has 24 bends and leads down to Airolo.
On the Trafoi side, the road up the Stelvio Pass in Italy has 48 numbered bends.
The Gotthard mountain railway line gains height near Wassen with spiral tunnels.
Spiral ramps in multi-storey car parks use the same principle as a serpentine road.

abschnitte.text: The word **serpentine** comes from the Latin serpens, which means snake. Like a snake, the road winds up the mountain in loops. The individual tight turning points are called **bends**. If a bend is so tight that the direction of travel almost reverses, it is called a **hairpin bend**. Serpentine roads are found on many pass roads in the Alps, but also on hiking trails on steep slopes.

In physics a slope is an **inclined plane**. The steeper it is, the more force you need to get a load up it. A serpentine road makes the route longer, but the **gradient** becomes smaller. The height you gain stays the same, but you spread the work over a longer distance. If a pass road climbs 300 metres in height over 4 km of road, the average gradient is about 7.5 per cent.

The **Tremola** is a section of the old Gotthard Pass road on the Ticino side. It leads from the Gotthard Pass in 24 bends through the Val Tremola down to **Airolo**. The road is paved with cobblestones and is considered one of the most beautiful historic pass roads in Switzerland. Many cyclists and motorcyclists ride it because of the many bends. Today it is protected as an important transport monument.

The road up the **Stelvio Pass** in South Tyrol is famous for its numbered bends. On the Trafoi side there are 48 bends, each with a sign showing its number. The Stelvio Pass is one of the highest road passes in the Alps. In Switzerland, too, there are winding pass roads, for example over the Furka Pass, the Grimsel Pass or the Susten Pass. In winter many of these passes are closed because of snow.

Railways can manage even less steep routes than cars. That is why spiral tunnels were built on the **Gotthard mountain line** near Wassen, in which the train goes round a loop inside the mountain and gains height. Travellers therefore see the church of Wassen three times from different angles. There are also such spiral tunnels on the Albula Railway in the Grisons. In multi-storey car parks, **spiral ramps** use the same principle: instead of a steep ramp, you drive upwards in a circle.

begriffe.erklaerung: A road that winds up a slope in bends.
A very tight curve where the road changes direction.
How steeply a road climbs, usually given in per cent.
A sloping surface that lets you raise loads with less force.
A railway tunnel in which the train goes round a loop to gain height.

gewusst: A gradient of 10 per cent means that you climb 10 metres for every 100 metres of road.
Many animals such as chamois and cows also walk in zigzags on steep slopes and form paths as they do so.
Thanks to the spiral tunnels, the church of Wassen has become one of the best-known railway sights in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In physics, floating means that a body stays on the surface of a liquid without going under. Whether something floats, hovers or sinks depends on buoyancy and weight. That is why a huge steel ship can float while a small stone goes under straight away.
wichtigste: A body sinks if its weight is greater than the buoyancy.
In a floating boat, buoyancy and weight are exactly equal.
A body hovers if its density is the same as that of water.
Substances with a lower density than water, such as candle wax, float.
About 90 per cent of an iceberg lies below the water surface.
A ball with a mass of 2 kg and a volume of 2.5 litres floats, because its density is lower than that of water.
If you breathe out completely, your body's volume becomes smaller and you sink deeper.

abschnitte.text: When a body dips into water, the water pushes more strongly from below than from above. This upward force is called **buoyancy**. More than 2000 years ago the Greek scholar Archimedes realised that the buoyancy is as great as the weight of the water pushed aside. That is why this law is called **Archimedes' principle**.

If the weight is greater than the buoyancy, the body sinks. If both are equal while the body is completely under water, it hovers. If the buoyancy is greater when it is under water, the body rises and then floats at the surface. When floating, it only dips in until the water pushed aside weighs exactly as much as the body itself.

**Density** tells you how much mass there is in a certain volume. Water has a density of about 1 kg per litre. Wood, candle wax and ice are lighter and therefore float. Ice has about nine tenths of the density of water, which is why only about one tenth of an iceberg sticks out of the sea.

A ship made of steel floats, even though steel is much heavier than water. The hull is hollow inside and filled with air, so it pushes aside a great deal of water. The average density of the whole ship is therefore lower than that of water. To dive, submarines flood their **ballast tanks** with water, and to surface they push it out again with compressed air.

In the **Cartesian diver**, a small tube with air in it floats in a closed PET bottle. If you squeeze the bottle, the air in the diver is compressed, water gets in and it sinks. If you let go, it rises again. A raw egg also shows the principle: it sinks in tap water, but floats in very salty water.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force with which a liquid pushes a body upwards.
Mass divided by volume, that is, how heavy a substance is for its size.
The buoyancy is as great as the weight of the liquid pushed aside.
Experiment in which a diver in a bottle sinks and rises when you squeeze it.

gewusst: In the Dead Sea the water is so salty that people can lie in it and read a newspaper.
Fish use their swim bladder to control whether they rise, sink or hover.
Ice floats because water takes up more space when it freezes and so becomes lighter.

teile.einleitung: A standing wave is a wave that does not travel, but vibrates up and down at fixed places. It forms when two identical waves travelling in opposite directions overlap. Every guitar string, every flute and even an alphorn produce their notes with standing waves.
wichtigste: A standing wave forms when two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions overlap.
There are places that stay still, the nodes, and places that vibrate strongly, the antinodes.
Two neighbouring nodes are half a wavelength apart.
Overall, an ideal standing wave carries no energy.
If you halve the vibrating length of a string, its fundamental frequency doubles.
A pipe closed at one end only forms odd multiples of the fundamental.
Kundt's tube and Chladni figures make standing waves visible.

abschnitte.text: Normally a wave travels, like a wave on a lake. But if a wave runs against a wall or a fixed end, it is **reflected** and travels back. The wave going out and the wave coming back overlap and form a **standing wave**. It seems to stay in place and only vibrates up and down.

At some places the two waves always cancel each other out; nothing moves there: these are the **nodes**. Between them are the **antinodes**, where the vibration is greatest. Two neighbouring nodes are always half a wavelength apart. Because energy only swings back and forth between nodes, no energy is carried on overall.

A string is fixed at both ends, and there are always nodes there. For the fundamental exactly half a wavelength fits on the string, so: fundamental frequency = wave speed divided by twice the length. So a string 0.65 m long with a wave speed of 286 m/s vibrates at 220 Hz. If you press the string down in the middle, the vibrating length is halved, and the note becomes an **octave** higher: the frequency doubles.

In flutes, organ pipes and alphorns the air vibrates as a standing **sound wave**. In a pipe closed at one end, a so-called **stopped pipe**, only a quarter of a wavelength fits in for the fundamental. Such a pipe 0.5 m long sounds at 170 Hz with a speed of sound of 340 m/s. It can only form odd multiples of the fundamental as overtones, which is why it sounds different from an open pipe.

In 1866 the German physicist August Kundt sprinkled fine powder into a glass tube and produced a standing sound wave in it. The powder gathers into little heaps at the nodes: this is **Kundt's tube**. Even earlier, in the 18th century, Ernst Florens Friedrich Chladni sprinkled sand on metal plates and stroked them with a violin bow. The sand gathers on the lines that stay still and forms beautiful **Chladni figures**.

Standing waves also form in a microwave oven, which is why there would be cold and hot spots in the food. The **turntable** makes sure that the food still gets evenly warm. In a bath you can make standing water waves if you rock back and forth at the right rhythm. With bridges and buildings, too, engineers make sure that no dangerous standing vibrations arise.

begriffe.erklaerung: Place in a standing wave that does not move.
Place in a standing wave that vibrates most strongly.
The distance from one wave crest to the next.
The lowest frequency at which something can vibrate, the fundamental note.
A higher note that sounds along with the fundamental.

gewusst: With a microwave without a turntable and a bar of chocolate, you can see the distances between the hot spots and use them to estimate the speed of light.
An alphorn has no keys or valves; its different notes come only from different standing waves in the column of air.
Around 1809 Chladni even showed his sound figures to the Emperor Napoleon.

teile.einleitung: A socket is the connection in the wall through which electrical appliances are supplied with electricity. Behind it are wires that reach all the way to the power station. Because there is a dangerous voltage in the socket, important safety rules apply when using it.
wichtigste: A normal Swiss socket has three holes.
In Switzerland the socket supplies a voltage of 230 volts.
The electricity comes through wires from a power station.
You must never put anything made of metal into a socket, or you risk an electric shock.
Plugging several multi-way adapters into each other is dangerous, because they can overheat.
The flat Europlug also fits into Swiss sockets.
Only an electrician repairs a broken socket.

abschnitte.text: A socket connects an appliance via its **plug** to the electricity network in the house. Inside the wall, cables lead to the fuse box and from there on through the power grid to a power station. In Switzerland the socket supplies **alternating current** at 230 volts and 50 hertz. This voltage is life-threatening for people.

Switzerland has its own plug system, often called **Type J**. The normal socket has three holes: two for the current and one in the middle, slightly offset, for the **earth**. The earth safely carries away current if a fault occurs in an appliance. The flat Europlug with two round pins also fits, but for many other foreign plugs you need a travel adapter.

If you put a piece of metal into the socket, an **electric shock** can flow through your body. If many multi-way adapters are plugged into each other with powerful appliances connected, cables can get too hot and catch fire. If there is a burning smell, the plug is hot or the socket gives off sparks, you must not use it any more. Then you tell an adult straight away.

A **socket cover** closes the holes of the socket so that children cannot put anything into them. Many new sockets have a built-in flap that only opens when a proper plug is pushed into several holes at the same time. In modern flats a **residual current device** also protects against dangerous accidents. It switches off the current in a flash if the current takes the wrong path.

You stop using an appliance with a damaged cable. You unplug chargers after charging, which saves electricity and is safer. When unplugging, you hold the plug and do not pull on the cable. Sockets in the garden or in the bathroom often have a **flip cover** so that no water gets in.

begriffe.erklaerung: Shows how strongly the current is driven, measured in volts.
Protective wire that safely carries away current if there is a fault.
Connector that lets foreign plugs fit into the socket.
Switch that turns off the current immediately if there is a fault.
Distributor to which you can connect several appliances.

gewusst: In Europe there are many different plug systems, which is why not every plug fits in every country.
As well as the normal socket, Switzerland also has sockets for more powerful appliances with 16 amperes, which have square pins.
The Swiss socket is especially narrow, which is why three of them often fit side by side in a single box.

teile.einleitung: Statics is a branch of mechanics that deals with forces on bodies at rest. It explains why a bridge does not collapse, a shelf holds and a crane does not topple over. Without statics, houses, towers or bridges could not be built safely.
wichtigste: Statics studies forces on bodies that are not moving.
A body is at rest when all the forces and turning effects cancel each other out.
A rigid body in a plane has 3 independent conditions for equilibrium.
Two forces acting at the same point are added with the parallelogram of forces.
In the bars of an ideal truss only tension or compression forces act.
In ancient Greece Archimedes was already studying the law of the lever.
Civil engineers need statics for every structure.

abschnitte.text: The word statics comes from the Greek word for “standing”. Statics describes bodies in **equilibrium**, that is, bodies that stay still. This does not mean that no forces are acting. In fact many forces act, but they cancel each other out exactly, as in a tug of war when both teams pull equally hard.

For a rigid body in a plane there are three **conditions for equilibrium**. The forces to the left and right must cancel out, and so must the forces up and down. In addition, the turning effects, the **moments**, must not add up, otherwise the body would turn. If a lamp of 50 N hangs in the middle of a rope whose halves are tilted at 30 degrees to the horizontal, each half of the rope carries 50 N.

Forces have a size and a direction, so they are drawn as arrows. Two forces acting at the same point are added with the **parallelogram of forces**. The other way round, a force can also be split up. On a slope tilted at 30 degrees, a **downhill force** of 50 N pulls a block of 100 N downwards.

Bridges and beams rest on **supports**. A fixed support holds the beam in place, while a sliding support in the plane can only take a force at right angles to the direction it slides in. This lets a bridge expand in the heat without being damaged. A **truss** consists of bars joined into triangles, and only tension or compression forces act in the bars, as in many railway bridges or the Eiffel Tower.

In the 3rd century BC the Greek scholar **Archimedes** was already studying the law of the lever. The saying “Give me a firm place to stand, and I will move the world” is attributed to him. Later scientists such as Simon Stevin developed the study of forces further. Today engineers calculate with computer programs based on the same basic laws.

A mountainous country like Switzerland needs many daring bridges, dams and tunnels.
