The Swiss engineer **Robert Maillart** built the Salginatobel Bridge near Schiers in the canton of the Grisons, which is regarded as a masterpiece today. At ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne, students learn how to calculate such structures safely. For every house, an expert has to prove that it is stable.

begriffe.erklaerung: State in which all forces cancel each other out and the body stays still.
Turning effect of a force; it is greater the further away the force acts.
Framework of bars joined into triangles.
Support on which a beam can slide back and forth a little.

gewusst: Triangles are especially stable, which is why cranes and many bridges are made of lots of triangles.
A seesaw in the playground is a lever on which you can try out statics.
A heavier child can seesaw with a lighter one if the heavier child sits closer to the middle.

teile.einleitung: Ski jumping is a winter sport in which athletes ski down a jumping hill, take off and fly through the air as far and as beautifully as possible. Physics and courage work together here: air resistance, lift and gravity decide the distance. In Simon Ammann, Switzerland has one of the most successful ski jumpers in history.
wichtigste: Ski jumpers jump from a structure called a ski jump.
They take off at an edge called the take-off table.
In the air the jumpers hold their skis in a V shape so that they fly further.
They land in the Telemark position, with one leg slightly in front.
On the largest hills, the ski flying hills, you fly more than 200 metres.
Simon Ammann won Olympic gold in ski jumping four times.
Since 2014 women's ski jumping has also been part of the Olympic Games.

abschnitte.text: A **ski jump** consists of the in-run, the take-off table and the landing slope. In the in-run on large hills the jumpers reach about 90 km/h. At the **take-off table** they push off powerfully. The landing slope is steep and roughly follows the flight path, so the jumper is never high above the ground and the landing is gentle.

In the in-run the jumpers crouch down low so that the air slows them down less. In the air they lean far forwards, almost like an aeroplane wing. This creates **lift**, which keeps them in the air for longer. A headwind can therefore help, while a tailwind shortens the jump.

In the past ski jumpers held their skis parallel next to each other. At the end of the 1980s the Swede Jan Boklöv made the **V style** famous, in which the ski tips point apart. At first jumpers even lost points for it. But because you fly much further in the V style, everyone jumps like this today.

On landing the jumpers put one leg slightly forward and bend their knees; this is called the **Telemark** landing. The name comes from the Telemark region in Norway, where ski jumping began. Points are given for the distance and for the style, which the judges assess. Today wind and the length of the in-run are also balanced out with points.

**Simon Ammann** from the Toggenburg won both individual events in Salt Lake City in 2002 and in Vancouver in 2010, so four Olympic golds in total. Andreas Küttel became world champion in 2009. Well-known ski jumps are in Engelberg, where World Cup events take place every year, and in Einsiedeln. Around New Year many fans follow the Four Hills Tournament in Germany and Austria.

On especially large hills, the **ski flying hills**, the athletes fly over 200 metres. The best flights even go over 250 metres, which is more than two football pitches. Famous ski flying hills are, for example, in Planica in Slovenia and in Vikersund in Norway. There a flight lasts several seconds.

begriffe.erklaerung: The structure with in-run, take-off edge and landing slope.
The edge at the end of the in-run where you take off.
Landing with one leg in front and the knees bent.
Flying position in which the skis spread apart like a V.
A force of the air that pushes a body upwards.

gewusst: Because the landing slope is so steep, a ski jumper is usually only a few metres above the ground, even though he flies very far.
At first the V style brought point deductions, until everyone realised how much further you get with it.
Simon Ammann won his first two Olympic titles in 2002, when hardly anyone had counted him among the favourites.

teile.einleitung: Soap is a cleaning product made from fats or oils. It loosens dirt and grease so that you can rinse them off with water. In physics soap is interesting, because it makes surfaces slippery and changes the surface tension of water.
wichtigste: Soap is traditionally made from fat or oil.
When washing your hands, it helps to loosen dirt and grease.
You should wash your hands with soap for about 20 to 30 seconds.
If you rub soap hard with water, lather forms.
A wet bar of soap slips easily out of your hand, because soap and water make things slippery.
Soapy water on the floor is slippery, so you wipe it up and put a non-slip mat in the shower.
With soap a tight ring is easier to pull off your finger.

abschnitte.text: Soap is made by boiling fats or oils with an **alkali**; this process is called **saponification**. With caustic soda you get hard soap, with caustic potash soft soap. In the past animal fat and wood ash were used for this, today often plant oils such as olive oil or coconut oil. Many liquid soaps and shower gels contain artificially made detergents instead of real soap.

A soap particle has two different ends. One end likes water, the other likes fat and avoids water. The fat-loving ends stick to grease and dirt and surround them in tiny little balls called **micelles**. The water can then simply rinse these little balls away.

Together with water, soap forms a thin film between two surfaces. This film reduces **friction**, similar to a lubricant. That is why a wet bar of soap slips out of your hand and a tight ring is easier to pull off with soap. For the same reason a shower floor with soapy water is dangerously slippery; a non-slip mat helps against this.

Water has **surface tension**: its surface behaves like a thin, stretched skin. Soap greatly reduces this tension. This lets water get into fabrics and cracks more easily. If you rub soap with water, air is trapped and lather forms, made of many small bubbles.

More than 4000 years ago the Sumerians in ancient Mesopotamia were already making soap-like products from oil and ash. In the Middle Ages cities such as Marseille and Aleppo were famous for their soaps. Today we know that washing your hands thoroughly with soap prevents many illnesses. It is important to soap every part, including thumbs, fingertips and the gaps between the fingers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Making soap from fat and an alkali.
Corrosive liquid that forms soap together with fat.
Tiny ball of soap particles that traps grease.
Force that makes the surface of water act like a thin skin.

gewusst: Hard water with a lot of limescale makes less lather with soap and leaves grey rings.
A pepper test shows the effect: pepper on water darts to the edge when you dip in a finger with soap on it.
Soap can destroy the fatty coat of some viruses and so make them harmless.

teile.einleitung: A solar power system is an installation that turns sunlight into useful energy. Usually this means solar panels that produce electricity, often on house roofs. In Switzerland more and more solar systems are being built, even high up in the mountains.
wichtigste: A solar power system needs sunlight to make electricity.
The dark panels of a solar system are called solar panels.
Solar systems are often built on house roofs.
At night a solar system makes no electricity.
Electricity that the house does not need flows into the power grid.
In Switzerland solar panels work best facing south.
In the mountains the sun often shines above the fog in winter, which is why systems are built there too.

abschnitte.text: A solar power system uses the energy of the Sun. The most common type is **photovoltaics**, which turns light directly into electricity. There are also **solar thermal** systems, which heat water with the Sun's warmth. When people talk about a solar system in everyday life, they usually mean the electricity system.

A **solar panel** consists of many solar cells, usually made of silicon. When light hits a cell, tiny charged particles inside it are set in motion and direct current flows. A device called an **inverter** turns it into the alternating current that comes out of the socket. The brighter the sun shines, the more electricity the system supplies.

Many detached houses, farms and school buildings in Switzerland have solar panels on the roof. You get the most electricity when the panels face **south** and are tilted. What the house does not need at the moment flows into the **power grid** and is used there by others. Some houses also store solar electricity in a battery in the cellar.

In winter there is often fog for weeks on the Swiss Plateau, while the sun shines in the mountains. The air is clearer there, and the snow also reflects extra light onto the panels. That is why **alpine solar systems** are also being built in Switzerland, for example on the dam wall of the Muttsee in the canton of Glarus. Such systems supply electricity precisely when it is scarce in winter.

Solar cells are not only found on roofs. **Satellites** and the International Space Station get their electricity from large solar wings. Parking ticket machines, road signs and garden lamps also often run on solar power. In sunny countries there are huge **solar farms** with hundreds of thousands of panels on open land.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technology for making electricity directly from sunlight.
A panel made of many solar cells connected together.
A device that turns direct current from the panels into alternating current for the socket.
The network of lines that brings electricity from power stations to houses.

gewusst: Solar panels supply a little more electricity in the cold than in great heat.
Even on cloudy days solar systems still produce some electricity.
In one hour the Sun sends more energy to the Earth than the whole of humanity uses in a year.

teile.einleitung: Household electricity use is the electrical energy a family needs at home for light, cooking, washing and appliances. It is measured in kilowatt-hours, and the electricity company sends a bill for it every year. With a little arithmetic and a few simple tricks you can find out which appliances use a lot and where you can save.
wichtigste: Energy is calculated as power times time, for example in kilowatt-hours.
A 2000 W kettle uses 0.1 kWh in 3 minutes.
A 10 W LED lamp used for 5 hours a day uses 18.25 kWh in a year.
If you replace a 60 W light bulb with an 8 W LED, you save 0.208 kWh in 4 hours.
An old appliance that constantly uses 150 W needs 1314 kWh a year.
Putting a lid on the pan saves electricity when cooking.
Appliances that run around the clock, such as a router, also add up to a lot of energy.

abschnitte.text: Every electrical appliance needs energy to work. How much energy an appliance needs per second is called its **power**, given in watts. The **energy** used is power times time. It is usually measured in kilowatt-hours, where one kilowatt-hour equals 1000 watts for one hour.

A 2000 W kettle, that is 2 kW, runs for 3 minutes, that is 0.05 hours, and uses 2 times 0.05 = 0.1 kWh. A 1500 W hairdryer used for 15 minutes every day uses 11.25 kWh in 30 days. A 2 W router running around the clock uses 1.44 kWh in 30 days. A washing machine using 0.5 kWh per wash costs 25 centimes for two washes at 25 centimes per kWh.

Appliances that heat or cool use a lot of electricity, such as the cooker, oven, tumble dryer, fridge and freezer. An electric **water heater** for hot water also uses a lot of energy. Small appliances such as a phone charger, on the other hand, use only a little. But appliances that run all the time, such as an old appliance with 150 W, add up to 1314 kWh in a year.

Depending on its size and heating, a household in Switzerland usually uses between about 2000 and 5000 kWh of electricity a year. Anyone who heats with a **heat pump** or charges an electric car uses much more. In 2026 the electricity price for many households was about 25 to 30 centimes per kWh, but it differs from one municipality to another. The **electricity meter** shows how much has been used.

An old **light bulb** turns most of its energy into heat and only a little into light. An **LED lamp** gives the same amount of light with far fewer watts. If you replace a 60 W bulb with an 8 W LED, you save 0.208 kWh in 4 hours. When buying new appliances, the **energy label** with letters from A to G shows how economical an appliance is.

When cooking, a **lid** on the pan saves a lot of energy, because the heat does not escape. Switching off the light when nobody is in the room also helps. Washing can often be done at 30 or 40 degrees instead of 60 degrees and dried in the air. Appliances on standby are best switched off completely with a power strip.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much energy an appliance needs per second, measured in watts.
Unit of energy, 1000 watts for one hour.
Coloured label that shows how economical an appliance is.
Light-emitting diode, a very economical source of light.

gewusst: With one kilowatt-hour you can bring about 10 litres of water to the boil in a kettle or keep a 10 W LED lamp shining for 100 hours.
A fridge runs day and night all year, which is why an economical model is especially worthwhile.
A light bulb gets so hot because it gives off most of its energy as heat.

teile.einleitung: Hydrostatic pressure is the pressure that builds up in a liquid or a gas because of the weight of the substance above. The deeper you dive, the greater it becomes. The air above us also presses on everything with its weight: that is air pressure.
wichtigste: Hydrostatic pressure is caused by the weight of the liquid or air above.
In water the pressure rises by about 1 bar for every 10 m of depth.
Pressure is measured in pascals; one pascal is one newton per square metre.
Standard air pressure at sea level is 1013.25 hPa.
At standard pressure, the mercury column of a barometer stands about 760 mm high.
A suction pump can lift water at most about 10 m.
Evangelista Torricelli invented the mercury barometer, and Otto von Guericke showed the force of air pressure.

abschnitte.text: Imagine there is a column of water above you, pressing on you with its weight. The taller this column, the greater the **hydrostatic pressure**, also called the pressure due to gravity. It depends only on the depth, the density of the liquid and the Earth's gravity. The shape of the container does not matter; this is known as the **hydrostatic paradox**.

Hydrostatic pressure equals density times gravitational acceleration times depth. In water 2 m deep it is about 19,600 **pascals**. On the 10 m² floor of such a pool, a force of about 196 kN therefore acts, without counting the air pressure. That is equal to the weight of about 20 tonnes.

Air has weight too and creates its own pressure: **air pressure**. At sea level it averages 1013.25 hectopascals. Higher up, for example on a mountain top, there is less air above, so the pressure there is lower. Air pressure can hold up a column of water about 10 m high, which is why a suction pump cannot lift water any higher.

In 1643 the Italian Evangelista Torricelli filled a glass tube with mercury and stood it upside down in a dish. The mercury sank to a height of about 760 mm, and so the first **barometer** was created. Around 1654 Otto von Guericke, the mayor of Magdeburg, put two half spheres together and pumped the air out. Afterwards even teams of horses could hardly pull the **Magdeburg hemispheres** apart.

Dams are much thicker at the bottom than at the top, because water pressure increases with depth. Divers feel the pressure on their ears only a few metres under water and have to equalise the pressure. Water towers use hydrostatic pressure so that water flows from the pipes into the houses. Submarines also have to be built to withstand the enormous pressure in the deep.

begriffe.erklaerung: The pressure in a still liquid caused by the weight of the liquid above.
Unit of pressure, 1 newton per square metre.
Instrument for measuring air pressure.
100 pascals, the usual unit in weather forecasts.

gewusst: At the deepest point of the ocean, about 11,000 m below the sea surface, the pressure is over a thousand times as great as at the surface.
The Grande Dixence in Valais is one of the highest dams in the world and much wider at the bottom than at the top.
Air pressure presses on every square centimetre of your skin about as hard as a weight of one kilogram.

teile.einleitung: A toaster is an electric kitchen appliance that toasts slices of bread. Glowing heating wires make the bread brown and crispy in a few minutes. When the toast is ready, it pops up by itself.
wichtigste: A toaster makes bread brown and crispy.
Inside the toaster heating wires glow red.
When the bread is ready, it pops up.
With the dial you control how brown the bread gets.
If you toast for too long, the bread turns black.
You must never put a metal fork into a toaster that is switched on.
Breadcrumbs collect at the bottom of the toaster.
On some toasters you can put a rack for warming rolls.

abschnitte.text: A toaster usually has two or four slots at the top into which you put slices of bread. When you press the lever down, the bread sinks into the appliance and the heating switches on. After one to three minutes the bread is brown and crispy. Then it pops up again with a click. Toasted bread is called **toast**.

Inside there are thin **heating wires**, usually made of a mixture of nickel and chromium. When current flows through them, they get so hot that they glow red. They give off **heat radiation**, which heats the surface of the bread. A timer or a heat sensor notices when the bread is ready and releases a spring that makes the bread shoot up. With the **dial** you set how long it toasts and how brown the bread should become.

At high heat, sugar and protein on the surface of the bread react with each other. This **Maillard reaction** creates the brown colour and the lovely toasted smell. Water also evaporates, which is why the toast becomes crispy. If you toast for too long, the bread chars and turns black. Burnt bread tastes bitter and should not be eaten.

You must never put a metal fork or knife into a toaster that is switched on. The heating wires are live, and you could get a dangerous **electric shock**. If a slice gets stuck, you first pull out the plug and wait until the appliance has cooled down. The **crumb tray** at the bottom should be emptied regularly, because old crumbs can burn and smoke. A toaster should never be near curtains or paper.

In the past bread was toasted over an open fire or on the stove. Electric toasters have existed since the end of the 19th century, but at first they had to be watched by hand. Around 1920 the American Charles Strite invented a toaster that pops the bread out automatically. Today there are also toasters with a **bun rack**, on which you can warm up croissants and rolls.

begriffe.erklaerung: Wire that gets hot when current flows through it.
Chemical change that turns food brown when it is heated.
Small drawer at the bottom of the toaster that catches crumbs.
When electric current flows through the body, which can be dangerous.

gewusst: The English word “toast” goes back to the Latin word for roasting.
The heating wires in a toaster get several hundred degrees hot.
There are toasters that toast pictures or patterns onto the bread.

teile.einleitung: Steel is a very strong and versatile material made mainly of iron. Bridges, cars, rails, tools and saucepans are made from it. Although steel is much heavier than water, huge ships made of steel can float.
wichtigste: Steel is a mixture of iron and a little carbon, usually under 2 per cent.
Steel is about eight times heavier than the same amount of water.
It is very strong, but can also be bent, forged and rolled.
Additives such as chromium make steel stainless.
Steel is made in blast furnaces and electric furnaces.
Steel can be recycled almost endlessly.
Ships made of steel float because they are hollow inside and push aside a lot of water.

abschnitte.text: Steel is an **alloy**, that is, a mixture of metals or of a metal with other substances. The main part is **iron**, with a small amount of **carbon** added. The carbon makes the soft iron much harder and stronger. Depending on additives such as chromium, nickel or manganese, thousands of different kinds of steel are made for different purposes.

A cube of steel with sides of 10 centimetres weighs almost 8 kilograms, while the same amount of water weighs only 1 kilogram. That is why a steel nail sinks in water at once. But a ship made of steel is mostly filled with air inside. It pushes aside so much water that **buoyancy** carries its weight. This principle was described by the Greek scientist **Archimedes** more than 2000 years ago.

First, liquid pig iron is produced from iron ore and coke in a **blast furnace**; it still contains too much carbon. Then oxygen is blown into it so that part of the carbon burns away, and steel is created. Today a lot of steel is also melted from scrap in an **electric furnace**. The liquid steel is then poured into moulds or rolled into sheets and bars.

Ordinary steel rusts when it comes into contact with water and air. If you add at least about 10.5 per cent **chromium**, a wafer-thin protective layer forms on the surface. This **stainless steel** is used for sinks, cutlery, saucepans and equipment in hospitals. Other steels are protected with paint or a layer of zinc.

Steel is found in bridges, skyscrapers, railway lines, cars, bicycles and tools. In **reinforced concrete**, steel bars strengthen the concrete so that buildings and tunnels are stable. In Switzerland there are steelworks, for example in Gerlafingen in the canton of Solothurn and in Emmenbrücke in the canton of Lucerne. They make their steel mainly from scrap.

Steel is one of the most recycled materials in the world. Old cars, tin cans and girders can be melted down and turned into new steel. Because steel is magnetic, it can easily be sorted out of rubbish with large **magnets**. Recycling saves a lot of energy and raw materials.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of a metal with other metals or substances.
A very tall furnace in which liquid iron is obtained from iron ore.
Especially pure or rust-free steel, for example for cutlery and saucepans.
Shows how heavy a substance is in relation to its size.

gewusst: Steel is about eight times as heavy as water, yet container ships made of steel float.
Steel can be melted down again and again without getting worse.
More than 2000 years ago smiths in various parts of the world were already making simple steel.

teile.einleitung: A spotting scope is a telescope for one eye that lets you watch animals and landscapes from a great distance. It magnifies much more than binoculars and still shows an upright image that is the right way round. In Switzerland it is used, for example, by game wardens, hunters and birdwatchers.
wichtigste: A spotting scope is a one-eyed observation telescope for nature.
A typical spotting scope magnifies about 20 to 60 times.
Prisms inside turn the image the right way round again.
Because of the strong magnification it is usually put on a tripod.
With a zoom eyepiece the magnification can be changed smoothly.
Taking photos through a spotting scope is called digiscoping.
The German word Spektiv comes from the Latin “spectare”, which means to look.

abschnitte.text: A spotting scope is a **telescope** for observing things on Earth, not mainly for the stars. You look into it with only one eye, unlike **binoculars** with their two tubes. In return a spotting scope usually magnifies about 20 to 60 times, binoculars only about 8 to 10 times. It is often waterproof and robustly built so that it can stand up to any weather outdoors.

At the front a large lens, the **objective**, collects the light. A simple astronomical telescope shows the image upside down. In a spotting scope, glass **prisms** redirect the light several times and turn the image upright and the right way round again. At the back the **eyepiece** magnifies the image for the eye.

At 40 times magnification, every tiny tremble of your hand also becomes 40 times bigger. That is why a spotting scope almost always stands on a **tripod**. Many devices have a **zoom eyepiece**, which lets you set the magnification smoothly. You first look for the animal with low magnification and then zoom in closer.

In the Swiss Alps, **game wardens** use spotting scopes to count ibex, chamois and red deer from a great distance without disturbing them. Hunters use them to check whether an animal is old or young. On the shores of Lake Constance or Lake Neuchâtel, birdwatchers recognise rare water birds. Sport shooters also use spotting scopes to see the hits on the target from far away.

If you hold a camera or a mobile phone to the eyepiece, you can take photos through the spotting scope. This technique is called **digiscoping**. It produces pictures of shy animals that you could otherwise only take with very expensive telephoto lenses. There are special holders for mobile phones so that the camera sits exactly behind the eyepiece.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lens you look into on a telescope.
The large front lens that collects the light.
A cut piece of glass that redirects light and here turns the image round.
A stand with three legs on which a device stands steady.

gewusst: With a good spotting scope you can still recognise an ibex several kilometres away.
With a spotting scope, ornithologists can even read the fine rings on birds' legs from a distance.
A spotting scope with a large objective lens still shows a bright image at dusk.

teile.einleitung: Total internal reflection means that light is completely sent back at a boundary, as if by a perfect mirror. This happens when light tries to pass at a very steep slant from a denser substance such as water or glass into a less dense substance such as air. Thanks to total internal reflection, diamonds sparkle and data races through fibre-optic cables.
wichtigste: Total internal reflection only happens when light tries to go from the optically denser to the optically less dense medium.
The angle of incidence must be greater than the so-called critical angle.
For light going from water into air the critical angle is about 49 degrees.
In total internal reflection practically all the light is sent back.
For the critical angle: sin θ equals n2 divided by n1.
Diamonds sparkle so strongly because their critical angle is only about 24 degrees.
Optical fibres, binoculars and bicycle reflectors use total internal reflection.

abschnitte.text: When light passes from one substance into another, it is usually refracted, that is, bent. A small part is always reflected as well. But if the light hits a boundary with air at a very steep slant from water or glass, nothing gets out at all. Then **practically all the light** is sent back, and this is called **total internal reflection**.

Whether a substance is optically dense is shown by its **refractive index** n: air has about 1.0, water about 1.33 and ordinary glass about 1.5. Total internal reflection only happens when light goes from the denser to the less dense medium. The **critical angle** is calculated with sin θ equals n2 divided by n1. For glass with n equal to 1.50 against air this gives about 41.8 degrees, and for flint glass with n equal to 1.70 about 36.0 degrees. Light going from air into water, on the other hand, can never be totally reflected.

A diver looking upwards at a steep slant sees the water surface as a **silver mirror**. Fish and stones from the bottom are reflected in it. Only in a circular window directly above can the diver see the sky. Outside this window the angle is greater than about 49 degrees, and total internal reflection takes place.

Diamond has a very high refractive index of about 2.42 and therefore a small critical angle of only about **24 degrees**. Light that enters a cut diamond is totally reflected many times inside. Only at certain surfaces does it come out again, often split into rainbow colours. The **brilliant cut** is calculated precisely so that as much light as possible comes back out of the top.

In an **optical fibre** light travels through a thin glass core and is totally reflected again and again at its edge. In this way it can even be guided round bends and travel many kilometres. Today internet data flows through such cables at enormous speed. In **prism binoculars**, too, glass prisms redirect the light by total internal reflection, and bicycle reflectors send light back in this way.

If you shine a laser pointer into a jet of water, the light follows the **curved jet of water**. This so-called light fountain was demonstrated by the Geneva physicist **Jean-Daniel Colladon** as early as around 1842. The light stays trapped in the jet, because it is totally reflected at the surface again and again. Modern fibre-optic cables work on the same principle.

begriffe.erklaerung: Number that shows how strongly a substance slows down and bends light.
Angle of incidence beyond which no light gets out and everything is sent back.
A substance in which light is slower, such as water compared with air.
Hair-thin glass thread that carries light over long distances.

gewusst: With flexible optical fibres doctors can look into the stomach without operating.
A single optical fibre is often thinner than a human hair.
The silvery shine of an air bubble in water also comes from total internal reflection.

teile.einleitung: A star is a huge, glowing ball of gas that produces its own light. In the night sky stars look like tiny points of light, because they are unimaginably far away. Our Sun is a star too.
wichtigste: Stars are huge balls of hot gas that shine by themselves.
The Sun is the star closest to the Earth.
Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky.
The Pole Star is almost exactly in the north.
The Plough is a well-known group of stars that looks like a cart with a handle.
Our galaxy is called the Milky Way and contains many billions of stars.
The hottest stars shine blue, cooler stars reddish.

abschnitte.text: A **star** is an enormous ball of gas, mainly hydrogen and helium. Inside it atomic nuclei fuse, and this produces light and heat. In this it differs from planets and moons, which only reflect the light of a star. The nearest star after the Sun is called Proxima Centauri. Its light takes a little over four years to reach us.

Stars shine in different **colours**, and the colour reveals the temperature. The hottest stars are blue or bluish white, medium ones like the Sun yellowish, cooler ones orange or red. There are tiny dwarf stars and giant stars that are a hundred times bigger than the Sun. An example of a red giant is Betelgeuse in the constellation of Orion. Stars live for millions to billions of years.

Our Sun belongs to a huge island of stars, the **Milky Way**. It is a galaxy shaped like a flat spiral and probably contains more than a hundred billion stars. On a clear, dark night you can see it as a bright, milky band across the sky. In the mountains of Switzerland, far from city lights, it can be seen especially well. In space there are countless other galaxies.

Thousands of years ago people were already joining stars together into **constellations**. The Plough is made of seven bright stars and looks like a cart with a handle. If you extend the back edge of the cart about five times, you find the **Pole Star**. It is almost exactly above the North Pole and therefore hardly seems to move. In the past sailors and travellers used it to find north at night.

**Sirius** in the constellation of the Great Dog is the brightest star in the night sky. It is a little over eight light years away, which makes it one of our neighbours. Vega, Arcturus and Rigel are also among the brightest stars. The Pleiades are a star cluster in which you can make out about six or seven stars with the naked eye. When a star seems to twinkle, this is because of the restless air of the Earth's atmosphere.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance that light travels in one year, almost ten trillion kilometres.
A huge collection of billions of stars, for example the Milky Way.
A group of stars that you join together in your mind to form a figure.
A star that is almost exactly in the north and is used to find your way.

gewusst: When you look at a star, you see light that was sent out years or even thousands of years ago.
Shooting stars are not stars at all, but small lumps of rock that burn up in the air.
The Pole Star is not the brightest star at all; it only stands out because it is always in the same place.

teile.einleitung: A fuse is a protective part in an electric circuit that cuts off the current when too much of it flows. In this way it stops cables from overheating and fires from starting. Every flat in Switzerland has a fuse box.
wichtigste: A fuse breaks the circuit when too much current flows.
It protects wires from overheating and prevents fires.
Fuses with a melting wire contain a thin wire that melts through.
Circuit breakers switch off and can be switched on again.
A residual current device protects people from dangerous electric shocks.
A fuse is triggered by a short circuit or by too many appliances at the same time.

abschnitte.text: If too much current flows through a cable, it gets hot. In the worst case the insulation melts and a fire starts. A **fuse** prevents this by breaking the circuit before it becomes dangerous. You can imagine it as a guard who slams the door shut at once when there is danger.

abschnitte.titel: The fuse with a melting wire
abschnitte.text: The oldest form is the **fuse with a melting wire**. Inside it is a thin wire that gets hot when there is too much current and melts through. This breaks the circuit, and the fuse has to be replaced. Such fuses are still found today in cars and in many electrical appliances.

In modern flats the fuse box usually contains **circuit breakers**, also called automatic fuses. When there is an overload or a short circuit, a lever flips down and cuts off the current. Once you have fixed the cause, you can simply flip the lever back up. Each circuit breaker protects a certain area, such as the kitchen or a room.

A **residual current device**, in Switzerland often called an FI switch, mainly protects people. It notices when current is flowing away along the wrong path, for example through a body. Then it switches off in a fraction of a second. In Switzerland it is required in bathrooms and for outdoor sockets.

A fuse often trips when too many powerful appliances such as a kettle, a hairdryer and an oven are running at the same time. A **short circuit** in a faulty cable also makes it react at once. If the same fuse keeps tripping, an electrician should take a look. In Switzerland only professionals are allowed to work on the electrical installation of a house.

begriffe.erklaerung: A direct connection between the poles without an appliance, through which a very large current flows.
More current flows for a longer time than the wire can take.
The box in a flat that holds all the fuses.
A safety switch that switches off at once when there are fault currents and protects people.

gewusst: In the past some people repaired blown fuses with wire, which is very dangerous and can cause fires.
An FI switch reacts to fault currents of just 30 milliamperes, which is a very small current.

teile.einleitung: A telescope is an instrument that collects light from very distant objects and so makes them look brighter and bigger. With telescopes people observe the Moon, planets, stars and distant galaxies. For more than 400 years they have been changing our picture of the universe.
wichtigste: A telescope collects light so that you can see distant stars.
The part you look into is called the eyepiece.
A reflecting telescope uses a curved mirror instead of a large lens.
Large telescopes are built on high mountains, because air and clouds get in the way less there.
The Hubble Space Telescope has been orbiting the Earth since 1990.
The James Webb Space Telescope was launched into space on 25 December 2021.
You must never look at the Sun through a telescope; you could be blinded instantly.
The Urania in Zurich is a well-known public observatory.

abschnitte.text: A telescope works like a big funnel for light. Its opening, the **objective**, collects much more light than our small eye. This makes even very faint stars visible. At the other end you look through the **eyepiece**, a small lens that magnifies the image. The bigger the opening of a telescope, the fainter and finer the things it can show.

There are two basic designs. A **refracting telescope**, or refractor, focuses the light with glass lenses. A **reflecting telescope**, or reflector, uses a curved mirror for this. Large mirrors are easier to build than huge lenses, which is why all large research telescopes today are reflecting telescopes. Around 1668 Isaac Newton built one of the first usable reflecting telescopes.

Around 1608 the first telescopes were built in the Netherlands. As early as 1609 the Italian scientist **Galileo Galilei** pointed a telescope he had built himself at the sky. He discovered craters on the Moon and four moons circling Jupiter. These observations helped to show that not everything circles the Earth.

The Earth's air shimmers and swallows part of the light, and clouds and city lights also get in the way. That is why large **observatories** are built on high, dry mountains, for example in the Atacama Desert in Chile. In Switzerland there are observatories such as the one on the Gornergrat near Zermatt. In the middle of Zurich there is the public observatory **Urania**, where everyone can look through a telescope.

Space telescopes work without any troublesome air at all. The **Hubble Space Telescope** has been orbiting the Earth since 1990 and has a mirror 2.4 metres across. On 25 December 2021 the **James Webb Space Telescope** was launched; its golden mirror measures 6.5 metres. It mainly observes infrared light and is about 1.5 million kilometres from the Earth. With it you can see some of the first galaxies that formed after the Big Bang.

You must never look at the Sun through a telescope or binoculars. The focused sunlight can badly injure the eye in an instant and make you blind. The Sun is only observed with special **solar filters** in front of the opening or by projecting it onto a sheet of paper. It is best to have experts at an observatory show you how to do it safely.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lens through which you look into a telescope.
The large opening with a lens or mirror that collects the light.
Building with telescopes for observing the sky.
Heat radiation that our eyes cannot see.

gewusst: The Extremely Large Telescope in Chile is to have a main mirror 39 metres across.
The light of some galaxies that the James Webb Telescope sees has been travelling for more than 13 billion years.
With a simple telescope Galileo Galilei discovered four moons of Jupiter.

teile.einleitung: The shoe sole is the bottom part of a shoe that touches the ground. It protects the foot, and its tread makes sure you do not slip. Depending on the sport and the surface, soles look very different.
wichtigste: Many shoe soles are made of rubber, because rubber grips the ground well.
A chunky tread gives walking boots better grip on earth and stones.
With smooth, worn soles you slip more easily.
When worn for a long time, the tread of a sole becomes flatter.
Footballers wear shoes with studs on grass.
Climbing shoes have a soft rubber sole that moulds itself to the rock.
Socks are slippery on parquet, which is why non-slip socks have rubber dots.

abschnitte.text: A shoe sole often consists of several layers. The **outsole** touches the ground, and above it lies the midsole, which cushions impacts. Inside the shoe there is usually also a soft insole. In sports shoes, the midsole is often made of light foam.

To be able to walk, you need **friction** between sole and ground. Rubber is soft and adapts to small bumps, which is why it grips well. The **tread**, with its grooves and knobs, digs into soft ground and channels away water and mud. If the sole is worn and smooth, the friction becomes smaller and you slip more easily.

Walking boots have a chunky, deep tread for grip on paths and rocks. Football boots have **studs** that dig into the grass. Climbing shoes have a soft, smooth rubber sole that puts a large area onto the rock. Indoor shoes have light-coloured soles, so that they do not leave black marks on the floor.

In socks on parquet or tiles you quickly slip, because fabric is smooth. **Non-slip socks** have rubber dots on the underside that improve grip. They are especially useful for small children and older people. With many soles, wet floors also become dangerously slippery.

In the past, soles were mostly made of leather or wood. Only after Charles Goodyear discovered the **vulcanisation** of natural rubber in 1839 did rubber become durable enough for shoes. Today, soles are also made of plastics such as polyurethane. For mountain boots, especially grippy rubber compounds developed in Italy are well known.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pattern of grooves and knobs on the underside of the sole.
A force that stops two surfaces from sliding easily over each other.
Pegs under sports shoes that press into the ground.
A process that turns natural rubber into firm, elastic rubber.

gewusst: The well-known yellow Vibram mountain boot sole was invented in Italy in 1937.
From the tread of footprints, investigators can sometimes tell which shoe left them.
Climbing shoes are worn so tight that the toes are slightly curled.

teile.einleitung: A transistor is a tiny electronic component that can switch and amplify electric current. Without transistors there would be no mobile phones, computers or games consoles. A modern chip contains billions of them.
wichtigste: Transistors have two main jobs: amplifying and switching.
They are made of semiconductors, usually silicon.
The transistor was invented in 1947 at Bell Labs in the USA.
A bipolar transistor has the terminals emitter, base and collector.
A field-effect transistor has the terminals source, gate and drain.
The MOSFET is the basic building block of almost all today's computer chips.
CMOS technology combines two kinds of MOSFET and so saves electricity.
Modern transistors are smaller than a virus.

abschnitte.text: A transistor is an electronic **component** with three terminals. With a small current or a small voltage at one terminal, you control a much larger current between the other two. You can imagine it as a tap that you turn on and off with your little finger. In this way the transistor can work as a **switch** or as an **amplifier**.

Transistors are made of **semiconductors** such as silicon. By deliberately adding foreign atoms, which is called **doping**, n-layers with extra electrons and p-layers with gaps for electrons are created. An npn transistor has the layers n, p, n. In a pnp transistor it is exactly the other way round.

In a **bipolar transistor** a small base current flows and controls a much larger collector current. The ratio is called the **current gain**. If a transistor has a current gain of 100, it turns 0.2 milliamperes of base current into 20 milliamperes of collector current. In this way, for example, quiet signals in loudspeakers and radios are made louder.

In computers transistors work as lightning-fast switches for zero and one. Almost all chips are made of **MOSFETs**, special field-effect transistors with source, gate and drain. **CMOS** technology combines n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs so that hardly any current flows when they are at rest. Modern transistors use the **FinFET** design, with an upright fin that the gate wraps around on three sides.

The first transistor was built in 1947 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley at Bell Labs. They received the **Nobel Prize** in Physics for it in 1956. Before that, large, hot **valves** were needed, which used a lot of electricity. The transistor made devices such as the pocket radio possible.

Transistors are among the most frequently made things that people have ever built. In a smartphone chip many billions of them work at the same time. Thanks to ever smaller transistors, computers have become faster, cheaper and more economical. This technology is also found in cars, washing machines and hearing aids.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance such as silicon that conducts electricity sometimes well and sometimes badly.
Deliberately building foreign atoms into a semiconductor.
A field-effect transistor, the basic building block of almost all chips.
How many times bigger the controlled current is than the controlling current.

gewusst: The name transistor is made up of the English words transfer and resistor.
The first transistor was about the size of a hand; today billions fit on a fingernail.
Before there were transistors, computers with thousands of valves filled whole rooms.

teile.einleitung: An electricity pylon is a tall framework that carries power lines high above the ground. Large steel pylons stand in long rows across fields, through forests and over mountains. Small wooden poles are often seen in the countryside.
wichtigste: Electricity pylons carry power lines high above the ground.
Large pylons are usually made of steel.
Small poles in the countryside are often made of wood.
The lines hang high up so that nobody can touch them.
The wires hang from insulators, which do not let electricity through.
You must never climb up an electricity pylon.
Storks sometimes build their nests on electricity pylons.

abschnitte.text: An **electricity pylon**, in technical language a transmission tower, carries the conductor cables of a power line. The large pylons for high voltage are often 40 to 80 metres tall. They are made of a **steel lattice**, that is, many steel struts joined into triangles. This makes them stable and yet fairly light.

For low voltages in the countryside **wooden poles** are often used, treated with preservatives against rot. There are also concrete poles. At the end of a line, or where it changes direction, there are especially strong **tension towers**. In between, lighter suspension towers carry the cables.

The conductor cables do not hang directly from the metal of the pylon, but from **insulators**. These are made of glass, porcelain or plastic and do not let electricity through. They often look like chains of plates. The higher the voltage, the longer the insulators have to be, so that the electricity cannot jump across.

The lines hang so high so that nobody can touch them by accident. With high voltage the electricity can even jump through the air if you get too close. That is why the rule is always: **never climb up**. You also never fly kites or drones near power lines.

In Switzerland many lines run over Alpine passes and through steep valleys. There are often no roads there that lorries can use. That is why the parts of the pylons are flown up by **helicopter**, and fitters put them together high in the air. In winter the pylons also have to withstand heavy loads of snow and ice.

The **white stork** likes to build its large nest on tall pylons, chimneys and roofs. Because birds on pylons can also get an electric shock if their wings touch two parts, electricity companies fit dangerous pylons with protective covers. Sometimes separate nesting poles are also put up for storks next to the electricity pylons. Today many storks breed in Switzerland again, after they almost disappeared in the 20th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technical term for a tower that carries power lines in the air.
Part made of glass, porcelain or plastic that does not let electricity through.
The thick metal cable through which the electricity flows.
Framework of struts joined into triangles.

gewusst: Some pylons are as tall as a tower block with more than 20 storeys.
The shape of many pylons is reminiscent of a fir tree or a giant figure with outstretched arms.
Fitters who work on pylons are secured with harnesses and ropes.

teile.einleitung: A hall of mirrors is a room full of mirrors in which you see yourself many times over, distorted or seemingly endlessly. You often find one at the Chilbi, the Swiss village fair, or in theme parks. Behind the fun there is physics: mirrors reflect light according to fixed rules and can trick our brain.
wichtigste: A hall of mirrors is a room full of mirrors.
In Switzerland halls of mirrors are often found at the Chilbi.
At the Glacier Garden in Lucerne there is a famous mirror maze.
In a mirror maze you easily get lost, because you do not know what is real.
Between two mirrors facing each other you see a great many mirror images one behind the other.
Distorting mirrors make you look fat, thin, tall or small.
In the Palace of Versailles in France there is a famous Hall of Mirrors.

abschnitte.text: A mirror is a very smooth surface, usually glass with a thin layer of metal on the back. Light that falls on it is sent back; this is called **reflection**. The **law of reflection** applies: the angle of incidence is the same as the angle of reflection. Our brain thinks the light comes in a straight line, which is why we see the **mirror image** apparently behind the mirror.

In many halls of mirrors there are **distorting mirrors**, which are not flat but curved. If a mirror curves inwards, the image looks bigger; if it curves outwards, it looks smaller. If a mirror is curved differently at the top than at the bottom, you suddenly see a huge head on tiny legs. Such mirrors make young and old laugh.

If two mirrors face each other exactly, each sends back the image of the other. This creates a great many **mirror images** one behind the other, which get smaller and darker. It looks like an endless tunnel. But it is not truly endless, because each mirror swallows a little light with every reflection.

In a **mirror maze** the walls are made of mirrors and panes of glass. Because the passages are reflected many times, you do not know what is a real path and what is only a reflection. That is why you easily get lost. So that you do not walk into a mirror, you stretch your hands out in front of you and feel your way forward slowly.

At the **Glacier Garden in Lucerne** there is a famous mirror maze in the Moorish style, reminiscent of the Alhambra palace in Spain. It was built for the 1896 Swiss National Exhibition in Geneva and then moved to Lucerne. At fairs such as the **Chilbi** or the autumn fair there are often travelling halls of mirrors. In some science museums, too, you can experiment with mirrors.

abschnitte.titel: The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles
abschnitte.text: One of the most famous rooms with mirrors is the **Hall of Mirrors** in the Palace of Versailles near Paris. King Louis XIV had it built in the 17th century, when large mirrors were extremely expensive. Hundreds of mirrors reflect the light from the windows back into the long hall. The peace treaty after the First World War was signed in the Hall of Mirrors in 1919.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sending back of light at a surface.
The image you see in a mirror; it is reversed.
A curved mirror that distorts the image.
A winding system of passages in which you have to find your way.

gewusst: In a mirror left and right seem to be swapped, but really it is front and back that are swapped.
In the 17th century large mirrors were so expensive that they were seen as a sign of wealth.
A tunnel between two mirrors often looks slightly greenish, because the glass lets through a little green light.

teile.einleitung: A plumb bob is a heavy weight on a string that you let hang freely. Because gravity pulls it downwards, the string points exactly vertically towards the Earth. It is one of the oldest measuring tools in the world and is also called a plumb.
wichtigste: A plumb bob is a weight on a string.
The string of a plumb bob hanging still points exactly vertically downwards.
This is because of gravity, which pulls the weight towards the Earth.
Bricklayers use it to check whether a wall is vertical.
The name comes from the fact that the weight used to be made of lead.
A shorter word for the plumb bob is plumb.
In the past sailors measured the depth of the water with a lead on a long line.

abschnitte.text: If you hang a weight on a string and wait until it is still, **gravity** pulls it exactly towards the centre of the Earth. The string then forms a **vertical**, also called a plumb line. Everywhere on Earth this direction is the direction in which things fall. The weight is often pointed at the bottom so that you can mark an exact point on the ground.

Bricklayers, carpenters and tilers hold the plumb bob against a wall or a post. If the distance between the string and the wall is the same at the top and the bottom, the wall is **vertical**. This is how walls are built that are not crooked and do not fall over. Today spirit levels and lasers are often used as well, but the plumb bob works without any battery.

The master builders of ancient Egypt were already using plumb bobs to build temples and pyramids. The Romans and the builders of the medieval cathedrals knew it too. The name comes from the Latin word for the metal **lead**, which the weight was usually made of in the past. Today plumb bobs are often made of brass or steel.

In the past sailors threw a **lead** on a long, marked line overboard. As soon as it touched the bottom, they could read the depth of the water on the line. In this way they recognised dangerous shallows. Today the depth is measured with an **echo sounder**, which sends sound waves to the bottom and measures the time until the echo returns.

Close to large mountain ranges, a plumb bob does not hang exactly towards the centre of the Earth. The huge mass of the mountains pulls the weight a tiny bit to the side. This **deflection of the vertical** is very small, but must be taken into account in precise land surveys. Surveyors have measured this effect in the Swiss Alps too.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for plumb bob, a weight on a string.
Line that points exactly in the direction of gravity.
Device that measures the depth of water with sound.
Small sideways pull on the plumb bob caused by large masses such as mountains.

gewusst: The word plumb, as in a plumb wall, means exactly the same as vertical.
The direction opposite the plumb line, directly above your head, is called the zenith.
A plumb bob works the same way on the Moon, but there it swings for longer before it comes to rest.

teile.einleitung: Sonography, also called an ultrasound scan, is a method doctors use to look inside the body. Very high sound waves that we cannot hear are sent into the body, and an image is made from their echoes. The principle is similar to the way bats find their way with echoes.
wichtigste: Medical sonography works with ultrasound of a few megahertz.
In the transducer the piezoelectric effect produces the ultrasound and receives the echoes.
From the travel time of the echoes, the device calculates how deep a boundary lies.
For soft tissue a speed of sound of about 1540 m/s is assumed.
In B mode the echoes are put together as shades of grey to form a cross-sectional image.
Sonography uses no ionising radiation, unlike X-rays and computed tomography.
Air-filled lungs and bones are hard to examine with ultrasound.

abschnitte.text: People hear sounds up to about 20,000 vibrations per second, that is 20 kilohertz. Sound with a higher frequency is called **ultrasound**. In medicine, frequencies of a few **megahertz**, that is millions of vibrations per second, are used. Higher frequencies give sharper images, but do not reach as deep.

The most important part is the **transducer**, which is held against the skin. Inside it are crystals that change shape through the **piezoelectric effect** when a current is applied, and so send out sound. When an echo comes back, the crystals do the opposite and produce a small electrical voltage. A gel is put between the transducer and the skin, because even a thin layer of air would reflect the sound back almost completely.

The sound travels into the body, is partly reflected at boundaries between tissues and comes back as an **echo**. The device measures the travel time and calculates with about 1540 m/s. If an echo comes back after 130 microseconds, the sound has travelled about 20 cm there and back, so the boundary is about 10 cm deep. In **B mode** many such echoes are put together as lighter and darker shades of grey to form a moving cross-sectional image.

Ultrasound is used to examine, for example, the heart, liver, kidneys, gall bladder, thyroid and blood vessels. With the **Doppler method** you can even see how fast and in which direction blood is flowing, often shown in colour. Sometimes tiny gas-filled **microbubbles** are injected as a contrast agent, because they reflect sound especially strongly. In engineering, too, ultrasound is used to check workpieces for hidden cracks.

Sonography is painless, quick, fairly cheap and shows movements in real time. A big advantage is that it uses **no ionising radiation**. However, ultrasound does not get through air and bone well, because these reflect or absorb the sound almost completely. That is why other methods are usually needed for the lungs or the brain in adults.

The **piezoelectric effect** was discovered by the brothers Pierre and Jacques Curie in 1880. In the First World War devices were developed to track down submarines with sound, the echo sounder. In the 1940s and 1950s researchers began to use ultrasound for medicine. Today there is an ultrasound machine in almost every doctor's surgery and hospital.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sound with such a high frequency that people cannot hear it.
The device held against the skin that sends and receives sound.
Certain crystals change shape with electricity and produce electricity when pressed.
Sound that is reflected back by a surface.
Method used to measure the speed of flowing blood.

gewusst: Bats and dolphins find their way with ultrasound echoes on a very similar principle.
The gel used in an ultrasound scan is needed because air blocks the sound almost completely.
Today ultrasound devices are so small that they can be connected to a smartphone.

teile.einleitung: In physics transparency means that a substance lets light through so that you can see through it. Window glass, clear water and air are transparent, but a wall is not. Whether something is see-through depends on how its particles deal with light.
wichtigste: A transparent substance lets light through almost unhindered.
Glass is a typical transparent material.
You can see through a window pane because glass lets light through, but a wall does not.
Substances that only let light through scattered are called translucent.
Substances that let no light through at all are called opaque.
A substance can be see-through for visible light but block other radiation.
Light is refracted when it passes into a transparent substance.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “trans” for “through” and “parere” for “to appear”. A **transparent** substance lets light through in such a way that you can make out clear images behind it. Examples are window glass, air, clear water and many plastics such as Perspex. But no substance is perfectly see-through; a small part of the light is always swallowed or sent back.

Three groups are distinguished. Transparent substances such as glass let light through undisturbed. **Translucent** substances such as frosted glass, baking paper or a thin candle let light through but scatter it, so that you only see shadows. **Opaque** substances such as wood, metal or a wall let no light through at all.

Light is made of small packets of energy. The particles in a substance can only swallow light if its energy matches them exactly. In glass, visible light does not match, so it flies through almost unhindered. Because glass also has no grains or fibres, the light is hardly **scattered** either.

When light enters a transparent substance at a slant, it changes direction. This effect is called **refraction**. That is why a straw in a glass of water looks bent. A small part of the light is also reflected at the surface, which is why you can see yourself in the window pane in the evening.

Window glass is see-through for visible light, but holds back a large part of **UV radiation**. That is why you hardly get sunburnt behind a pane of glass. X-rays, on the other hand, pass through skin and muscles, but hardly through bones. This is how X-ray pictures are made.

See-through materials are everywhere: in windows, glasses, camera lenses and screens. **Fibre-optic cables** carry light over many kilometres and so transmit internet data. In nature some animals are almost see-through, for example jellyfish or glass frogs, and protect themselves from enemies in this way. In a figurative sense, people speak of transparency when something is open and easy to follow.

begriffe.erklaerung: See-through; you can see clearly through it.
Light comes through, but you cannot see clear shapes.
Not see-through; no light comes through.
The change in the direction of light when it passes into another substance.

gewusst: The glass frog has such see-through belly skin that you can see its heart beating.
Pure ice is see-through, but snow is white, because the many small crystals scatter light in all directions.
Optical fibres for the internet are so clear that light can travel many kilometres in them.

teile.einleitung: Skis are long, narrow boards that let you glide over snow. They stop you from sinking in deeply and make fast descents and long winter hikes possible. For Switzerland, skiing is an important part of leisure, tourism and sporting history.
wichtigste: With skis you sink in less deeply, because your weight is spread over a large area.
Sharp steel edges on the sides make sure that the skis grip in bends.
Some cross-country skis have scales under the middle so that they do not slip backwards when you push off.
On a ski tour you stick skins under the skis to go uphill.
Beginners brake with the snowplough, in which the ski tips are together.
In the downhill, a ski racer crouches down to have less air resistance.
Most ski resorts in Switzerland are in the Alps.

abschnitte.text: In shoes your whole body weight presses on a small area, and you sink deep into the snow. Skis spread the weight over a much larger **area**, so the pressure on the snow becomes smaller. When gliding, friction creates a wafer-thin film of water under the ski, on which it slides easily. With **ski wax** on the base it glides even better.

On their sides skis have sharp **steel edges**, which dig into the snow and ice in turns. Modern **carving skis** are narrower in the middle than at the front and back, so on their edge they make a curve by themselves. Beginners brake with the **snowplough**: the ski tips point together and the ends apart. In the downhill, racers crouch down so that the air slows them down less.

Alpine skis are built for pistes and are used with stiff boots in a binding. **Cross-country skis** are light and narrow, and the heel stays free. Some have scales under the middle so that they do not slip backwards when you push off. For a **ski tour** you stick skins under the skis and climb uphill under your own steam, then ski down through untouched snow.

Skis are very old: in Scandinavia and Russia skis have been found that are several thousand years old. For a long time they were mainly a way for hunters to get around in winter. Skiing as a sport developed in Norway in the 19th century, for example with the Telemark technique. In Switzerland one of the first ski clubs was founded in Glarus in 1893, and soon afterwards the first ski resorts appeared in the Alps.

Most Swiss ski resorts are in the **Alps**, for example in Zermatt, Davos, St Moritz, Verbier or Adelboden. In the Jura, too, there are smaller ski areas and many cross-country trails. Famous races are the **Lauberhorn race** in Wengen and the World Cup on the Chuenisbärgli in Adelboden. Swiss ski stars such as Vreni Schneider, Lara Gut-Behrami or Marco Odermatt have won many World Cup races.

A **ski helmet** protects your head in falls and is especially important for children. On the piste there are rules, such as skiing at a suitable speed and showing consideration for slower skiers. Away from the marked pistes there is a **risk of avalanches**, so you only ski there with the right equipment and experience. The binding releases in a fall so that you do not injure your legs.

begriffe.erklaerung: The device that holds the ski boot on the ski and opens in falls.
Skis with a narrow middle that turn especially easily.
Strips with slanting hairs under the skis that stop you slipping back when going uphill.
A braking and skiing position in which the ski tips point towards each other.
A prepared track for cross-country skis.

gewusst: Skins for ski touring got their name because seal skins really were used in the past.
In the downhill, racers reach speeds of well over 100 kilometres per hour.
The word ski comes from Norwegian and originally meant a split piece of wood.

teile.einleitung: Thermal energy is the energy contained in the heat of a body. It exists because the tiny particles of a substance are constantly moving and jiggling. The faster they move, the warmer the substance is.
wichtigste: Thermal energy is the kinetic energy of the particles of a substance.
Heat can be transferred by conduction, convection and radiation.
A metal spoon in hot tea also gets warm at the handle through conduction.
A radiator spreads the heat in the room through convection of the air.
The heat of a campfire reaches you through radiation.
To warm 2 kg of water by 10 °C you need 84 kJ.
A heat pump brings heat from the outside air or the ground into the house.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of tiny **particles**, that is atoms and molecules. These particles are never completely still; they jiggle, vibrate and dart about. The energy of this movement is called **thermal energy** or heat energy. The higher the temperature, the faster the particles move. Only at absolute zero, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, would the movement almost come to a stop.

abschnitte.titel: Three ways for heat to travel
abschnitte.text: In **conduction** the particles pass their movement on to their neighbours; this is how a metal spoon in hot tea gets warm right up to the handle. In **convection** warm water or warm air is carried along, as with a radiator, above which the warm air rises and circulates in the room. In **radiation** heat travels without any substance at all; this is how you feel the heat of a campfire or the sun on your skin. Heat always flows from the warmer to the colder body.

Energy is measured in **joules**. To warm 1 kilogram of water by 1 degree Celsius you need about 4.2 kilojoules. So for 2 kilograms of water and 10 degrees it is 2 times 10 times 4.2, which makes 84 kilojoules. Water can store an especially large amount of heat, which is why in many heating systems it is pumped through the radiators as a **heat carrier**.

Houses lose heat through walls, roof and windows. Double or triple-glazed windows keep the heat in better, because the layer between the panes conducts heat poorly. Good **insulation** saves a lot of heating energy. In Switzerland more and more houses are heated with a **heat pump**, which takes heat from the outside air, the ground or groundwater and brings it into the house.

Thermal energy can be turned into other forms of energy. In a power station water is heated into steam, which drives turbines and so produces electricity. The other way round, friction turns kinetic energy into heat; you notice this when you rub your hands together. With every conversion, part of the energy becomes heat that spreads out into the surroundings.

begriffe.erklaerung: Unit of energy.
Passing heat on from particle to particle in a substance.
Transport of heat by flowing air or liquid.
Transfer of heat by invisible rays, with no substance in between.
Device that uses heat from the surroundings for heating.

gewusst: An iceberg contains more thermal energy in total than a cup of hot tea, because it is so huge.
Water needs much more energy to warm up than almost any other substance, which is why lakes warm up slowly in spring.
The heat of the Sun travels through empty space to the Earth as radiation.

teile.einleitung: An inertial force is a force you feel when you are in an accelerating vehicle, for example in a braking bus or a moving lift. It is not caused by another body, but by the inertia of your own body. That is why it is also called a fictitious force.
wichtigste: Inertial forces occur in accelerating frames of reference.
The inertial force points against the acceleration of the system.
If a bus brakes hard, the standing passengers are pushed forwards.
If a lift going down brakes, you feel heavier than usual.
In a freely falling lift, bathroom scales show zero.
D'Alembert's principle brings the inertial force into the balance of forces as an extra force.
An inertial force has no counter-force according to Newton's third law.
Centrifugal force is a well-known inertial force.

abschnitte.text: Anyone sitting in a vehicle that speeds up, brakes or goes round a bend feels a force pushing or pulling them. This force is called an **inertial force** or **fictitious force**. It always points against the acceleration of the vehicle. If a bus brakes hard, the standing passengers are pushed forwards. When a train starts, you are pressed into your seat.

How you explain it depends on the **frame of reference**, that is, on where you are watching from. An observer on the platform sees no mysterious force: the seat accelerates the passenger's inert body forwards, just as the law of inertia says. The passenger in the train, on the other hand, feels pressed into the seat and describes this with an inertial force. Both descriptions lead to the same result. But unlike real forces such as gravity, an inertial force has no **counter-force** according to Newton's third law.

When a lift starts going up or brakes on the way down, you feel heavier, and bathroom scales show more. When it starts going down or brakes on the way up, you feel lighter. If a lift fell freely, the scales would show zero and you would be **weightless**. This is exactly what astronauts experience in the space station, which is constantly falling around the Earth. On parabolic flights in aeroplanes, people also train for weightlessness in this way.

In a bend or on a roundabout you feel a force pushing outwards, the **centrifugal force**. This is also an inertial force, because the body really wants to keep flying in a straight line. A salad spinner and the spin cycle of a washing machine use this effect. Because of the Earth's rotation there is also the **Coriolis force**, which deflects the winds around high and low-pressure areas.

In the 18th century the French mathematician **Jean-Baptiste le Rond d'Alembert** had the idea of simply counting the inertial force as an extra force in the balance of forces. This **d'Alembert's principle** makes many problems in engineering easier. An example: in a car accelerating at 3 metres per second squared, a pendulum hangs at a slant towards the back. Because 3 divided by 9.81 is about 0.31, it leans about 17 degrees away from the vertical.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point of view from which you observe and describe a movement.
Another name for inertial force, because it is not caused by another body.
Inertial force that you feel pushing outwards in bends.
State in which you no longer feel any weight, for example in free fall.

gewusst: Astronauts in the space station do not float because there is no gravity there, but because they are constantly falling around the Earth.
Roller coasters are built so that in loops you are pressed into your seat by inertial forces.
In an emergency stop a body can push forwards with many times its own weight.

teile.einleitung: An aerofoil is a specially shaped wing that keeps an aeroplane in the air. When air flows around it, an upward force is created: lift. Aerofoils are found on aeroplanes, gliders, birds and even on fast boats.
wichtigste: In a flow of air an aerofoil produces an upward force, lift.
The straight line from the front edge to the back edge of a wing section is called the chord line.
If the centre line of the section curves upwards, this is called camber.
Flaps make sure there is enough lift during take-off and landing despite the low speed.
At the wing tips, wingtip vortices form because air flows from the underside to the upper side.
Winglets at the wing tips reduce induced drag.
In the NACA 0012 section, the last two digits give the greatest thickness as a percentage of the chord length.
Otto Lilienthal studied curved wings and made gliding flights from 1891.

abschnitte.text: If you cut straight across an aeroplane wing, you see its **section**: thick and rounded at the front, thin and pointed at the back. The straight line joining the front edge and the back edge is called the **chord line**. If the centre line of the section curves upwards, this is called **camber**. The shape of the section decides how much lift and how much drag a wing produces.

The wing is tilted slightly upwards; this angle is called the **angle of attack**. Because of its shape and the angle of attack, the air is deflected downwards, and in reaction the wing is pushed upwards. Above the wing the air flows faster and the pressure is lower; below the wing the pressure is higher. This difference in pressure gives the **lift**. The faster an aeroplane flies, the greater the lift becomes.

During take-off and landing an airliner flies slowly. Then it extends its **flaps**, which make the wing larger and more strongly curved, so that enough lift is still produced. At the wing tips air flows from the underside, where the pressure is higher, to the upper side, and **wingtip vortices** form. These vortices cost energy, the so-called induced drag. Small upturned **winglets** at the tips reduce it and save fuel.

Sections are often named with numbers, for example from the American NACA series. In the **NACA 0012**, the first two zeros mean that the section is not cambered, that is symmetrical, and 12 means that it is at most 12 per cent as thick as it is long. The **aspect ratio** is also important: wingspan times wingspan divided by wing area. A glider with a wingspan of 20 metres and an area of 16 square metres has an aspect ratio of 25. Long, slender wings like those of gliders glide especially well.

People learned how to fly by watching birds. The German aviation pioneer **Otto Lilienthal** studied curved wings systematically and from 1891 made over a thousand gliding flights with aircraft he built himself. In 1903 the Wright brothers in the USA made the first controlled powered flight. Today the Airbus A380 has wings with a span of almost 80 metres.

The Swiss solar aircraft **Solar Impulse 2** had wings with a span of 72 metres, covered with more than 17,000 solar cells. In 2015 and 2016 Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg flew it around the whole world on solar energy alone. In Stans in the canton of Nidwalden the company Pilatus builds aircraft that are sold to many countries. There are also aerofoils under water, by the way, for example on hydrofoils, which lift themselves out of the water at high speed.

begriffe.erklaerung: Upward force that keeps an aeroplane in the air.
The cross-sectional shape of a wing.
Angle at which the wing is tilted against the flow of air.
Distance from one wing tip to the other.
Small upturned wing tip that saves fuel.

gewusst: The wings of Solar Impulse 2 were wider than those of a jumbo jet, even though the aircraft was only about as heavy as a car.
Wingtip vortices behind large aeroplanes are so strong that following aircraft have to keep their distance.
Otto Lilienthal is regarded as the first person to make repeated successful gliding flights.

teile.einleitung: The tesla is the unit used to measure how strong a magnetic field is. It is named after the inventor Nikola Tesla and belongs to the International System of Units, SI. One tesla is a very strong field, which is why in everyday life people often calculate in millitesla or microtesla.
wichtigste: The tesla is the SI unit of magnetic flux density.
The unit is named after Nikola Tesla, who is known above all for alternating current technology.
In SI base units one tesla equals kg/(A · s²).
One tesla is equivalent to 1 N/(A · m).
One tesla equals 10,000 gauss.
0.25 T is 250 mT, and 0.05 mT is 50 µT.
If you multiply 1 tesla by 1 square metre, you get 1 weber.

abschnitte.text: The tesla, **T** for short, gives the **magnetic flux density**, that is, how strong a magnetic field is at a certain place. A strong field exerts large forces on magnets, iron and moving electric charges. A field of 1 tesla exerts a force of 1 newton on a wire 1 metre long carrying 1 ampere. That is why 1 T equals 1 N/(A · m).

Because a tesla is very large, smaller units are often used. A **millitesla** (mT) is a thousandth of a tesla, a **microtesla** (µT) a millionth. So 0.25 T equals 250 mT, and 0.05 mT equals 50 µT. An older unit is the **gauss**, where 1 tesla equals 10,000 gauss. In SI base units a tesla can be written as kg/(A · s²), and 1 tesla times 1 square metre gives a magnetic flux of 1 weber.

The Earth's magnetic field is weak: at the surface it is only about 25 to 65 microtesla. Even so, it is enough to turn a compass needle towards the north. A small fridge magnet reaches a few millitesla. Strong neodymium magnets reach about one tesla at their surface. An **MRI scanner** in a hospital usually works with 1.5 or 3 tesla, which is tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth's magnetic field.

**Nikola Tesla** was born in 1856 in Smiljan in what is today Croatia and died in New York in 1943. He was a brilliant inventor and electrical engineer. He is known above all for **alternating current technology**, which is used to distribute electricity almost everywhere in the world today. Among other things he developed an alternating current motor and the Tesla coil, which produces huge sparks.

The unit tesla was set in 1960 by the General Conference on Weights and Measures, together with the new International System of Units, SI. Before that, the gauss, named after the mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss, was mainly used in physics. Because the unit is named after a person, its symbol T is always written as a capital letter.

begriffe.erklaerung: Quantity that shows how strong a magnetic field is at a certain place.
The International System of Units with the metre, kilogram, second and more.
Older unit for magnetic fields; 10,000 gauss are 1 tesla.
Unit for the magnetic flux through a surface.
Current that keeps changing its direction.

gewusst: The strongest magnets in research laboratories reach more than 40 tesla continuously.
The Earth's magnetic field is about 50,000 times weaker than 1 tesla.
The car maker Tesla also takes its name from Nikola Tesla.
