teile.einleitung: A transformer is an electrical device that raises or lowers the voltage of alternating current. Without transformers, electricity could not be carried over long distances from the power station to your socket. Many chargers also contain a small transformer.
wichtigste: A transformer changes the voltage of alternating current.
It consists of two coils and a shared iron core.
It works through a constantly changing magnetic field that induces a voltage.
The ratio of the numbers of turns decides how much the voltage is changed.
An ordinary transformer does not work with direct current.
High voltage makes carrying electricity over long distances low in losses.
In Switzerland household electricity comes out of the socket at 230 volts.

abschnitte.text: A transformer converts electrical voltage without anything moving. It can step a voltage up or down. The word comes from the Latin “transformare”, which means “to change the shape of”. Transformers come tiny in chargers and huge in **substations**.

A transformer has two coils of wire wound around a shared **iron core**. When alternating current flows through the first coil, the primary coil, a magnetic field forms that is constantly changing. This changing field produces a new voltage in the second coil, the secondary coil. This process is called **induction**.

How much the voltage is changed depends on the ratio of the **numbers of turns**. If the second coil has ten times more turns than the first, the voltage there is ten times higher. At the same time the current becomes about ten times smaller, because energy does not come from nowhere. A good large transformer loses only very little energy in the process.

abschnitte.titel: From the power station to the socket
abschnitte.text: For transport, electricity is brought up to **high voltage**, in Switzerland up to 380,000 volts. This means that less current flows through the lines, and less energy is lost as heat. In substations and transformer stations in the neighbourhood the voltage is lowered step by step. At the end, 230 volts come out of the socket.

The basis, electromagnetic induction, was discovered by the Englishman Michael Faraday in 1831. Usable transformers for power grids were developed in the 1880s by, among others, engineers of the Ganz company in Budapest. Thanks to them, **alternating current** won out over direct current. To this day transformers are at the heart of every power grid.

You can find small transformers in the power supplies of model railways, doorbells and older chargers. Modern mobile phone chargers work with switched-mode power supplies, which also contain a small transformer. Large transformers in substations can be as heavy as several lorries. Because they get warm, they are often cooled with **oil**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The electrical “pressure” that drives the current, measured in volts.
A wound-up wire that can produce a magnetic field.
The creation of a voltage by a changing magnetic field.
A facility in which large transformers change the voltage in the power grid.

gewusst: The typical hum of a transformer happens because the iron core vibrates very slightly in time with the alternating current.
A transformer has no moving parts and can therefore work for decades.
In Switzerland the railway runs on a voltage of 15,000 volts, which is stepped down by a transformer in the locomotive.

teile.einleitung: Schwingen is a traditional Swiss form of wrestling and counts as a national sport. Two wrestlers grab each other by their wrestling shorts and try to put their opponent on his back. Strength, technique and a lot of physics play a part, such as balance and leverage.
wichtigste: Schwingen is a traditional Swiss form of wrestling.
A bout takes place in a round ring with sawdust.
The sawdust cushions the falls.
Over their clothes, wrestlers pull on short trousers made of strong cloth, the wrestling shorts.
The wrestlers grab each other by these shorts.
A wrestler stands low with his legs wide apart, because this makes him more stable.
The winner is the one who brings his opponent to the ground with both shoulder blades.
The biggest festival is the Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival.

abschnitte.text: Schwingen is a kind of **wrestling** that has been popular with herders and farmers in Switzerland for centuries. A bout is called a **Gang** and usually lasts only a few minutes. At the start, each wrestler grabs the belt of his opponent's wrestling shorts with his right hand and the rolled-up trouser leg with his left. Then both try to bring the other to the ground with a throw. The bout is won when the opponent touches the ground with both **shoulder blades**.

The fight takes place in a round ring thickly covered with **sawdust**. The soft sawdust cushions the falls and so protects against injuries. Over their clothes the wrestlers wear short trousers made of strong drill, a tough fabric. Sennen wrestlers traditionally fight in dark trousers and coloured shirts, gymnast wrestlers all in white. After the bout the winner often brushes the sawdust off the loser's back as a sign of respect.

A wrestler stands low with his legs wide apart, so his **centre of gravity** is close to the ground and above a wide base. This makes him much harder to knock over. In a throw he uses **leverage**, for example by pushing his hip under his opponent and tipping him over it. Well-known throws are called Kurz, Hüfter, Brienzer or Übersprung. Whoever cleverly uses the opponent's momentum needs less strength of his own.

The season is made up of many wrestling festivals in all parts of the country, often in the open air with music and yodelling. Every three years the **Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival** takes place, one of the biggest sporting events in Switzerland. The best wrestler there is crowned **king of Schwingen**. The best competitors receive a wreath of oak leaves. The traditional winner's prize is a live bull, the Siegermuni.

**Stone throwing** is often also part of the wrestling festivals. The best known stone is the Unspunnen stone, which weighs over 80 kilograms and is thrown at the Unspunnen Festival near Interlaken. The Federal Wrestling Association was founded in 1895 and organises the big festivals. For several decades there have also been competitions for women. Many children start training in a young wrestlers' club.

begriffe.erklaerung: The name for a single bout between two wrestlers.
A very strong, coarse fabric from which the wrestling shorts are sewn.
The point where you can imagine the whole weight of a body to be concentrated.
The winner of the Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival.

gewusst: Tens of thousands of people watch in the stadium at the Federal Wrestling Festival.
The winner's prize at the Federal Festival is traditionally a live bull.
After the bout the winner brushes the sawdust off the loser's back.

t1vyj4j5.t: Straw in a glass of water

teile.einleitung: If you put a straw into a glass of water at a slant, it looks as if it is bent at the water surface. In reality it is perfectly straight; our eye is just being fooled. The reason is refraction, which happens when light passes from water into air.
wichtigste: The straw looks bent because light is refracted when it passes from water into air.
With cooking oil instead of water the bend is greater, because oil refracts light more strongly.
If the straw stands upright and you look exactly straight down from above, there is no bend.
A swimming pool looks less deep from above than it really is.
A pool 2 m deep looks only about 1.5 m deep from straight above.
A fish in the water is deeper than it appears.
A round glass of water acts like a converging lens and magnifies.

abschnitte.text: For this experiment you only need a clear glass, water and a **straw**. You put the straw into the glass at a slant and look at it from the side or at an angle from above. At the water surface the straw seems to have a bend. The part under water looks raised, as if it were closer to the surface.

Light travels more slowly in water than in air. So when a ray of light hits the boundary between water and air at a slant, it changes direction; this is called **refraction**. But our brain assumes that light always comes in a straight line. That is why we see the part of the straw under water in a different place from where it really is. If the light hits the surface exactly at right angles, it is not bent, and then there is no bend either.

How strongly a substance refracts light is given by its **refractive index**. Air has a refractive index of almost exactly 1, water about 1.33 and cooking oil about 1.47. If you fill the glass with oil instead of water, the apparent bend is therefore greater. The rule by which light is refracted is called the **law of refraction** and was described in the 17th century by the Dutchman Willebrord Snellius.

A swimming pool also looks less deep from above than it is, because the light from the bottom is refracted at the surface. As a rule of thumb, you divide the real depth by the refractive index 1.33. So a pool 2 metres deep looks only about 1.5 metres deep from straight above. This is one reason why you should never jump into unknown water without checking.

If you put a coin in a cup so that it is just hidden by the rim and then pour in water, the coin suddenly appears. The refracted light makes it visible over the rim. A fish in a pond is deeper than it appears, so you easily miss it if you aim at an angle from above with a spear. Herons and other fish hunters have learned to make up for this error.

If you look from the side through a round glass filled with water, a spoon inside often looks bigger. The curved glass with water acts like a **converging lens**, that is, like a magnifying glass. Glasses, cameras and microscopes work on the same principle. The **rainbow** is also created by refraction of light in raindrops.

begriffe.erklaerung: Change in the direction of light when it passes from one substance into another.
Number that shows how strongly a substance refracts light.
Curved, transparent piece that brings light rays together and makes things look bigger.
When our eyes see something differently from how it really is.

gewusst: In water light is about a quarter slower than in air.
If you put your arm into the water, it looks shorter than it is.
A diamond sparkles so strongly because it refracts light very strongly.

teile.einleitung: Snell's law of refraction describes how sharply a ray of light bends when it passes from one substance into another, for example from air into water. It is named after the Dutch scientist Willebrord van Roijen Snell, who found it around 1621. It can be used to explain glasses, lenses and even the rainbow.
wichtigste: Light is refracted when it passes at an angle from one transparent substance into another.
The law is n1 · sin α = n2 · sin β.
The angle of incidence and the angle of refraction are always measured from the normal.
The refractive index n tells you how strongly a substance slows down light.
When light goes from air into water or glass, it is bent towards the normal.
The law is named after Willebrord van Roijen Snell, who found it around 1621.
Fermat's principle explains the law: light takes the path with the shortest travel time.

abschnitte.text: Light travels at different speeds in different substances, for example more slowly in water than in air. So when a ray of light hits the boundary at an angle, it changes direction; this is called **refraction**. That is why a spoon in a glass of water looks as if it has a bend in it. And a swimming pool looks less deep from above than it really is.

You draw a helper line at right angles to the boundary, the **normal**. The angle of incidence α and the angle of refraction β are measured from this normal. The law is n1 · sin α = n2 · sin β, where n1 and n2 are the **refractive indices** of the two substances. The greater the difference between the refractive indices, the more sharply the ray bends.

Air has a refractive index of about 1.00, water 1.33 and ordinary glass about 1.5. If light from air hits water at 45°, then sin β = sin 45° divided by 1.33. This gives an angle of refraction of about 32°, so the ray is bent **towards the normal**. If light goes the other way, from glass into air, it is bent away from the normal.

When light passes from a denser substance such as glass into air, the angle can become too shallow. Beyond a certain **critical angle**, the light no longer comes out at all, but is reflected back completely. This **total internal reflection** is used in fibre-optic cables, which carry internet data as light over long distances. The sparkle of diamonds, which have a refractive index of about 2.4, also comes from this.

As early as around the year 984 the Persian scholar Ibn Sahl in Baghdad described a similar law. In Europe Willebrord van Roijen Snell found it around 1621, but did not publish it. René Descartes made it known in 1637, which is why in France it is named after him. Later Pierre de Fermat showed that light always chooses the **quickest path**, like a lifeguard who would rather run further along the beach and swim less.

Without refraction there would be no **lenses**, so no glasses, cameras, microscopes or telescopes. Our own eye also refracts light with the cornea and the lens so that a sharp image is formed. In a rainbow, sunlight is refracted in drops of water and split into its colours. In this way a simple law explains many things we see every day.

begriffe.erklaerung: Change in the direction of light when it passes into another substance.
An imaginary line at right angles to the boundary.
A number that shows how strongly a substance slows down light.
Complete reflection of light back at a boundary.
Rule according to which light takes the path with the shortest travel time.

gewusst: Fish in the water are not quite where you see them, which is why herons aim a little lower when catching them.
The law of refraction had already been described by Ibn Sahl more than 600 years before Snell.
A diamond sparkles so strongly because it refracts light much more than glass does.

teile.einleitung: A thermal is warm air rising from the ground. It forms on sunny days, when the ground warms up and heats the air above it. Glider pilots, paragliders and large birds use thermals to climb high without an engine or flapping their wings.
wichtigste: A thermal is rising warm air.
Warm air rises because it has a lower density than colder air.
Thermals form most easily over dry, dark surfaces such as a ploughed field.
On a summer day, thermals are usually strongest in the early afternoon.
At the top of a column of rising air a cumulus cloud often forms.
Paragliders, glider pilots, storks and birds of prey use thermals.
In a thermal, heat transfer by convection is at work.

abschnitte.text: The Sun warms the ground, and the ground warms the air directly above it. Warm air expands and has a **lower density** than colder air, so it is lighter. That is why it rises, similar to a hot-air balloon. This kind of heat transfer by flowing air is called **convection**.

Not every kind of ground warms up equally. Dry, dark surfaces such as a freshly ploughed **field**, rock faces, roads or villages heat up quickly. Meadows, forests and lakes stay cooler. Above the warm places the air breaks away from the ground as a **thermal bubble** or as a rising column.

If the moist warm air rises high enough, it cools down, and the water vapour turns into droplets. Then a **cumulus cloud**, a white fair-weather cloud, forms at the top of the column. For pilots it is a signpost to the next thermal. On a summer day thermals are usually strongest in the early afternoon, when the ground is warmest.

**Glider pilots** and **paragliders** circle in thermals and gain height in this way, often many hundreds of metres. Then they glide to the next thermal and can fly long distances like this. Glider pilots in German-speaking countries also call a thermal a **“Bart”**, which means beard. An instrument called a variometer beeps when you are going up, so the pilot can feel the rising air without seeing it.

Storks, eagles, buzzards and vultures often circle in thermals without a single beat of their wings. In this way they save a lot of energy. That is why in autumn storks prefer to migrate over land rather than over the sea, because there are hardly any thermals over water. If you look up at the sky on a summer day, you sometimes see several birds of prey circling together in a rising current of air.

In the Swiss Alps there are strong thermals on sunny days, because sunny mountain slopes heat up quickly. That is why Switzerland is very popular with paragliders, for example around Interlaken or Fiesch in Valais. But very strong thermals can also grow into tall towering clouds and **thunderstorms**. That is why pilots watch the weather closely and land in good time.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rising warm air.
Transport of heat by flowing air or liquid.
How much mass there is in a certain space.
A white, cauliflower-shaped heap cloud.
An instrument that shows whether an aircraft is rising or sinking.

gewusst: Thanks to thermals, gliders can fly hundreds of kilometres without any engine at all.
On their way to Africa storks prefer to take the detour via Gibraltar, because there are hardly any thermals over the sea.
Smoke from a chimney sometimes also shows where the air is rising at the moment.

teile.einleitung: The Standard Model of particle physics is the theory that describes what all matter is made of at the very smallest level and how these tiny particles act on each other. It is like nature's construction kit, with a few basic building blocks and the forces that hold them together. Many of its predictions have been confirmed very precisely at CERN near Geneva.
wichtigste: The Standard Model describes the smallest known building blocks of matter, the elementary particles.
It contains 12 elementary matter particles, namely 6 quarks and 6 leptons.
Three of the four fundamental forces are explained: the electromagnetic, the weak and the strong interaction.
Gravitation, that is gravity, is not part of the Standard Model.
The forces are carried by gauge bosons, such as the photon, the gluons and the W and Z bosons.
The Higgs boson was discovered at CERN in 2012 and was the last missing particle of the model.
The theory was developed in the 1960s and 1970s through the work of many physicists.

abschnitte.text: The Standard Model is a physical theory about the **elementary particles**, that is, particles that cannot be split any further. Atoms consist of electrons and a nucleus, and the nucleus consists of protons and neutrons. But protons and neutrons are themselves built from even smaller particles, the **quarks**. The Standard Model sorts all these particles and explains how they influence each other.

Matter is made of 12 basic building blocks, the **fermions**. They include 6 quarks called up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom. Then there are 6 **leptons**: the electron, the muon, the tau and three kinds of neutrinos. Almost everything we see in everyday life is built only from up quarks, down quarks and electrons. In addition, each of these particles has an antiparticle.

In the Standard Model, forces are carried by special particles, the **gauge bosons**. The **photon**, a particle of light, carries the electromagnetic force, which explains magnets and electric current, for example. The **gluons** carry the strong interaction, which holds the quarks in the atomic nucleus together like glue. The W and Z bosons are responsible for the weak interaction, which acts in some kinds of radioactivity.

The strong interaction is described by **quantum chromodynamics**. Sheldon Glashow, Abdus Salam and Steven Weinberg showed that the electromagnetic and the weak interaction belong together, and for this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1979. This unification is called the **electroweak interaction**. Later Peter Higgs and others predicted a further particle that gives particles their mass.

At **CERN**, the European research centre on the border between Switzerland and France, there is the largest particle accelerator in the world. The **Large Hadron Collider** is a ring about 27 kilometres long deep underground. There protons are made to collide at almost the speed of light. In 2012 the **Higgs boson** was detected there, and in 2013 Peter Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel Prize.

Although the Standard Model is very successful, it does not explain everything. **Gravitation** does not fit into it so far. Nor does the mysterious **dark matter**, which is observed indirectly in space. That is why scientists are looking for an even more complete theory.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle that, according to what we know today, cannot be split into smaller parts.
A basic building block that protons and neutrons are made of.
A particle that carries a force between other particles.
The particle of the strong force; it holds the quarks together like glue.
A particle linked to the mechanism that gives particles their mass.

gewusst: The word gluon comes from the English word glue, “Leim” in German.
The name quark comes from a novel by the Irish writer James Joyce.
The top quark is the heaviest known elementary particle and is about as heavy as a whole gold atom.

teile.einleitung: We call it sunshine when the Sun's light shines directly to the ground without clouds in the way. How much sunshine a place gets is measured as the sunshine duration in hours. It depends on the season, the weather and the location, and in Switzerland there are big differences.
wichtigste: Sunshine duration is given in hours.
In summer there are more hours of sunshine, because the days are longer.
Around 21 June we have the longest day of the year.
Ticino is often called the “sun parlour of Switzerland”.
In winter there is often a sea of fog over the Swiss Plateau, while the sun shines in the mountains.
In the weather forecast “fair” means a lot of sun and few clouds.
The UV index shows how strong the Sun's radiation is.

abschnitte.text: We speak of **sunshine** when sunlight hits the ground directly and is not hidden by clouds. Weather services only count an hour of sunshine if the direct radiation is strong enough. If not a single cloud can be seen, the sky is called **cloudless**. In the weather forecast a yellow sun shows fine, sunny weather.

In the past sunshine duration was measured with a **glass ball**, which focuses sunlight like a magnifying glass. The focal point burned a track into a strip of paper, and from the length of the track you could read off the hours of sunshine. Today weather services such as MeteoSwiss use electronic sensors. They measure automatically when the sun is shining strongly enough.

Because the Earth's axis is tilted, the days are long in summer and short in winter. Around 21 June, the **summer solstice**, it is light in Zurich for almost 16 hours. Around 21 December it is only about 8.5 hours. That is why there are many more possible hours of sunshine in summer than in winter.

**Ticino**, south of the Alps, is known as the “sun parlour of Switzerland”, and Valais and the Engadine are also very sunny. There the sun often shines for over 2000 hours a year. On the Swiss Plateau, on the other hand, it is often grey in winter, because cold, damp air settles as **high fog**. If you go up a mountain then, you often see a white sea of fog below you while you yourself stand in the sun.

In the weather forecast **“sunny”** means there are almost no clouds. **“Fair”** means a lot of sun with only a few clouds. With “cloudy” or “overcast”, on the other hand, little or no sun gets through. Often the UV index is given too, which shows how strong the Sun's radiation is and how well you should protect yourself.

Sunlight lifts many people's mood and helps the body to make **vitamin D**. But too much sun can cause sunburn and harm the eyes. That is why sun cream, a hat and sunglasses are important on sunny days. Especially in the mountains and on snow, the sun is stronger than you think.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time during which the sun shines directly, measured in hours.
The longest day of the year, around 21 June.
A layer of fog that does not lie on the ground, but a little above it.
A sea of fog that you see from above from a mountain.
A number that shows how strongly the Sun's radiation affects the skin.

gewusst: If you want to escape the fog in Switzerland in winter, a trip up a hill about 1000 metres high is often enough.
The old glass ball for measuring hours of sunshine worked without any electricity.
In theory the sun could shine for at most about half of all the hours in a year, because it is dark at night.

teile.einleitung: Diving depth tells you how far below the water surface a diver, an animal or a submarine is. The deeper it goes, the more strongly the water presses from all sides. This water pressure decides how deep people and machines can dive.
wichtigste: For every 10 metres of water depth the pressure rises by about 1 bar.
At a depth of 10 metres the total pressure including air pressure is about 2 bar, at 30 metres about 4 bar.
At the deepest point of the sea, about 11 kilometres down, the pressure is more than 1000 bar.
Air in a balloon is squeezed together in the deep; at 20 metres to about a third.
A dive computer measures the diving depth from the water pressure.
Diving on a single breath is called freediving.
Submarines need a thick, strong hull to withstand the water pressure.

abschnitte.text: Water is heavy: a litre weighs about one kilogram. The deeper you dive, the more water there is above you pressing down. Every 10 metres, about 1 **bar** of pressure is added. At the surface the air already presses with about 1 bar, so at a depth of 10 metres it is about 2 bar in total and at 30 metres about 4 bar.

Gases can be squeezed together, but water hardly at all. If you take a balloon filled with air down to a depth of 20 metres, the pressure there is about three times as great, and the balloon shrinks to about a third. This law is called **Boyle's law**. That is why divers already feel pressure on their ears a few metres down and have to equalise the pressure.

Recreational divers with a compressed air cylinder usually do not dive deeper than about 40 metres. A **dive computer** on the wrist measures the depth from the water pressure and calculates how long you may stay. Anyone who comes up too fast risks the dangerous decompression sickness, because gas bubbles form in the blood. In **freediving** you dive without equipment on a single breath; top athletes reach depths of over 100 metres in this way.

Submarines have a thick, round hull made of steel or titanium so that they are not crushed. At the deepest point of the oceans, in the **Mariana Trench** in the Pacific, the water is about 11 kilometres deep. There it presses with over 1000 bar, which is as if a car were standing on every thumbnail. People first reached this place in 1960.

The Swiss physicist **Auguste Piccard** invented the bathyscaphe, a submersible for the deep sea. In 1960 his son Jacques Piccard, together with the American Don Walsh, dived in the bathyscaphe Trieste to the bottom of the Mariana Trench. The Piccard family is also known for records in the air. In Swiss lakes such as Lake Geneva or Lake Maggiore the water is several hundred metres deep.

Deep-sea fish are not crushed by the huge water pressure. Inside their bodies the pressure is the same as outside, and they usually have no air-filled spaces. If they are brought to the surface quickly, this often harms them badly. Sperm whales can dive more than 1000 metres deep to hunt squid.

begriffe.erklaerung: Unit of pressure; air pressure at the surface is about 1 bar.
Pushing air into the ears so that the pressure inside and outside is the same.
Diving while holding your breath, without breathing equipment.
Submersible that can go very deep into the deep sea.
Deepest known place in the oceans, in the Pacific.

gewusst: A Swiss man, Jacques Piccard, was one of the first two people at the deepest point of the sea.
At a depth of 11 kilometres the water presses more than a thousand times harder than the air at the surface.
A sperm whale can stay under water for more than an hour.

teile.einleitung: A reflecting telescope is a telescope that collects light with a curved mirror instead of a lens. All the large telescopes in the world today are reflecting telescopes. With them astronomers look as far as the most distant galaxies.
wichtigste: A reflecting telescope collects light with a curved primary mirror.
Mirrors do not produce coloured fringes, because all colours are reflected in the same way.
In a Newtonian telescope a small slanted secondary mirror directs the light sideways to the eyepiece.
In a Cassegrain telescope the light reaches the eyepiece through a hole in the primary mirror.
Telescope mirrors are usually coated with aluminium.
The largest mirrors are made of many hexagonal segments.
ESO's Extremely Large Telescope in Chile is getting a mirror about 39 metres across.
Adaptive optics correct the blurring caused by the shimmering of the air.

abschnitte.text: A reflecting telescope catches the light from stars with a large, inwardly curved **primary mirror**. The mirror focuses the light at one point, the **focal point**. There an image forms, which you look at with an eyepiece or record with a camera. The bigger the mirror, the more light it collects and the fainter the objects you can see.

In 1668 the English scientist **Isaac Newton** built one of the first usable reflecting telescopes. In a **Newtonian telescope** a small slanted secondary mirror directs the light sideways out of the tube to the eyepiece. In a **Cassegrain telescope** a second mirror sends the light back through a hole in the middle of the primary mirror. This keeps the instrument shorter and easier to handle.

A simple glass lens refracts blue and red light by different amounts, which is why **coloured fringes** form around bright stars. A mirror, on the other hand, reflects all colours in the same way. You can also support a mirror from behind, whereas a lens can only be held at its edge. That is why mirrors can be built much bigger; the largest lens of a telescope measures only about one metre.

Large mirrors are often made of many hexagonal **segments** fitted together like a honeycomb. The Keck telescopes on Hawaii are each 10 metres across. The **Extremely Large Telescope** of the European Southern Observatory ESO in Chile's Atacama Desert will have a mirror of about 39 metres. Switzerland is a member of ESO and is taking part in the project.

Telescope mirrors are made of special glass that is coated with a wafer-thin layer of **aluminium**. This layer reflects the light and is renewed every few years. The restless air makes stars twinkle and images blurry. That is why **adaptive optics** bend a thin mirror hundreds of times a second to cancel out the shimmering.

begriffe.erklaerung: The large curved mirror that collects the light in the telescope.
The point where the focused light rays meet.
A small mirror that redirects the focused light to the eyepiece.
A technique that cancels out the shimmering of the air with mirrors that can change shape.

gewusst: The James Webb Space Telescope has a mirror made of 18 hexagonal segments coated with gold.
Telescopes stand on high mountains and in deserts, because the air there is dry and calm.
Many amateur astronomers grind their telescope mirrors themselves.

teile.einleitung: Thomas Young was an English doctor, physicist and language scholar who lived from 1773 to 1829. With his experiments he showed that light behaves like a wave. He also helped to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs and did research on colour vision.
wichtigste: Thomas Young was English and worked as a doctor.
At the beginning of the 19th century he presented his interference experiments with light.
With them he called into question Isaac Newton's particle theory of light.
He made important contributions to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs.
The three-colour theory of vision goes back to Young and Hermann von Helmholtz.
In English the elastic modulus is named after him: “Young's modulus”.
The Young-Laplace equation describes the difference in pressure at curved liquid surfaces.

abschnitte.text: Thomas Young was born in 1773 in Milverton in south-west England and died in London in 1829. Even as a child he learned incredibly quickly, and as a young man he knew many languages, including Latin, Greek and Hebrew. He studied medicine in London, Edinburgh and Göttingen and later worked as a **doctor** in London. Alongside this he did research in so many fields that he is called a **polymath**.

Isaac Newton had taught that light is made of tiny particles. At the beginning of the 19th century Young let light pass through two narrow slits. On a screen behind them light and dark stripes appeared. This pattern forms when waves overlap, strengthening and cancelling each other; this is called **interference**. The **double-slit experiment** became one of the most famous experiments in physics and is still important in quantum physics today.

Young suspected that there are only three kinds of colour receptors in the eye. The brain puts all colours together from the signals of these three kinds. The German scientist Hermann von Helmholtz later developed this idea further, which is why it is called the **Young-Helmholtz three-colour theory**. Today we know that the retina really does have three kinds of cones, which react mainly to red, green and blue.

In 1799 the **Rosetta Stone** was found in Egypt, with the same text on it in three scripts, including hieroglyphs and Greek. Young studied it and realised that some hieroglyphs stand for sounds, especially in the names of kings. In this way he deciphered some signs, for example in the name of King Ptolemy. The decisive breakthrough was then made in 1822 by the Frenchman Jean-François Champollion.

Young also studied how much materials stretch when you pull on them. The quantity that describes this is called the **elastic modulus**, in English “Young's modulus”. Together with the Frenchman Pierre-Simon Laplace, he gave his name to the Young-Laplace equation, which describes the difference in pressure at curved liquid surfaces, as in soap bubbles. He was also one of the first to use the word energy in its present-day meaning in physics.

begriffe.erklaerung: Overlapping of waves, in which they strengthen or cancel each other.
Experiment in which light passes through two slits and makes stripes.
Number that shows how stiff a material is.
Person who knows about a great many fields of knowledge.
Stone slab with the same text in three scripts.

gewusst: Thomas Young is said to have been able to read at the age of two.
A biography of him has the title “The Last Man Who Knew Everything”.
At first his wave theory of light was fiercely rejected by many scholars.

teile.einleitung: A particle accelerator is a machine that brings tiny electrically charged particles such as electrons or protons up to extremely high speeds. Scientists make them collide or use their radiation to study the building blocks of matter. The largest accelerator in the world is at CERN near Geneva.
wichtigste: Particle accelerators give charged particles high energy using electric fields.
A proton that passes through a voltage of 2000 volts gains 2 keV of energy.
Ernest Lawrence invented the cyclotron in the 1930s.
The old cathode ray television also contained a small particle accelerator.
On circular paths, electrons lose a lot of energy as synchrotron radiation.
The Swiss Light Source at the Paul Scherrer Institute uses electrons to produce intense X-ray light.
At the Paul Scherrer Institute tumours are treated with accelerated protons.
The Future Circular Collider planned at CERN is to have a circumference of about 91 kilometres.

abschnitte.text: Charged particles are attracted or pushed away by electric fields and so get faster. If a proton passes through a voltage of 2000 volts, it gains an energy of 2000 **electronvolts**, that is 2 keV. In modern facilities the particles are pushed again and again in **radio-frequency cavities**, similar to a child on a swing. Strong magnets steer the particles along their path and focus the beam. So that the particles do not collide with air molecules, they fly in tubes with a vacuum.

There are straight accelerators, the **linear accelerators**, and ring-shaped facilities. In the 1930s in California, Ernest Lawrence invented the **cyclotron**, in which the particles circle outwards in a spiral. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1939. In a circular accelerator the particles can go round many times and gain energy on every lap. But on circular paths electrons lose a lot of energy as **synchrotron radiation**, which is why circles are not good for bringing them to the very highest energies.

CERN is a European research centre that was founded in 1954 and lies on the border between Switzerland and France. Its largest accelerator is the **Large Hadron Collider** (LHC), with a circumference of about 27 kilometres, which runs about 100 metres underground. There protons crash into each other at almost the speed of light. In 2012 the Higgs particle was discovered at the LHC. As a successor, CERN is planning the Future Circular Collider, with a circumference of about 91 kilometres.

The Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen in the canton of Aargau is the largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering in Switzerland. It runs a powerful proton accelerator, which is also used to produce neutrons and other particles for research. The **Swiss Light Source** (SLS) is a ring in which electrons circle and give off very bright X-ray light. With it scientists study, for example, the structure of proteins, batteries and new materials.

Not all accelerators are huge. The old **cathode ray television** contained a picture tube in which electrons were accelerated and made dots on the screen light up. Hospitals have linear accelerators that produce beams for treating cancer. At PSI tumours are treated with protons; this is called **proton therapy**, and it can be especially gentle on healthy tissue.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy an electron gains when it passes through a voltage of 1 volt.
Accelerator in which particles circle in a spiral.
Light given off by fast charged particles on a curved path.
Positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
A space from which almost all the air has been removed.

gewusst: In the LHC, protons go round the 27-kilometre ring more than 11,000 times a second.
The World Wide Web was invented at CERN in 1989 so that scientists could share their data more easily.
An old cathode ray television was also a small particle accelerator.

teile.einleitung: Subtractive colour mixing explains how new colours are made from dyes, inks and watercolours. Every dye swallows part of the light, and only the colour we see is left over. Without this principle there would be no colourful newspapers, books or paintings.
wichtigste: The three primary colours of subtractive mixing are cyan, magenta and yellow.
Cyan and yellow together make green.
Magenta and yellow together make red.
Cyan and magenta together make blue.
All three primary colours on top of each other ideally make black.
The mixing is called subtractive because each dye swallows, that is takes away, part of the light.
Painting with watercolours and printing use subtractive colour mixing.

abschnitte.text: White light, for example sunlight, is made of all the colours of the rainbow. A dye **absorbs** some of these colours, that is, it swallows them. It sends the rest back, and this rest reaches our eye. The more dyes you mix, the more light is swallowed and the darker the mixture becomes.

The primary colours of subtractive mixing are **cyan** (a light blue-green), **magenta** (a strong pink) and yellow. Cyan swallows red light, magenta swallows green light and yellow swallows blue light. If you mix two of them, only one colour of light is left: cyan and yellow let only green through, magenta and yellow only red, cyan and magenta only blue. When all three come together, almost all the light is swallowed and black is the result.

Colour printers and printing presses work with four colours called **CMYK**. C stands for cyan, M for magenta, Y for yellow and K for key, the key colour black. Real dyes are not perfect, so mixing cyan, magenta and yellow usually gives only a muddy dark brown. That is why real black is printed as well; it is also cheaper and makes text sharper. If you look at a printed picture through a magnifying glass, you can see many tiny dots of colour.

With screens, mobile phones and spotlights it works exactly the other way round. There coloured light is added together, which is why it is called **additive colour mixing**. Its primary colours are red, green and blue, RGB for short. There all three together do not make black, but white. The primary colours of one kind of mixing are exactly the mixed colours of the other.

A tomato looks red because it mainly sends back red light and swallows the other colours. If you light it only with green light, it finds hardly any red light to send back and looks almost black. That is why clothes often look quite different in coloured disco lights than in daylight. When you paint with **watercolours** in the classroom, you are also mixing subtractively: blue and yellow become green.

For thousands of years painters have mixed pigments, that is coloured powders, to get new shades. In the past people at school mostly learned red, yellow and blue as the primary colours, but this is only an imprecise simplification. With cyan, magenta and yellow far more colours can be mixed. Modern four-colour printing became established in the 20th century and shapes magazines, posters and packaging today.

begriffe.erklaerung: When a substance swallows light instead of sending it back.
Light blue-green, one of the three primary colours in printing.
Strong pinkish red, one of the three primary colours in printing.
The four printing colours cyan, magenta, yellow and black.
Coloured powder from which paints are made.

gewusst: The K in CMYK does not stand for the last letter of the English word black, but for “key”, the key colour.
A set of printer cartridges with cyan, magenta, yellow and black can produce thousands of different shades.
Under green light a ripe tomato looks almost black.

teile.einleitung: The pole vault is an athletics event in which athletes jump over a high bar with a long, flexible pole. In doing so, the energy of a fast run-up is turned into height. Today the best vaulters clear more than six metres, which is as high as a two-storey house.
wichtigste: In the pole vault kinetic energy is turned into potential energy.
A fast run-up is decisive, because more speed means more energy for height.
Modern poles are usually made of glass fibre or carbon fibre.
At take-off the vaulter plants the pole in the box.
In 1985 in Paris, Sergey Bubka was the first person to clear 6 metres.
Armand Duplantis has held the men's world record since 2020 and has improved it several times.
A thick mat cushions the landing from a great height.

abschnitte.text: In the pole vault the athlete runs towards the equipment with a long **pole**. Shortly before the bar he plants the end of the pole in the **box**, a hollow in the ground. The pole bends strongly and flings the vaulter upwards. Above the **bar** he turns, pushes himself off the pole and falls onto a thick mat.

During the run-up the vaulter collects **kinetic energy**. When planting the pole, part of it is stored for a moment in the bent pole as elastic energy. The pole straightens again and passes the energy on to the vaulter as **potential energy**. Using the formula h = v² / (2g), with a run-up at 10 m/s and g = 10 m/s², the body's centre of gravity rises by 5 metres, purely in theory.

Long ago people already jumped over streams and ditches with poles, and in the Netherlands this is still a popular sport today. Pole vaulting was already part of the first modern Olympic Games in 1896. Back then people jumped with poles made of wood and later of **bamboo**. From the 1960s, flexible poles made of **glass fibre** took over, later also of carbon fibre, and the heights rose sharply.

In 1985 in Paris, the Ukrainian **Sergey Bubka** was the first person to clear 6 metres, and he set many world records. Since 2020 the Swede **Armand Duplantis** has held the men's world record and keeps improving it by one centimetre at a time. At the 2025 World Championships in Tokyo he cleared 6.30 metres. Among women, the Russian Yelena Isinbayeva was the first to jump over 5 metres, in 2005.

Because the vaulters fall from more than six metres, they land on a very thick, soft **mat**. The bar only rests loosely and falls down if it is touched. A good vaulter needs speed, strength, body tension and gymnastic skill. In Switzerland the pole vault is trained in many athletics clubs, and even children practise with short, soft poles.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hollow in the ground into which the vaulter plants the pole at take-off.
The energy a body has because it is moving.
The energy a body has because it is high up.
The point where you can imagine the whole weight of the body to be concentrated.

gewusst: Sergey Bubka improved the world record 35 times in total, indoors and outdoors together.
A pole for top athletes is about 5 metres long and is chosen to suit the vaulter's body weight.
Armand Duplantis's record is higher than a giraffe's head, which is about 5 to 6 metres above the ground.

teile.einleitung: An LC circuit, also called a resonant circuit, is an electric circuit made of a coil and a capacitor in which energy swings back and forth. This creates an electrical oscillation with a certain frequency. Resonant circuits are found in radios, transmitters, clocks and many other devices.
wichtigste: In an LC circuit the energy swings between the electric field of the capacitor and the magnetic field of the coil.
If you multiply the capacitance by four, the natural frequency is halved.
In a real resonant circuit the ohmic resistance turns energy into heat, which is why the oscillation dies away.
An adjustable resonant circuit is used in a radio to tune in to a station.
At resonance the impedance of a series resonant circuit is at its minimum, and that of an ideal parallel resonant circuit is very large.
The Q factor shows how weakly a resonant circuit is damped and how sharp its resonance is.
The Meissner circuit is used to produce undamped electrical oscillations.

abschnitte.text: First the **capacitor** is charged; its energy is stored in the electric field. Then it discharges through the **coil**, and the current builds up a magnetic field there. When the magnetic field collapses, it keeps the current flowing and charges the capacitor up again the other way round. So the energy swings back and forth, similar to a pendulum swinging between potential and kinetic energy.

How fast the energy swings depends on the **capacitance** of the capacitor and the inductance of the coil. The formula for this is called Thomson's oscillation equation, after the British physicist William Thomson. The greater the capacitance and inductance, the lower the **natural frequency**. If you multiply the capacitance by four, the frequency becomes half as big.

Every real wire has an **ohmic resistance**, which turns part of the energy into heat. That is why the oscillations get smaller and smaller until they stop completely. The **Q factor** describes how little a resonant circuit is damped. A circuit with a high Q factor oscillates for a long time and reacts only to a very narrow range of frequencies.

If a resonant circuit is excited from outside at its natural frequency, it oscillates especially strongly; this is called **resonance**. In a classic radio you change the capacitance, and with it the natural frequency, using a variable capacitor. In this way you pick out from many stations exactly the one whose frequency matches. In a series resonant circuit the impedance is at its minimum at resonance; in an ideal parallel resonant circuit it is very large.

To keep an oscillation going permanently, you have to feed back the lost energy at the right rhythm. In 1913 the German Alexander Meissner presented a **feedback circuit** for this, which is named after him today. An amplifier, in the past an electron valve, always gives a small push at the right moment. Such oscillators produce the carrier waves of radio stations and clock signals in electronic devices.

begriffe.erklaerung: Component that stores electric charge and energy.
Wound-up wire that produces a magnetic field.
Frequency at which a system oscillates by itself.
Especially strong oscillation when the excitation matches the natural frequency.
Measure of how little a resonant circuit is damped.

gewusst: A resonant circuit works on the same principle as a child on a swing who is pushed at the right rhythm.
Radio tags on goods in shops often contain a tiny resonant circuit that is detected at the till or the exit.
Heinrich Hertz also experimented with resonant circuits when he proved the existence of radio waves in 1886.

teile.einleitung: Grit is everything that is spread on slippery roads and paths in winter so that nobody slips. It includes road salt, sand and chippings. Salt makes the ice melt, while sand and chippings make the smooth surface rougher.
wichtigste: Grit means materials such as salt, sand or chippings that are spread on black ice and snow.
Sand gives more grip but does not melt the ice; it only makes it rougher.
Road salt makes ice melt.
Because salt can harm plants and soil, some places prefer to spread sand or chippings.
On large roads a gritter spreads the salt.
In spring the chippings are swept off the roads again.
Many locomotives also have a sander so that their wheels do not spin.

abschnitte.text: **Grit** is material spread on roads, pavements and steps when there is snow and ice. A distinction is made between **de-icing** materials such as salt and **gripping** materials such as sand, chippings or fine gravel. Both are meant to stop people slipping or cars skidding. Which grit is used depends on the place and the weather.

**Road salt** is usually ordinary table salt, that is sodium chloride. When salt dissolves in water, this salt water only freezes at lower temperatures than pure water. That is why the ice melts even though it is below zero. But in very severe cold, salt works less and less well. Often salt water, called **brine**, is also sprayed onto the road, because it works faster.

Sand and chippings do not melt the ice, but make the smooth surface rough. The hard, sharp grains act like sandpaper under shoes and tyres. That is why sand is much more suitable than, say, flour, which is soft and soon turns to mush. **Chippings** are crushed rock with sharp edges that grips especially well.

Salt can harm **plants**, trees and soil when it gets into the ground with the meltwater. It also attacks cars, bridges and concrete, because it speeds up rusting. Dogs' paws can be irritated by salt. That is why many municipalities prefer to spread sand or chippings on footpaths, and some ask house owners not to use salt.

In winter a municipality's **winter service** clears snow and grits the roads. The staff often set out early in the morning so that the roads are safe before the rush hour. On large roads a **gritter** spreads the salt evenly with a spinning disc. In spring, road sweepers sweep away the chippings that are left lying.

Locomotives also need grit, namely sand. On wet or icy rails, or rails covered with leaves, the steel wheels can spin. That is why many locomotives have a **sander**, which blows sand onto the rails in front of the wheels. This helps the wheels grip better, especially when starting off and on steep lines.

begriffe.erklaerung: Material such as salt, sand or chippings that is spread against slippery surfaces.
Small, sharp pieces of crushed rock.
Salt water that is sprayed onto roads.
People and vehicles that clear snow and grit in winter.

gewusst: Salt water only freezes at lower temperatures than pure water, which is why the sea also freezes over less easily.
Part of the road salt in Switzerland comes from the Swiss salt works on the Rhine and in Bex.
In spring the swept-up chippings can often be cleaned and used again the next winter.

teile.einleitung: An oven cloth or pot holder is a thick piece of fabric used to hold hot pots, pans and baking trays. It protects your hands from burns. Behind it is physics: a good pot holder conducts heat only very poorly.
wichtigste: With a pot holder you can hold hot pots without burning yourself.
A thick pot holder protects well, because it conducts heat poorly.
A pot holder should be dry, because a wet one conducts heat faster.
Pot holders are often made of cotton.
You use an oven glove to take hot trays out of the oven.
A small loop is for hanging it up.
You never hold a pot holder close to an open flame, because it can catch fire.

abschnitte.text: A pot holder is usually a square or round piece made of several layers of fabric. It is often knitted, crocheted or sewn from **cotton** and padded inside with a thick filling. At one corner it has a small **loop** so that you can hang it up next to the cooker. One variety is the **oven glove**, which covers the whole hand and is used to take hot trays out of the oven.

Materials conduct heat differently. Metal, such as a pan handle, conducts heat very well, which is why it gets hot. Fabric, wool and above all the **air** between the fibres conduct heat poorly; they are called **thermal insulators**. A thick pot holder contains a lot of trapped air, so the heat only reaches your hand slowly. The thicker the cloth, the longer it keeps the heat away.

A wet pot holder is dangerous. Water conducts heat much better than air and fills the gaps between the fibres. As a result the heat quickly reaches the skin. In addition, the water can turn into **steam** when it touches a hot pot, and steam is very hot and causes painful scalds.

Fabric pot holders can catch fire, so you never hold them close to an open gas flame or on a hot hotplate. You do not put a hot pan directly on the table, but on a **trivet**, so that the table is not damaged. Pan handles are turned towards the back so that nobody gets caught on them. Children should always cook at the cooker together with an adult.

Crocheting or knitting a pot holder is a classic project in textile lessons at many schools. You learn stitches and patterns. Today there are also pot holders made of **silicone**, which are heat-resistant, non-slip and easy to wash. Some oven gloves are also reinforced with especially heat-resistant fibres.

begriffe.erklaerung: Material that conducts heat poorly and therefore protects against heat.
Passing heat on through a material.
Plant fibre from which many fabrics are made.
Mat or stand on which you put hot pots.

gewusst: Trapped air is one of the best thermal insulators, which is also why down jackets are so warm.
A wet pot holder can be more dangerous than none at all.
Crocheted pot holders are among the most popular first pieces of handicraft at school.

teile.einleitung: A thermostat is a controller that keeps a temperature constant automatically. It is found on radiators, in fridges, in irons and in many other devices. It constantly measures the temperature and switches the heating or cooling on or off.
wichtigste: A thermostat keeps a temperature constant.
The temperature you set is called the set point.
Setting 3 on many radiator thermostats is about 20 °C.
Many thermostatic valves contain an expanding element.
If you lower the room temperature by 1 °C, you save about 6 per cent of heating energy.
A radiator thermostat must not be covered by furniture or curtains.
In the fridge a thermostat keeps the inside temperature low.
With night setback the room temperature is controlled at a lower level at night.

abschnitte.text: A thermostat is a **temperature controller**. You set how warm or cold it should be; this desired value is called the **set point**. The thermostat constantly measures the actual temperature, the actual value. If it is too cold, it switches the heating on; when it is warm enough, it switches it off again. In this way the temperature always swings around the desired value; this is called a **control loop**.

Many thermostats use the fact that substances expand when warm. In the thermostatic valve on a radiator there is an **expanding element** with wax, liquid or gas. When the room gets warmer, the substance expands and slowly pushes the valve closed, so that less hot water flows into the radiator. Other thermostats use a **bimetallic strip** made of two different metals, which bends when warm and opens a switch. Modern devices measure electronically with a sensor.

The numbers on the knob are not degrees, but settings. On many radiator thermostats setting 3 is about 20 degrees Celsius, and each setting up or down changes the temperature by a few degrees. The thermostat measures the air directly around it. If it is covered by furniture or curtains, heat builds up there and it measures the wrong temperature, and then the room does not heat properly.

In the **fridge** a thermostat makes sure that it stays cool inside, usually at about 5 degrees Celsius. Ovens, irons, kettles, water heaters and aquarium heaters also have thermostats. In an iron it stops the soleplate from getting too hot and burning the fabric. In a car a thermostat makes sure that the engine quickly reaches its proper working temperature.

Just 1 degree lower room temperature saves about 6 per cent of heating energy. For living rooms experts in Switzerland recommend about 20 degrees, and less for bedrooms. With **night setback** the temperature is automatically controlled at a lower level at night. When airing the room, it is best to turn the thermostat down and open the window wide for a short time, rather than leaving it tilted open for a long time. Smart thermostats can even be controlled with a mobile phone.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature you want and set.
The temperature that is actually being measured at the moment.
Strip made of two metals that bends when warm.
Part containing a substance that expands when warm and moves a valve.
System that keeps measuring and adjusting until the desired value is reached.

gewusst: The numbers on a radiator thermostat are not degrees Celsius, only settings.
Turning the thermostat right up does not heat the room faster; it only makes it warmer in the end.
Many radiator thermostats have a snowflake symbol, which protects against freezing.

teile.einleitung: Boiling is the change of a liquid into a gas in which vapour bubbles form everywhere in the liquid. At sea level water boils at 100 °C. Whether cooking pasta or using a kettle, we come across boiling in the kitchen every day.
wichtigste: When boiling, vapour bubbles form in the liquid and rise to the top.
At normal air pressure water boils at 100 °C.
The higher you go into the mountains, the lower the boiling point.
While water is boiling, it does not get hotter than its boiling point.
If you let water boil for a long time, it evaporates and there is less and less of it.
A kettle switches itself off as soon as the water boils.
Boiling water can cause serious burns, so care is important.

abschnitte.text: When you heat water, small bubbles first form on the bottom of the pan. Shortly before it boils you hear a **rushing and bubbling** sound, because vapour bubbles form and collapse again. When the water is bubbling hard, large bubbles rise. These bubbles are not air, but **water vapour**.

The **boiling point** is the temperature at which a liquid boils. For water at sea level it is 100 °C. As long as water is boiling, the temperature stays the same; the heat added is needed to turn water into vapour. Other substances have other boiling points: alcohol (ethanol) boils at only about 78 °C, liquid nitrogen even at minus 196 °C.

The boiling point depends on the **air pressure**. In the mountains the air pressure is lower, so water boils there sooner. At about 3000 metres, water already boils at about 90 °C, which is why eggs and pasta take longer there. In a **pressure cooker** it is the other way round: the pressure is higher, the water gets as hot as about 120 °C and the food cooks faster. A well-known pressure cooker, the Duromatic, comes from the company Kuhn Rikon in the canton of Zurich.

Water can also turn into vapour without boiling, for example a puddle in the sun. This is called **evaporation**; it happens only at the surface and slowly. When boiling, on the other hand, the vapour forms throughout the liquid and very quickly. That is why there is less and less water in the pan when it boils for a long time.

Pasta, potatoes or rice become soft in boiling water. If the water bubbles too hard, you turn the heat down, otherwise a pan that is too full can **boil over**. A kettle uses a switch that reacts to the hot steam to notice when the water is boiling, and switches itself off. This saves electricity and stops the appliance from boiling dry.

Boiling water and steam can **scald** the skin badly. That is why you turn the pan handle inwards, so that nobody knocks the pan off. You should not pour boiling water into a thin, cold glass, because the glass can crack from the sudden heat. Younger children should only cook at the cooker with adults.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature at which a liquid boils.
Water in the form of a gas, invisible like air.
Slow change into a gas at the surface, even below the boiling point.
The weight of the air pressing on everything.
A tightly sealed pan in which water gets hotter than 100 °C.

gewusst: The white “steam” above a saucepan is not really steam, but tiny drops of water; real water vapour is invisible.
On Mount Everest water boils at only about 70 °C, so tea never gets really hot there.
In a microwave, water can sometimes get hotter than 100 °C without boiling and then suddenly bubble out.

teile.einleitung: The centre of mass theorem is a basic law of mechanics. It says that the centre of mass of a body or a group of bodies moves as if all the mass were gathered there and all external forces acted exactly at that point. This makes it possible to describe even complicated movements surprisingly simply.
wichtigste: The centre of mass moves as if all external forces acted on it.
Internal forces between the parts of a system cannot change the movement of the centre of mass.
If a firework rocket explodes, the centre of mass of all the pieces keeps following the original curved path of the throw.
If 2 kg lie at x = 0 m and 6 kg at x = 4 m, the shared centre of mass is at x = 3 m.
The shared centre of mass of the Earth and the Moon lies inside the Earth.
If a 60 kg person in a 120 kg boat walks 3 m forwards, the boat slides 1 m backwards.
The theorem is closely linked to the conservation of momentum.

abschnitte.titel: What is the centre of mass?
abschnitte.text: The **centre of mass** is the point where you can imagine the entire mass of a body to be gathered. In an even ball it lies exactly in the middle. For several bodies you calculate it as a weighted average of their positions. Heavy bodies pull the centre of mass more strongly towards themselves than light ones.

The centre of mass theorem follows from Isaac Newton's laws of motion. Only **external forces**, such as gravity or friction with the ground, can change the movement of the centre of mass. **Internal forces**, with which the parts push or pull each other, cancel each other out in pairs. If no external force acts, the centre of mass moves steadily in a straight line or stays at rest.

If a firework rocket explodes in the sky, the pieces fly off in all directions. But without air resistance their shared centre of mass keeps flying along the old **curved path of the throw** until the first piece reaches the ground. If a body of 1 kg moves at 4 m/s and a second one of 3 kg is at rest, their centre of mass moves at 1 m/s. If someone walks forwards in a rowing boat, the boat moves backwards so that the centre of mass stays in its place.

Celestial bodies also turn around their shared centre of mass, which is called the **barycentre**. Because the Earth has about 81 times as much mass as the Moon, this point still lies inside the Earth, about 4700 km from the Earth's centre. So every month the Earth wobbles a little around this point. With this method astronomers even find planets around distant stars, because the star wobbles slightly back and forth.

In the high jump, athletes use the **Flop technique**, which Dick Fosbury made famous at the 1968 Olympic Games in Mexico. The body is bent strongly over the bar, so that parts of it are already below the bar. In this way the centre of mass can stay below the bar even though the whole body gets over it. Gymnasts and ski jumpers also use their understanding of the centre of mass for their movements.

begriffe.erklaerung: Point where you can imagine the whole mass of a body to be gathered.
Force acting on a system from outside, for example gravity.
Force between the parts of a system itself.
Shared centre of mass of two celestial bodies.

gewusst: The Sun also circles around a shared centre of mass with the planets, which sometimes even lies outside the Sun.
A cat can turn while falling without the path of its centre of mass changing.
An astronaut in space cannot shift their centre of mass without pushing off from something.

teile.einleitung: A match is a thin stick of wood with a head that catches fire when you strike it. In Switzerland people usually call it “Zündholz” in German. It is a brilliant little invention that lets you make fire quickly and easily, but you have to use it carefully.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the match is usually called “Zündholz” in German.
When you strike it, friction makes the head hot until it catches fire.
A safety match only lights on the striking surface of the box.
A wet match is hard to light, because the head does not get hot enough.
A used match must be put out completely.
Children should only light matches with an adult.
Andersen wrote the fairy tale The Little Match Girl.

abschnitte.text: When you strike the head across the striking surface, **friction** produces heat. This heat starts a chemical process in which the head gets very hot and catches fire. The head contains a substance that gives off **oxygen** and a fuel. Then the wood catches fire; it is often soaked in paraffin wax so that it keeps burning well.

In a **safety match**, part of the igniting chemicals is in the striking surface of the box. That is where the **red phosphorus** is, while the head contains a substance that supplies oxygen. Only when the two come together does the match light. That is why it only lights on the box and not by accident in your trouser pocket.

Before there were matches, people made fire with flint, steel and tinder. Around 1826 the Englishman John Walker invented a friction match. Early matches contained poisonous **white phosphorus**, which made the workers in the factories ill and was therefore banned later. The safety match was developed in **Sweden** in the 19th century and sold from there all over the world.

If a match is wet, much of the heat from friction is used up to evaporate the water. So the head does not get hot enough to catch fire. In addition, the igniting mixture can dissolve in water. That is why there are **storm matches** for hikes and camps, which burn even in wind and wet weather.

Children should only light matches together with an **adult**. You always strike away from your body and hold the match tilted slightly downwards. A used match must be put out completely, for example by blowing it out or putting it in a glass of water. Matches belong in a place that small children cannot reach.

In 1845 the Danish writer **Hans Christian Andersen** wrote the fairy tale The Little Match Girl. It tells of a poor girl who has to sell matches on a freezing cold New Year's Eve. To warm herself, she lights one after another and sees beautiful pictures in their light. The fairy tale is sad and reminds us how hard life was for poor children at that time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss German word for a match.
The rough surface on the box on which you strike the match.
A chemical element that catches fire easily.
When two surfaces rub against each other and heat is produced.

gewusst: A match only burns for about ten to twenty seconds.
In the old days matches were also called sulphur matches, because their head contained sulphur.
Some people collect matchboxes with beautiful pictures; this is called phillumeny.

teile.einleitung: Solar radiation is the energy that the Sun sends into space as light and heat. A small part of it reaches the Earth and makes life there possible in the first place. It warms us, makes plants grow and can even supply electricity and hot water.
wichtigste: Solar radiation consists of visible light, infrared radiation and UV radiation.
The Sun's light takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth.
Dark surfaces take in a lot of radiation; a black T-shirt gets warmest in the sun.
The Sun's rays are strongest around midday on a summer's day.
In winter the Sun is low in the sky, so it warms less.
Sun cream protects the skin from too much UV radiation.
A solar collector uses solar radiation to heat water.

abschnitte.titel: What the radiation is made of
abschnitte.text: The Sun is a huge ball of hot gas, about 5500 °C at the surface. It sends out **electromagnetic radiation**, which travels at the speed of light and covers the 150 million kilometres to the Earth in about 8 minutes. A large part of it is visible light, and almost as much is **infrared radiation**, which we feel as heat. Only a small part is UV radiation, which tans or burns the skin.

Dark surfaces **absorb** the radiation: they swallow it and get warm. Light surfaces send a lot of light back: they **reflect** it. That is why a black T-shirt gets much warmer in the sun than a white one. A metal slide can also get so hot on a hot summer's day that you burn yourself on it.

Sunlight passes through the windows of a car and warms the seats and the dashboard. But the heat can hardly get out again, so it gets very hot inside, sometimes over 60 °C. That is why you must never leave children or animals in a car in the sun. In the shade of a tree, on the other hand, it is cooler, because the Sun's rays do not reach you there.

abschnitte.titel: The Sun's position and the seasons
abschnitte.text: Around midday the Sun is at its highest and its rays are strongest. In winter it is low; the rays hit the ground at a **slant** and spread over a larger area. That is why it is often cold even on sunny winter days. For the same reason snow melts faster on a **south-facing slope** than on a north-facing slope, because it gets more sun.

The **ozone layer** high up in the atmosphere filters out a large part of the dangerous UV radiation. What still gets through can cause sunburn and, over time, skin cancer. That is why you protect yourself with sun cream, clothing, a hat and sunglasses. In the mountains UV radiation is stronger, and snow reflects it as well.

Plants use sunlight for **photosynthesis** and make sugar and oxygen from it. A **solar collector** on the roof uses solar radiation to heat water for showers and heating. Solar cells, also called photovoltaics, turn sunlight directly into electricity. In Switzerland more and more roofs are being fitted with such systems.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible radiation that we feel as heat.
Invisible, high-energy radiation that can cause sunburn.
To take in radiation and get warm as a result.
To send radiation back like a mirror.
A layer in the atmosphere that keeps out a lot of UV radiation.

gewusst: The sunlight you see right now left the Sun about 8 minutes ago.
Fresh snow reflects most of the sunlight, which is why you need sunglasses when skiing.
In only about an hour and a half the Sun sends as much energy to the Earth as all people together use in a whole year.

teile.einleitung: A synchronous motor is an electric motor whose turning part rotates exactly in time with the alternating current, that is, synchronously. It always runs at the same speed, whether it has little or a lot of work to do. Almost all large power stations produce their electricity with the same machine, just run the other way as a generator.
wichtigste: In a synchronous motor the rotor turns exactly at the speed of the rotating field.
With one pair of poles, the rotating field on the 50 Hz grid turns 3000 times a minute.
With two pairs of poles, a synchronous motor on the 50 Hz grid runs at 1500 revolutions per minute.
The rotor is magnetised by permanent magnets or by a winding supplied with direct current.
A simple synchronous motor does not start by itself on a fixed grid.
If it is loaded too heavily, it falls out of step and stops.
In most large power stations a synchronous machine is installed as the generator.

abschnitte.text: A synchronous motor consists of a fixed part, the **stator**, and a turning part, the **rotor**. In the stator there are copper windings through which three-phase current flows. This produces a magnetic field that travels round in a circle, the **rotating field**. The rotor is itself a magnet, either with permanent magnets or with a winding through which direct current flows.

The rotating field pulls the magnetic rotor along with it, just like a magnet that you move in a circle around a compass needle. The rotor turns **exactly as fast** as the rotating field, hence the name synchronous. The speed depends only on the grid frequency and the number of **pole pairs**: revolutions per minute equal 60 times the frequency divided by the number of pole pairs. On the 50 Hz grid that is 3000 revolutions with one pole pair and 1500 with two.

abschnitte.titel: Starting and falling out of step
abschnitte.text: A simple synchronous motor has a problem: from standstill, the sluggish rotor cannot follow the fast rotating field and simply stays still. That is why engineers build in an extra **starting winding** or let it run up slowly with a **frequency converter**. If the motor is loaded too heavily while running, the rotor can lose touch. Then it falls **out of step** and stops.

If you turn a synchronous machine from outside, for example with a water turbine, it produces electricity and works as a **generator**. Almost all large power stations, whether hydro, nuclear or gas, use such synchronous generators. The generators in hydroelectric power stations in the Swiss Alps turn rather slowly and have many pole pairs instead. An over-excited synchronous machine can supply the grid with **reactive power** as well as real power and so keep the voltage stable.

In the past small synchronous motors drove many electric **clocks**. Because their speed is firmly linked to the grid frequency, they kept good time as long as the frequency was right. Today synchronous motors with permanent magnets are found in many **electric cars**, e-bikes, locomotives and industrial robots. They are very efficient and can be controlled precisely with modern electronics.

begriffe.erklaerung: A magnetic field that turns in a circle.
The turning part of a motor.
The fixed part of a motor.
A pair of north and south poles of a magnet or a winding.
A machine that turns movement into electricity.

gewusst: A motor and a generator are basically the same machine, just used in the opposite direction.
All the large generators in the European power grid turn together at the same rhythm, like a giant orchestra.
The Swiss railways use their own power network with a different frequency from the sockets at home.

teile.einleitung: Elastic potential energy is energy stored in an elastically deformed body. A drawn bow, a compressed spring or a stretched rubber band are full of elastic energy. When you let go, it is released again and can set something in motion.
wichtigste: Elastic energy is found in elastically deformed bodies.
Examples are drawn bows, springs, rubber bands and trampolines.
When you let go, elastic energy usually turns into kinetic energy.
If you stretch a spring twice as far, the elastic energy becomes four times as large.
The formula is: elastic energy equals one half times spring constant times extension squared.
According to Hooke's law the spring force is proportional to the extension.
Without losses, all of the elastic energy is turned into kinetic energy.

abschnitte.text: **Elastic potential energy** is the energy stored in an **elastically** deformed body. Elastic means that the body springs back into its old shape when you let go. A drawn bow, a spring or a rubber band store energy in this way. The work you put in when stretching comes back out when you let go.

When you jump on a **trampoline**, the mat stretches and stores elastic energy. As it springs back, this turns into kinetic energy and flings you upwards. If a rubber band stores 2 joules, a paper pellet can get at most 2 joules of kinetic energy. In the pole vault the strongly bent pole stores elastic energy and lifts the vaulter over the bar.

In the 17th century the Englishman Robert Hooke described how the force of a spring is proportional to its extension. This means: double the extension, double the force. How stiff a spring is is given by the **spring constant** D in newtons per metre. If you hang two identical springs of 200 N/m each one after the other, the whole arrangement has only 100 N/m.

You calculate elastic energy as one half times D times extension squared. So a spring of 200 N/m that is stretched by 0.1 m stores 1 joule. Because the extension is squared, the energy becomes four times as large when the extension is doubled. If you compress a spring of 800 N/m by 5 cm and use it to shoot a ball of 20 g, without losses the ball reaches 10 m/s.

The suspension fork of a mountain bike briefly stores elastic energy when the bike goes over a root and cushions the bump. Mattresses, ballpoint pens with a push button and clothes pegs also contain springs. With the **crossbow**, like the one William Tell uses in the legend, an arrow is shot off by the elastic energy of the bow. Wind-up toy cars also run on spring power.

Inside mechanical watches there is a coiled steel spring, the **mainspring**. When the watch is wound, it is tightened and stores elastic energy. It releases this slowly and evenly and so drives the gear wheels and hands. The Swiss watch industry in the Jura is world-famous for such fine movements.

begriffe.erklaerung: A body that goes back to its shape after being deformed.
A number that shows how stiff or soft a spring is.
The unit of energy.
The coiled spring that drives a mechanical watch.

gewusst: If a rubber band is stretched too far, it is permanently deformed or snaps, and then elastic energy is lost.
A football also briefly stores elastic energy when it hits something, because it is squashed a little.

teile.einleitung: The Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system. It is a huge ball of glowing hot gas that gives us light and warmth. Without the Sun there would be no life on Earth.
wichtigste: The Sun is a star and the centre of our solar system.
