About 109 Earths would fit side by side across the Sun.
The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away from the Earth.
It is about 4.6 billion years old.
More than 99 per cent of the whole mass of the solar system is in the Sun.
Darker patches on its surface are called sunspots.
You must never look directly at the Sun with the naked eye or through binoculars.

abschnitte.text: The Sun is a perfectly ordinary **star**, like many we see in the night sky. It only looks so bright to us because it is much closer than all the other stars. Its diameter is about 1.4 million kilometres, so about 109 Earths fit side by side across it. More than 99 per cent of the whole mass of the **solar system** is in the Sun. Its gravity keeps all eight planets in their orbits.

The Sun is made mainly of hydrogen and helium. In its core the temperature is about 15 million degrees, and the pressure is enormous. There hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium; this is called **nuclear fusion**. This releases a huge amount of energy, which radiates outwards as light and heat. At the visible surface it is still about 5500 degrees hot.

Sometimes darker patches can be seen on the Sun, the **sunspots**. They are a little cooler than their surroundings and so look darker. The number of spots rises and falls in a rhythm of about eleven years. In strong eruptions the Sun hurls charged particles into space. If they hit the Earth, they can set off **auroras**, which can sometimes even be seen in Switzerland.

On average the Earth is about 150 million kilometres away from the Sun. Sunlight takes a little over 8 minutes to travel this distance. The Earth circles the Sun in one year, and because the Earth's axis is tilted, there are **seasons**. Plants use sunlight to grow and so form the basis for almost all life. In Switzerland more and more electricity is being produced with **solar systems** on roofs and dams.

The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a huge cloud of gas and dust. Today it is about halfway through its life. In about five billion years the hydrogen in its core will start to run out. Then it will swell up into a **red giant** and later become a small, dense white dwarf. But that will take an unimaginably long time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge, glowing ball of hot gas that produces its own light.
The fusing of small atomic nuclei into larger ones, which releases a lot of energy.
A slightly cooler and therefore darker patch on the Sun's surface.
The Sun with all the planets, moons and other bodies that circle it.

gewusst: The sunlight you see right now left the Sun a little over 8 minutes ago.
A car driving non-stop at 100 kilometres per hour would need more than 170 years to reach the Sun.
During a total solar eclipse it becomes almost dark for a short time in the middle of the day.

teile.einleitung: A stone is a solid piece of rock, like the ones you find everywhere in streams, on paths and in the mountains. In physics stones are interesting, because they show clearly what sinks and what floats. A pebble goes under in water, but a pumice stone floats.
wichtigste: An ordinary pebble sinks in water, because it is heavier than the same amount of water.
Pumice stone is so light and full of air that it floats on water.
If you throw a stone into water, circular waves form.
Flat stones can be thrown so that they skip several times across the water.
Pebbles in streams are rolled and polished by the water for a long time and so become round and smooth.
There are many stones on the bottom of streams, because they sink.
If a stone lies on a wooden board, the board can carry it in the water.

abschnitte.text: A **stone** is a piece of **rock** made of minerals. There are a great many kinds, for example granite, limestone, sandstone and gneiss. Large blocks of stone are called boulders, small round stones pebbles. In Switzerland the Alps and the Jura are built of different kinds of rock.

Whether something floats depends on its **density**, that is, on how heavy a substance is compared with its volume. A litre of water weighs about 1 kilogram, but a litre of granite about 2.7 kilograms. When the stone dips in, it pushes water aside and so gets **buoyancy**, but this is less than its weight. That is why it sinks to the bottom, and why there are so many stones in every stream.

**Pumice** forms in volcanic eruptions when foaming lava cools down very quickly. Countless small gas bubbles stay trapped in the rock. That is why pumice is so light that it can float on water. After large volcanic eruptions, huge rafts of pumice have drifted on the sea. In the bathroom pumice is used to rub hard skin off the feet.

When a stone falls into water, you usually hear a **splash**. The stone pushes the water aside and **circular waves** form, which spread out in all directions. The bigger the stone, the higher the waves. If you throw a flat stone at a slant and fast, it bounces off the water and skips on several times before it sinks.

Stones in streams and rivers are swept along by the water and roll over the bottom. As they do, they knock against each other and wear down, so that corners and edges disappear. After a long time they are round and smooth; they are then called **river stones** or pebbles. In Switzerland, glaciers have also carried large blocks of stone a long way; these are called **erratic boulders**.

People have used stones since the earliest times, as tools as far back as the Stone Age. Today houses, walls and roads are built from stone and gravel. Stones also store heat well, which is why there are stone ovens and warm stone slabs. Many children collect special stones such as crystals or fossils.

begriffe.erklaerung: Natural solid material made of one or more minerals.
How heavy a substance is in relation to its size.
Force with which water pushes an object that is dipped in upwards.
Large block of stone that a glacier has carried far away.

gewusst: Pumice has so many small holes that it feels almost like a sponge made of stone.
A stone on a board can float, because the board together with the stone pushes aside enough water.
Some erratic boulders on the Swiss Plateau were brought from the Alps by glaciers thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge was a suspension bridge in the US state of Washington that collapsed in the wind in 1940, only about four months after it opened. Because it had already been moving strongly up and down before that, it got the nickname “Galloping Gertie”. The film of its collapse is one of the most famous pictures in the history of engineering.
wichtigste: The first Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed in 1940.
It stood in the US state of Washington.
The collapse happened after about four months in use.
Because of its swaying it was called “Galloping Gertie”.
It collapsed at a wind speed of about 65 km/h, which is not a particularly strong storm.
The main cause was aeroelastic flutter, a self-reinforcing vibration in the wind.
Nobody was killed in the collapse, but a dog was.

abschnitte.text: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge spanned the **Tacoma Narrows**, a strait of Puget Sound near the city of Tacoma. It opened on 1 July 1940 and was then one of the longest **suspension bridges** in the world, with a main span of about 850 metres. The deck was very **slender** and flexible, to save material and money. This elegant but light design was its downfall.

Even while it was being built, the deck moved noticeably up and down in the wind. That is why people called the bridge **“Galloping Gertie”**. Some even drove there specially to experience the wavy ride. Engineers tried to slow down the vibrations with cables and dampers, but it did not help enough.

On 7 November 1940 a wind of about 65 km/h was blowing. Suddenly the deck began to twist about its long axis, a **torsional vibration** in which one side rose while the other sank. After about an hour, parts of the suspension broke, and large pieces of the deck fell into the water. Nobody died, but a dog called Tubby, who was sitting in a car left behind on the bridge, was killed.

For a long time school books said that the bridge collapsed because of simple **resonance**, like a glass shattered by a note. Today we know that the main cause was **aeroelastic flutter**. In this, wind and movement strengthen each other: the twisted deck redirects the wind in such a way that it makes the twisting even bigger. The Swiss bridge builder Othmar Ammann was a member of the commission that investigated the collapse.

After the disaster, bridges were tested as models in a **wind tunnel** much more often. New suspension bridges were given stiffer decks or a shape that lets the wind slip past. In 1950 a new, much stiffer bridge opened at the same place, and in 2007 a second one was added next to it. The wreckage of the old bridge still lies on the seabed and has become an artificial **reef** for fish and other sea creatures.

begriffe.erklaerung: Bridge whose deck hangs from large cables between towers.
A vibration in which something twists back and forth.
Self-reinforcing vibration caused by a flow of air.
Strong vibration when something is pushed at the right rhythm.
Facility in which models are tested with artificial wind.

gewusst: The collapse was filmed, and the film is still shown in physics and engineering lessons today.
The bridge did not collapse in a hurricane, but in a wind that you would rather call a strong breeze.
The remains of the bridge are protected in the USA so that nobody takes them from the seabed.

teile.einleitung: Day and night take turns because the Earth spins on its own axis like a top. On the side facing the Sun it is day, and on the other side it is night. Together a day and a night last about 24 hours.
wichtigste: Day and night happen because the Earth spins on its own axis.
A day and a night together last about 24 hours.
When it is midday in Switzerland, it is night on the other side of the Earth.
In our part of the world the days are longest in summer and shortest in December.
At the equinoxes in March and September, day and night are about the same length.
Far in the north the sun even shines at midnight in summer.
Some animals, such as the owl, are mainly awake at night.

abschnitte.text: The Earth turns once on its own axis in about 24 hours; this is called the **Earth's rotation**. It turns from west to east. That is why it looks as if the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west. In reality it is not the Sun that moves round us; we turn with the Earth towards the Sun and away from it again.

The Sun always lights up only one half of the globe, where it is **day**. On the half facing away it is **night**. When it is midday in Switzerland, for example, it is the middle of the night in New Zealand. That is why the world has different **time zones**; in Switzerland Central European Time applies.

The Earth's axis is tilted, by about 23.5 degrees. In summer the northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so our days are long and the nights short. Around 21 June the day in Switzerland lasts almost 16 hours, around 21 December only a little over 8 hours. These days are called the **solstices**. Around 20 March and 23 September, day and night are about the same length; these are the **equinoxes**.

The further north you travel, the bigger the differences become. North of the **Arctic Circle** the sun does not set for days in summer; this is called the **midnight sun**. In winter, on the other hand, it stays below the horizon for days, and then there is polar night. At the equator, by contrast, day and night are about the same length all year round.

abschnitte.titel: Life by day and by night
abschnitte.text: Many animals, and we humans too, are active during the day and sleep at night. An inner clock in the body makes sure that we get tired in the evening. Other animals are **nocturnal**, for example owls, bats, hedgehogs and badgers. They have especially good eyes, ears or noses for finding their way in the dark.

Even in ancient times people arranged their daily lives around day and night. With sundials they could tell the time from the shadow. Today the day is divided into 24 hours. In Switzerland the clocks are put forward by one hour in summer; this is **summer time**, so that it stays light for longer in the evening.

begriffe.erklaerung: The turning of the Earth on its own axis.
The day of the year with the longest or shortest daylight.
A day in spring or autumn on which day and night are the same length.
An imaginary line far in the north beyond which there is midnight sun; in the south it is the Antarctic Circle.
Animals that are awake at night and sleep during the day.

gewusst: At the equator the Earth's surface turns at more than 1600 kilometres per hour, without us feeling anything.
Astronauts on the ISS see about 16 sunrises a day.
On the planet Venus a single day lasts longer than a whole Venus year.

teile.einleitung: In physics, floating means that an object stays on the surface of the water and does not sink. A cork floats, a stone sinks, and yet a huge steel ship floats. Behind all this is an invisible force: buoyancy.
wichtigste: A body floats if the buoyancy is at least as great as its weight.
The buoyancy is as great as the weight of the water pushed aside.
Bodies that are lighter than the same amount of water float on top.
A cork, a dry leaf and an empty, closed bottle float.
If you fill the bottle completely with sand, it becomes too heavy and sinks.
If you breathe in deeply and lie still, you float more easily.
In the game Float or sink you test what stays on top and what goes under.

abschnitte.text: When an object dips into water, it pushes water aside: it **displaces** it. In return, the water pushes upwards against the object from below. This force is called **buoyancy**. If the buoyancy is as great as the object's weight, it floats; otherwise it sinks.

The Greek scholar **Archimedes** lived more than 2200 years ago in Syracuse on Sicily. He realised that the buoyancy is exactly as great as the weight of the water pushed aside. That is why this law is called **Archimedes' principle**. According to legend, he had the idea in the bath and shouted excitedly Eureka, which means I have found it.

Whether something floats depends on its **density**, that is, how heavy a certain piece of it is. One litre of water weighs about one kilogram. Cork, wood and air are lighter than the same amount of water and therefore float. An empty, closed plastic bottle is full of air and floats. If you fill it with sand, it becomes heavier than the same amount of water and sinks.

A piece of steel sinks at once, but a large steel ship floats. This is because of its shape: the hollow **hull** is full of air and pushes aside a great deal of water. This creates a large buoyancy that carries the ship's weight. If you load a ship, it sinks deeper into the water until enough water is pushed aside again.

Ducks can drift on the water without paddling. Their feathers trap a lot of air and are made water-repellent with an oily secretion. The human body, too, has almost the same density as water. If you breathe in deeply, your lungs fill with air and you float more easily. In the very salty **Dead Sea** you even float almost by yourself, because salt water is denser.

In the game **Float or sink** you put different objects into a bowl of water. First you guess what will stay on top, then you try it out. An apple, a cork and a block of wood float; a coin, a key and a stone sink. A ball of modelling clay sinks, but if you shape it into a little boat, it floats.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which water pushes an object upwards.
How much a certain volume of a substance weighs.
To push water aside when you dip something into it.
The rule that the buoyancy is as great as the weight of the water pushed aside.

gewusst: Icebergs float because ice is a little lighter than water, but about nine tenths of them lie below the surface.
A submarine dives by filling tanks with water and surfaces by pushing the water out again with air.
A fresh egg sinks in tap water, but floats in very salty water.

teile.einleitung: Standby consumption is the electricity an electrical appliance uses even though it is not being used at the moment. The appliance is not completely switched off, but stays on and waits for a command, for example from the remote control. For each appliance this is not much, but across many households a surprising amount of energy adds up.
wichtigste: In standby an appliance stays on and waits for a command.
You can often recognise standby by a small indicator light.
A television on permanent standby at 5 W uses 43.8 kWh a year.
At 25 centimes per kWh this costs about 10.95 francs a year.
A charger in the socket without a phone also usually uses a little electricity.
With a power strip with a switch you can disconnect several appliances from the mains at once.
Because of regulations, new appliances may only use very little electricity on standby.

abschnitte.text: The English word **standby** means something like “ready and waiting”. An appliance on standby is not completely off, but is waiting for a signal. A television, for example, has to notice when someone presses the **remote control**. For this a small part of the electronics stays switched on all the time and uses electricity.

Many appliances in the home have a standby mode: televisions, games consoles, printers, coffee machines, routers and computers. Often a red or orange **indicator light** shows that an appliance is waiting. **Power supplies** and chargers plugged into the socket also often get warm, because they convert a little electricity. Some appliances also show a clock that uses electricity all the time.

You calculate energy as power times time. A television of 5 watts is on standby for 365 times 24 hours a year, that is 8760 hours. That makes 43,800 watt-hours or **43.8 kilowatt-hours**. At an electricity price of 25 centimes per kWh, this costs 10.95 francs. Eight appliances of 2 W each already have a standby power of 16 W together.

A single appliance uses only a little on standby. But because many appliances are waiting at the same time in millions of households, it adds up to a large amount of energy. This energy has to be produced in power stations. So anyone who **saves electricity** helps the environment and their purse.

In the European Union and in Switzerland there are rules for the electricity use of new appliances. These **ecodesign regulations** require many appliances to use at most about 0.5 to 1 watt on standby. Older appliances often use much more. When buying, it is therefore worth looking at the **energy label**.

The easiest way is a **power strip with a switch**, which lets you switch several appliances off completely at once. Unplug chargers from the socket after charging. Some appliances have a real off switch on the appliance itself. But with routers or appliances that make recordings, you should ask your parents first whether they need to stay switched on.

begriffe.erklaerung: State of readiness in which an appliance stays on and waits for a command.
Unit of power, that is, how much energy an appliance uses per second.
Unit of energy, for example 1000 watts for one hour.
Strip with several sockets, often with a switch for turning off all the appliances.

gewusst: An old appliance with 10 W on standby uses almost as much electricity in a year as an LED lamp that is on for many hours every day.
Many appliances that look switched off are really on standby.
If you touch a charger in the socket and it is warm, it is using electricity.

teile.einleitung: The moment of inertia shows how hard it is to set a body turning or to slow down its turning. In rotation it plays the same part as mass does in straight-line motion. It depends not only on the mass, but also on how far this mass is from the axis of rotation.
wichtigste: In rotation the moment of inertia corresponds to mass in straight-line motion.
It depends on the mass and on how the mass is distributed around the axis of rotation.
For a point mass J = m · r²; the SI unit is kg·m².
A thin-walled hollow cylinder has J = m · r², a solid cylinder J = ½ · m · r².
A solid sphere has J = ⅖ · m · r², a thin rod about its middle J = 1/12 · m · l².
Torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration: M = J · α.
The Basel mathematician Leonhard Euler introduced the term in the 18th century.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who wants to push something notices that heavy things are more sluggish. With turning it is similar, only here it also matters where the mass sits. If the mass is far out, the body is harder to set turning. This quantity is called the **moment of inertia** and is written as J or I; its unit is **kg·m²**.

For a small point mass J = m · r², where r is the distance from the axis. So a mass of 2 kg at a distance of 0.5 m has J = 2 · 0.25 = 0.5 kg·m². In a thin-walled **hollow cylinder** all the mass is on the outside, so J = m · r². A solid cylinder has J = ½ · m · r², a solid sphere J = ⅖ · m · r², and a thin rod about its middle J = 1/12 · m · l².

Just as a force accelerates a mass, a **torque** accelerates a rotation. The rule is M = J · α, where α is the angular acceleration. If 10 N·m acts on a body with 2 kg·m², the angular acceleration is 5 rad/s². The greater the moment of inertia, the more slowly a body gets up to speed.

A figure skater spins faster in a **pirouette** when she pulls her arms in, because her moment of inertia then becomes smaller. Tightrope walkers hold a long pole, because its large moment of inertia makes tipping over slower. If you let a solid and a hollow cylinder roll down a ramp at the same time, the solid cylinder wins. Thanks to its large moment of inertia, a **flywheel** in machines stores a lot of rotational energy.

In the 18th century the Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler** studied the rotation of rigid bodies in detail. He coined the term moment of inertia. Later the parallel axis theorem was discovered, named after the Swiss mathematician Jakob Steiner. It is used to calculate the moment of inertia for axes that do not pass through the centre of mass.

begriffe.erklaerung: The imaginary line around which a body turns.
The turning effect of a force, measured in newton metres.
How quickly a rotation becomes faster or slower.
How the mass in a body is spread out, more on the inside or more on the outside.

gewusst: Two Swiss mathematicians, Leonhard Euler and Jakob Steiner, played a decisive part in shaping the study of the moment of inertia.
A raw egg spins less well than a boiled one, because the liquid inside does not turn along with it straight away.
Cats usually land on their feet partly because they cleverly change the moments of inertia of parts of their body.

teile.einleitung: Solar energy is the energy that the Sun sends to the Earth as light and heat. It is the most important source of energy for almost all life on our planet. Today people use it to produce electricity and to heat water.
wichtigste: The Sun supplies the Earth with light and heat.
The energy is produced inside the Sun by nuclear fusion.
Plants use sunlight for photosynthesis.
Solar cells turn sunlight into electricity.
Solar collectors use the Sun to heat water.
Solar energy is one of the renewable energies.
Wind and water power also come from the Sun in the end.

abschnitte.text: The **Sun** is a huge star made of hot gas, mainly hydrogen. In its core the temperature is about 15 million degrees Celsius. There hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium; this is called **nuclear fusion**. This releases an enormous amount of energy, which radiates into space as light and heat.

Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to travel the roughly 150 million kilometres to the Earth. It brings not only **light**, but also **heat**. Without this heat the Earth would be an icy planet without life. The Sun also drives the weather: it evaporates water and moves the air.

Plants catch sunlight with their green pigment and use it to build up sugar; this is called **photosynthesis**. In doing so they give off oxygen, which people and animals breathe. Animals eat plants and so use solar energy indirectly. Coal, oil and natural gas are also stored solar energy from plants and tiny organisms of millions of years ago.

abschnitte.titel: Electricity and heat from the Sun
abschnitte.text: **Solar cells** turn sunlight directly into electricity; this is called photovoltaics. **Solar collectors** on roofs, on the other hand, heat water for showering or heating. In very sunny regions such as Spain, large fields of mirrors focus the light to produce steam for turbines. Solar energy is **renewable**: it does not run out and causes no exhaust fumes while in use.

Switzerland has been greatly expanding its use of solar energy for years. By around 2024 solar power was already covering about a tenth of Switzerland's electricity needs. Valais and Ticino are especially sunny. One disadvantage is that in winter, when a lot of electricity is needed, the sun shines for less time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fusing of atomic nuclei, which releases a lot of energy.
Plants use sunlight to build up sugar and give off oxygen.
An installation that heats water with the Sun's warmth.
Energy from sources that do not get used up.

gewusst: In one hour the Sun sends more energy to the Earth than the whole of humanity uses in a year.
The Sun is so big that more than a million Earths would fit inside it.

teile.einleitung: Specific heat capacity tells you how much energy is needed to warm one kilogram of a substance by one degree. Some substances, such as water, soak up a great deal of energy for this, while others, such as metals, need only a little. This explains why a lake makes the winter climate milder and why a spoon in hot tea warms up quickly.
wichtigste: Specific heat capacity says how much heat 1 kg of a substance needs for each degree it is warmed.
Its SI unit is J/(kg·K).
Liquid water has an especially high value of about 4.2 kJ/(kg·K).
Ice has only about half as much heat capacity as liquid water.
The amount of heat is calculated with Q = c · m · ΔT.
Large lakes such as Lake Geneva store a lot of heat and make the winters on their shores milder.
According to the Dulong-Petit rule, many solid elements have a molar heat capacity of about 25 J/(mol·K).

abschnitte.text: When you warm a substance, you have to add energy to it: **heat**. The **specific heat capacity**, c for short, says how much heat one kilogram of the substance needs to become one kelvin warmer. A difference of one kelvin is the same size as a difference of one degree Celsius. The unit is therefore joules per kilogram and kelvin, written J/(kg·K).

At about 4.2 kJ/(kg·K), liquid **water** has one of the highest values of all substances. Aluminium needs only about 0.9 kJ/(kg·K), iron and steel about 0.45 kJ/(kg·K). That is why a metal pan gets hot much faster than the water in it. **Ice**, by the way, has only about half as much heat capacity as liquid water.

The formula is **Q = c · m · ΔT**, that is heat equals heat capacity times mass times change in temperature. To warm 1 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C you need 4.18 kJ times 80, so about 334 kJ. A 2000-watt kettle does this in about 167 seconds without losses. The other way round: if 0.5 kg of aluminium takes in 9 kJ, its temperature rises by 20 K.

Large lakes such as **Lake Geneva** store huge amounts of heat in summer. In winter they give this heat back only slowly. That is why winters on the shore are often milder than in places far from large bodies of water. For the same reason the climate on sea coasts is more even than inland on the continents; this is called a **maritime climate**.

In the 18th century the Scottish scientist **Joseph Black** realised that different substances take in different amounts of heat. He was one of the first to distinguish clearly between temperature and quantity of heat. In 1819 Pierre Louis Dulong and Alexis Thérèse Petit found the **Dulong-Petit rule**. It says that one mole of many solid elements needs about 25 J/(mol·K).

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that flows from a warmer to a colder body.
The SI unit of temperature; a difference of one kelvin equals one degree Celsius.
The unit of energy and heat.
A certain, very large number of particles, which chemists use to give amounts of substance.

gewusst: A hot water bottle is filled with water because it can store so much heat.
In a fresh apple cake, the pastry is often already lukewarm while the juicy pieces of apple are still hot.
The human body is made largely of water, which is why body temperature changes only slowly.

teile.einleitung: Resistivity is a property of a material that shows how strongly a substance slows down electric current. With it you can work out what resistance a wire of a certain length and thickness has. This is how we know, for example, why power cables are made of copper and heating wires of other alloys.
wichtigste: Resistivity ρ (rho) is a property of the material.
The resistance of a wire is R = ρ · l / A.
A longer wire has more resistance, a thicker one less.
The SI unit is Ω·m; in engineering Ω·mm²/m is often used.
At room temperature silver has the lowest resistivity of all metals.
In metals the resistance rises with temperature.
The alloy constantan hardly changes its resistance with temperature.

abschnitte.text: Every wire slows down the current a little; this is called **electrical resistance**. How much depends on three things: the material, the length and the cross-section. **Resistivity** ρ describes only the influence of the material. It gives the resistance that a cube or a standard wire made of this substance would have.

The rule is **R = ρ · l / A**, where l is the length and A the cross-sectional area. So a copper wire 20 m long with a cross-section of 0.75 mm² and ρ = 0.0178 Ω·mm²/m has about 0.47 Ω. If you double the length, the resistance doubles. If you double the diameter, the area becomes four times as large, which is why the resistance is halved with double the length and double the diameter.

**Silver** has the lowest resistivity, closely followed by copper. Because silver is expensive, cables are usually made of **copper**, with about 0.0178 Ω·mm²/m. At about 0.028 Ω·mm²/m aluminium conducts less well, but is lighter and cheaper, which is why overhead power lines often hang on aluminium cables. For the same resistance an aluminium conductor needs about 1.6 times the cross-section of copper.

In metals the resistance rises when they get warmer, because the atoms vibrate more strongly and get in the way of the electrons. The platinum **Pt100 sensor** makes use of this: it has exactly 100 Ω at 0 °C and about 119 Ω at 50 °C. The alloy **constantan**, made of copper and nickel, on the other hand hardly changes its resistance. That is why precision resistors for measuring instruments are made from it.

If some substances are cooled down very strongly, their resistance suddenly disappears completely. This **superconductivity** was discovered in mercury in 1911 by the Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes. Today superconducting coils produce strong magnetic fields, for example in MRI scanners in hospitals. The particle accelerator at CERN near Geneva also uses superconducting magnets.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly a component slows down the current, measured in ohms (Ω).
The surface you see when you cut straight across a wire.
A mixture of two or more metals.
A state in which a very cold substance conducts current with no resistance at all.

gewusst: A constantan wire with a cross-section of 0.2 mm² only needs to be 4 metres long to have a resistance of 10 Ω.
Glass and plastic have an unimaginably higher resistivity than copper and are therefore used as insulators.
Because thin cables have more resistance and get warm, cables for powerful appliances have to be thicker.

teile.einleitung: A drinking straw is a thin, hollow tube used to suck drinks out of a glass. It is called a straw because in the past hollow stalks of cereal plants really were used for this. A straw is a good way to see how air pressure works.
wichtigste: A straw is hollow so that the drink can flow through it.
The name comes from hollow cereal stalks that people used to drink with.
When you suck, the air outside pushes the drink up the straw.
If you hold your finger over the top of a straw and lift it out of the water, the water stays in the straw.
If a straw has a hole, air flows in and drinking does not work well.
You cannot drink water from the ground with a straw 10 metres long.
More environmentally friendly straws are often made of paper.

abschnitte.text: A **drinking straw** is a tube, usually about 20 centimetres long and a few millimetres thick. The name straw reminds us that people used to drink through hollow **cereal stalks** of rye or wheat. Today there are straws made of plastic, paper, glass, metal, bamboo or even pasta. Some have a **bend** near the top so that you can drink comfortably from a glass.

When you suck on the straw, you draw air out of the tube into your mouth. This makes the **air pressure** in the straw lower. But the air above the drink in the glass keeps pressing on the surface with full force. This pressure pushes the drink up the straw into your mouth. So you do not really pull the drink up; the air pushes it up.

If you put a straw into water, hold your finger over the top and lift it out, the water stays in the straw. The air pressure from below holds it there, because no air can flow in at the top. If you take your finger away, the water runs out at once. If a straw has a **hole**, air flows in through the hole when you suck, and hardly any drink reaches the top.

Air pressure can push water up at most about 10 metres, even if you could suck perfectly. That is why you cannot drink water from the ground with a straw 10 metres long. In reality a person's mouth can only create a much smaller drop in pressure. For the same reason, simple **suction pumps** can only lift water from a shallow depth.

Thousands of years ago people in Mesopotamia were already drinking beer through long tubes. In the 19th century straws made of **rye straw** were used, but they soon went soft and tasted of straw. In 1888 the American **Marvin Stone** patented a drinking straw made of wound paper. Later came the bendy straw and finally cheap plastic straws.

Plastic straws are usually used for only a few minutes and then end up in the rubbish. If they get into nature, they break down only very slowly and can harm animals in the sea. Since 2021 single-use plastic straws have been banned in the **European Union**. That is why today there are many paper straws or **reusable** straws made of glass or metal that you can wash.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force with which the air presses on everything around us.
When there is less air pressure in one place than all around it.
Hollow stem of grasses and cereal plants.
Right to be the only one to use an invention for a certain time.

gewusst: On the Moon you could not drink with a straw, because there is no air pressing on the drink.
The bend in the drinking straw was invented in the USA in the 1930s.
With a straw and your finger you can carry water like a pipette.

teile.einleitung: A ski jump is a steep structure on which ski jumpers take a run-up, take off and fly far through the air. In ski jumping physics and courage work together: speed, air resistance and lift decide the distance. In Switzerland, Engelberg with its large hill is a well-known World Cup venue.
wichtigste: A ski jump consists of the in-run, take-off table, landing slope and outrun.
The size of a hill is given by its hill size, for example HS 140.
The K in K point stands for construction point.
In the in-run jumpers crouch low to go faster.
In flight they hold their skis in a V shape, because this gives more lift.
Jan Boklöv made the V style famous at the end of the 1980s.
A light headwind is helpful, because it gives more lift.
A World Cup event takes place every year on the Gross-Titlis hill in Engelberg.

abschnitte.titel: How a ski jump is built
abschnitte.text: At the top the steep **in-run** begins, a track in which the jumpers pick up speed. At the end is the **take-off table**, from which they take off. Then comes the curved **landing slope**, which roughly follows the flight path, so that the jumpers are never high above the ground. At the bottom they slow down in the flat outrun.

The **K point**, or construction point, marks a distance the hill is built for. Anyone who lands exactly there gets 60 distance points in many competitions, and for every metre more or less, points are added or taken away. The **hill size**, HS for short, shows how far you can still land safely. So a hill with HS 140 is meant for jumps of up to about 140 metres.

In the in-run the jumpers go into a deep **crouch**, so that the air resistance stays small and they go faster. At the take-off table on large hills they reach almost 100 kilometres per hour. In flight they lean far forward; body and skis then act like a wing and create **lift**. A light headwind increases this lift, which is why differences in wind are balanced out with points today.

In the past ski jumpers held their skis parallel next to each other. At the end of the 1980s the Swede **Jan Boklöv** spread them into a V and at first lost style points for it. But the **V style** brought much more lift and greater distances. Soon everyone was jumping like this. Because of lift there are also strict rules for the suits, as wide suits would carry the jumper like a sail.

In **Engelberg** there is the Gross-Titlis hill, where a World Cup event takes place every December. In **Einsiedeln** there is a modern ski jump complex where many young jumpers train. The Swiss **Simon Ammann** won four Olympic gold medals, two each in Salt Lake City 2002 and in Vancouver 2010. This makes him one of the most successful ski jumpers of all time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The end of the in-run, from which the jumper takes off.
The construction point, a marked distance the hill is built for.
The distance up to which you can still land safely on a hill.
A force of the air that carries the jumper upwards.

gewusst: On the largest ski flying hills in the world, ski jumpers fly further than the length of two football pitches.
Ski jumpers land in the Telemark style, with one leg in front and one behind, otherwise they lose points.
At big competitions the track in the in-run is often made of ice, so that it is always equally fast.

teile.einleitung: The dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled so that the invisible water vapour in it turns into tiny drops of water. Then dew, fog or misted-up windows form. The dew point explains many everyday observations, from wet grass in the morning to steamed-up glasses.
wichtigste: At the dew point the air is saturated with water vapour.
If the air temperature and the dew point are the same, the relative humidity is 100 per cent.
If air cools below the dew point, part of the water vapour turns into water.
In the morning dew forms on the grass, because the grass cools below the dew point during the night.
A bottle from the fridge mists up because the air next to it cools below the dew point.
If the air contains more water vapour, the dew point rises.
If the dew point is below zero, frost forms instead of dew.

abschnitte.text: Air always contains some **water vapour**, that is, water in an invisible gas form. Warm air can take up much more water vapour than cold air. When air cools down, at some point it reaches a limit where it cannot hold any more vapour. This temperature is called the **dew point**. If the air gets even colder, part of the vapour turns into tiny droplets; this is called **condensation**.

On clear nights the ground and the blades of grass give off heat into space and cool down a lot. The air right next to the grass cools below the dew point. The water vapour settles on the blades as glistening drops: this is **dew**. If it is so cold that the dew point is below zero, fine ice crystals form instead: **frost**. When there are clouds or wind there is usually less dew, because the ground then cools down less.

If you take a cold bottle out of the fridge, it soon gets wet. The warm room air cools below the dew point next to the cold bottle, and water settles on it. The same happens to your **glasses** when you come into a warm room from outside in winter. Window panes also mist up on the inside in winter, especially in the kitchen and bathroom. Airing rooms regularly stops damp and **mould** from forming on cold walls.

**Relative humidity** shows what percentage of the possible amount of water vapour the air contains at the moment. If the air temperature and the dew point are close together, the air is very humid. If they are the same, the relative humidity is 100 per cent. If the air contains more water vapour, the dew point rises. A high dew point in summer, say above 18 degrees, feels muggy and oppressive.

When air rises, it cools until it reaches the dew point, and then **clouds** form. A rule of thumb says: the cloud base in metres is about 125 times the difference between the temperature and the dew point. So at 20 degrees with a dew point of 12 degrees, the cloud base is about 1000 metres up. If the air right at the ground cools below the dew point, **fog** forms, like the fog that often lies over the Swiss Plateau in autumn. That is why weather services such as MeteoSwiss give the dew point as well as the temperature.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water in gas form, which you cannot see.
When water vapour cools down and turns back into liquid water.
What percentage of the possible moisture the air contains at the moment.
Fine ice crystals that form when the dew point is below zero.

gewusst: The cloud you see when you breathe out in winter forms because the moist breath cools below the dew point in the cold.
The white trail behind an aeroplane, the contrail, also forms through condensation of water vapour.
In the desert the dew point can be far below zero, even though it is hot.

teile.einleitung: Weightlessness is the state in which you no longer feel your own weight and float freely. Astronauts on the International Space Station ISS experience it every day. The surprising thing is that the Earth's gravity has not disappeared up there at all.
wichtigste: In weightlessness people and objects float; a pen you let go of does not fall to the floor.
On the ISS, at a height of about 400 km, the Earth's gravity is still about 90 per cent of its value at the Earth's surface.
You float because the space station and the people inside are falling freely around the Earth together.
The ISS flies at about 7.7 km/s and circles the Earth in about 90 minutes.
In weightlessness liquids form balls, and candle flames burn round.
On Earth you can float for about 20 seconds at a time on a parabolic flight.
In weightlessness the body loses muscle and bone mass, which is why astronauts exercise every day.

abschnitte.text: Many people think there is no gravity in space. But at a height of 400 km the Earth still pulls almost as strongly as on the ground. The ISS is constantly falling towards the Earth, but at the same time it is flying sideways so fast that it always falls past the Earth. This state is called **free fall**. Because the station and everything in it fall at exactly the same speed, nothing presses against the floor, and everything floats. That is why physicists also speak of **microgravity**.

On the space station everything has to be fastened down, or it floats away. Tools are secured with **Velcro** or cords. Astronauts sleep in sleeping bags fixed to the wall. Instead of bread they often eat tortillas, because these do not make crumbs that could get into the equipment. The toilet sucks everything away with an **air flow**, because without gravity nothing would flow downwards.

In weightlessness a drop of water becomes a floating ball, because **surface tension** holds it together. A candle flame also looks completely different: it is round and bluish. On Earth hot air rises and stretches the flame upwards; this is called **convection**. Without buoyancy this flow does not happen, so the flame stays round and burns more weakly.

If you cannot fly into space, you can experience weightlessness on a **parabolic flight**. A plane climbs steeply and then flies an arc like a thrown ball. During this arc everyone in the cabin floats for about 20 seconds. One flight is made up of many such arcs one after another. In **drop towers**, too, experiments are made weightless for a few seconds.

Because the muscles no longer have to carry the body's weight, they become weaker, and the bones lose mass too. Astronauts therefore exercise for about two hours every day on a treadmill and strength machines. Ordinary scales do not work, so **body mass** is measured with a springy oscillation and calculated with the formula F = m·a. Many space travellers feel a bit sick for the first few days, because their sense of balance is confused.

**Claude Nicollier** from the canton of Vaud was the first Swiss astronaut. In the 1990s he flew into space four times on the Space Shuttle and, among other things, helped to repair the Hubble Space Telescope. Since 2022, with **Marco Sieber**, a Swiss person has once again been part of the astronaut corps of the European Space Agency ESA. Many experiments in weightlessness also come from Swiss universities.

begriffe.erklaerung: State in which you do not feel your weight and float freely.
Falling without anything slowing you down, with everything falling at the same speed.
A flight in an arc during which you are weightless for a short time on Earth.
Technical term for almost complete weightlessness, for example on the ISS.
A flow in which warm air or warm water rises upwards.

gewusst: The crew of the ISS sees about 16 sunrises every day, because they circle the Earth so fast.
In weightlessness astronauts grow a few centimetres taller, because their spine stretches.
In space tears do not run down your cheeks, but stay stuck to your eye as a small bubble of water.

teile.einleitung: The seat belt is a belt in a car that holds people in their seat in an accident. It is one of the most important inventions for road safety. How it works can be explained by the inertia of the body.
wichtigste: The seat belt is needed because of the inertia of the body.
The Swede Nils Bohlin is regarded as the inventor of the modern three-point belt.
A belt pretensioner pulls the belt tight in a flash in an accident.
A belt force limiter gives way in a controlled manner to protect the chest.
The belt should fit tightly, and the lap belt should run low across the pelvis.
In Switzerland children need a child seat up to the age of 12 or a height of 150 cm.
A crash at 50 km/h is about the same as a fall from a height of 10 m.

abschnitte.text: A body keeps moving at the same speed as long as no force slows it down; this is called **inertia**. If a car crashes into an obstacle, it stops almost immediately. But the people in the car keep flying forwards at the old speed. Without a belt they would crash into the steering wheel, the windscreen or the front seat.

In 1959 the Swedish car maker Volvo brought out the modern **three-point belt**, developed by the engineer Nils Bohlin. It holds the body at three points, with a shoulder belt across the chest and a lap belt. Volvo made the invention freely available so that all manufacturers could use it. It is estimated that since then this belt has saved a great many lives around the world.

Modern cars have a **belt pretensioner**, which pulls the belt tight in a fraction of a second in a crash. This way the body is slowed down along with the car as early as possible. Afterwards a **belt force limiter** gives way a little in a controlled manner, so that the force on the chest does not become too great. Together with the airbag, they spread the braking force as gently as possible.

The belt must fit tightly against the body and must not be twisted. The shoulder belt runs over the shoulder and the chest, never over the neck or under the arm. The **lap belt** lies low across the pelvis and not over the tummy. You should take off thick winter jackets so that the belt does not sit too loosely.

An adult belt does not yet fit children properly: it runs across the neck and tummy. That is why in Switzerland children need a suitable **child seat** up to the age of 12 or until they are 150 cm tall. Small children travel most safely facing backwards. Even on short journeys the rule is: everyone is buckled up before the car sets off.

begriffe.erklaerung: Property of a body to keep its movement.
Belt that secures the shoulder and pelvis at three points.
Device that tightens the belt in a flash in an accident.
Part that lets the belt give way in a controlled manner.

gewusst: In a crash at 50 km/h, a body is pushed forwards for a brief moment with many times its own weight.
In aeroplanes there are only lap belts, because different forces act there than in a car.
A belt that has been through a serious accident must be replaced.

teile.einleitung: A stopwatch is a watch that measures how long something takes. You start it at the beginning, it counts up from zero, and at the end you stop it. In sport, at school and in experiments it is an important measuring device.
wichtigste: A stopwatch measures how long something takes.
After starting, it counts up from zero.
With the reset button you set it back to zero.
In ski races a light barrier measures the time to a hundredth of a second.
In experiments a stopwatch is used to measure how long processes take.
Switzerland is known all over the world for its watches.
Today almost all mobile phones have a built-in stopwatch.

abschnitte.text: A **stopwatch** does not show the time of day, but a length of time. With the start button it begins counting from zero. With the stop button it stops, and you can read off the measured time. With the **reset button** you set it back to zero so that you can measure again.

In the past there were only mechanical stopwatches with hands, gear wheels and a spring that had to be wound up. Today most stopwatches are **digital** and show the time with numbers. Inside them a tiny **quartz crystal** vibrates very regularly, and the electronics count these vibrations. Wristwatches with a built-in stopwatch function are called **chronographs**.

You can also do calculations with a stopwatch. If Nina needs 30 seconds for one lap around the square, two laps at the same pace take 1 minute. If you measure how long a bike takes for 100 metres, you can work out its **speed** from that. In experiments you measure, for example, how long a pendulum takes for ten swings and then divide by ten.

In ski races the time has to be very precise, because **hundredths of a second** often decide who wins. That is why times are no longer taken by hand, but electronically. At the start a starting gate sets off the clock, and at the finish the skier breaks a **light barrier**. By hand you would always press the button a little too late because of your reaction time.

Switzerland is known all over the world for its **watch industry**. Many watch companies are based in the Jura, for example in the Vallée de Joux, in La Chaux-de-Fonds or in Biel. Swiss companies such as Omega and Longines have long been responsible for timekeeping at big sporting events such as the Olympic Games. The timing at ski races also often comes from Switzerland.

Today there is a stopwatch in almost every mobile phone, in sports watches and in fitness bands. Many can save **split times**, for example for each lap on the running track. Professionals use systems that measure thousandths of a second. For school, though, a simple stopwatch is usually enough.

begriffe.erklaerung: Watch that measures a length of time from start to stop.
Beam of light that sets off a signal when someone breaks it.
Wristwatch with a built-in stopwatch function.
The short time until you react to something, for example by pressing a button.

gewusst: A person's reaction time is usually about 0.2 seconds, which is why hand timing is imprecise.
A hundredth of a second is shorter than the blink of an eye.
At the 2014 Olympic Games, Dominique Gisin of Switzerland and Tina Maze of Slovenia shared gold in the downhill, because they were equally fast to the hundredth of a second.

teile.einleitung: The protective earth conductor is a special wire in electric cables that protects people from electric shocks. It can be recognised by its green and yellow colour. Normally no current flows through it; it only becomes important when there is a fault.
wichtigste: The protective earth conductor is green and yellow and is abbreviated to PE.
It is connected to the metal casing of a device.
The neutral conductor is blue, and the line conductor carrying the voltage is usually brown.
If a line conductor touches the casing, the current flows away through the protective earth conductor and the fuse blows.
If the protective earth conductor is broken, the casing can become live when there is a fault.
Class II devices are double insulated and do not need a protective earth conductor.
In Switzerland, the middle pin of the three-pin plug is the protective earth conductor.

abschnitte.text: A device cable usually contains three wires with fixed colours. The **line conductor**, also called the phase, carries the voltage and is usually brown. The **neutral conductor** is blue and carries the current back. The protective earth conductor has green and yellow stripes and is labelled PE in circuit diagrams, from the English Protective Earth.

The protective earth conductor connects the metal casing of a device to the house's **earthing**. If a wire comes loose inside the device and touches the casing, the current flows away immediately through the protective earth conductor. This produces such a large current that the fuse blows and breaks the circuit. Without the protective earth conductor, the casing would be live, and anyone touching it would get a dangerous shock.

Devices are divided into **protection classes**. Class I devices have a metal casing and need a protective earth conductor, for example washing machines, cookers or metal kettles. Class II devices are double insulated: their live parts are covered twice. That is why they often have only a two-pin plug, for example mobile phone chargers or hairdryers.

On the three-pin Swiss plug, the middle pin, which is slightly offset, is the protective earth conductor. In newer houses, a **residual current device**, RCD for short, also provides protection. It compares the current flowing out and back and switches off in a flash at even small differences. Work on a house's wiring may only be carried out by trained professionals.

Cables with damaged insulation should no longer be used. A plug with three pins must never be altered so that the protective earth conductor is missing. Adapters that do not pass on the protective earth conductor are also dangerous. If a device tingles when you touch it, pull out the plug at once and have it checked.

begriffe.erklaerung: The wire that carries the electrical voltage, often brown.
The blue wire through which the current flows back.
A conducting connection to the ground, through which fault currents flow away.
A grouping of devices according to how they protect against electric shock.
A switch that cuts off the current at once when there are fault currents.

gewusst: The green and yellow colour is reserved for the protective earth conductor and may not be used for any other wire.
The symbol for protection class II is two squares, one inside the other.
A residual current device reacts in fractions of a second.

teile.einleitung: Thermography is a method of making heat visible. A thermal imaging camera measures the invisible infrared radiation that every object gives off and shows it as a coloured picture. This lets you see where it is warm and where it is cold, even in complete darkness.
wichtigste: A thermal imaging camera makes the heat radiation of surfaces visible.
Red and yellow areas on a thermal image usually show warmer places.
In technical language a picture from a thermal imaging camera is called a thermogram.
Thermography is used to find badly insulated places on houses.
The fire brigade uses thermal imaging cameras to find people in smoke.
A thermal imaging camera cannot see through an ordinary window pane.
Electricians use thermal imaging cameras to track down overheated connections.

abschnitte.text: Every object gives off radiation, and the warmer it is, the more it gives off. At everyday temperatures this is mainly **infrared radiation**, which our eyes cannot see. It was discovered in 1800 by the astronomer William Herschel, when he measured warming with a thermometer beyond the red end of the Sun's spectrum. **Thermography** uses this radiation.

Instead of an ordinary image sensor, a **thermal imaging camera** has a sensor that reacts to infrared radiation. A computer turns the measured temperatures into colours; these are called **false colours**. Usually warm places are red, yellow or white and cold ones blue or violet. The finished picture is called a **thermogram**.

A thermal imaging camera cannot see through walls, not even through an ordinary **window pane**. Glass hardly lets through the heat radiation the camera measures; on the picture it looks almost like a mirror. It cannot see through water either. Through smoke and darkness, on the other hand, it can see very well.

With thermography you can find **badly insulated places** on houses, leaky windows or thermal bridges through which heat from the heating is lost. A cold **winter night** is best for this, when it is warm inside and cold outside and no sun is warming the walls. Then the places where heat escapes light up clearly on the picture. In this way house owners can insulate exactly where it is needed and save energy.

The **fire brigade** uses thermal imaging cameras to find people in thick smoke and to track down hidden pockets of embers. Electricians use them to discover **overheated connections** before they cause a fire. During epidemics thermal imaging cameras were used, for example at airports, to spot people with a raised body temperature. The police and rescue services also use them at night to search for missing people.

In Switzerland farmers and volunteers search the meadows with **drones** and thermal imaging cameras before mowing. In this way they find young fawns hiding in the tall grass and carry them to safety. Scientists also use thermography to watch nocturnal animals without disturbing them. Some snakes, such as rattlesnakes, can even sense heat radiation themselves.

begriffe.erklaerung: Method that makes heat visible with a camera.
Invisible heat radiation that every object gives off.
A picture taken with a thermal imaging camera.
Colours that are not real but stand for temperatures.
Place on a house through which especially large amounts of heat escape to the outside.

gewusst: On a thermal image you can sometimes still see where someone was sitting a moment ago, because the chair is still warm.
To a thermal imaging camera a pane of glass looks almost like a mirror.
Thanks to drones with thermal imaging cameras, many fawns are saved from death by mowing in Switzerland every year.

teile.einleitung: In electrical engineering a coil is a wound-up wire through which current can flow. When current flows through it, a magnetic field forms, like that of a bar magnet. Coils are found in electric motors, loudspeakers, transformers and many other devices.
wichtigste: A coil consists of many turns of an insulated wire.
The copper wire is coated with varnish so that the turns are insulated from each other.
From the outside, the magnetic field of a coil looks like that of a bar magnet.
Inside a long coil the magnetic field is almost uniform.
Twice as many turns with the same current and the same length give a magnetic field twice as strong.
The unit of inductance is the henry.
A coil without an iron core is called an air-core coil, and a long cylindrical coil is also called a solenoid.

abschnitte.text: A coil is made by winding a wire many times round a cylinder. Each round is called a **turn**. Usually **copper wire** is used, coated with a thin layer of varnish. The varnish insulates the turns from each other; otherwise the current would simply flow straight across the coil.

When current flows through a coil, a **magnetic field** forms. From the outside it looks like that of a bar magnet, with a north and a south pole. Inside a long coil the field is almost **uniform**, that is, equally strong and pointing the same way everywhere. If you put an **iron core** inside, the field becomes much stronger, and an electromagnet is created.

The field strength inside depends on the current, the number of turns and the length of the coil. If you double the number of turns from 200 to 400 with the same current and the same length, the field becomes twice as strong. If a coil has 25 layers of 40 turns each, that makes 1000 turns altogether. A long, cylindrical coil is also called a **solenoid**.

A coil resists every change in the current; this property is called **inductance**. Its unit is the **henry**, named after the American physicist Joseph Henry. In 1831 Michael Faraday discovered that a changing magnetic field produces a voltage in a coil. This **electromagnetic induction** is the basis of generators and transformers.

In every **electric motor** coils turn in a magnetic field. A **loudspeaker** has a small voice coil that moves a membrane in time with the music. Transformers on railway lines and in chargers are made of two coils on a shared iron core. Induction hobs, doorbells and the charging coils of wireless phone chargers also use coils.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single round of the wire around the coil.
The property of a coil to resist changes in current, measured in henries.
A coil without an iron core inside.
A coil with an iron core that is only magnetic when current flows.

gewusst: Huge electromagnets in scrapyards lift whole cars and drop them when the current is switched off.
A smartphone contains tiny coils for the loudspeaker, vibration and wireless charging.
The particle accelerator at CERN near Geneva uses thousands of superconducting coils as magnets.

teile.einleitung: The centre of gravity is the point of a body where you can imagine its whole weight to be concentrated. If you support an object exactly there, it stays balanced. Whether a tower stands, a racing car takes a bend safely or a roly-poly toy rights itself depends on the centre of gravity.
wichtigste: At the centre of gravity you can imagine the whole weight of a body to be concentrated.
In an evenly made ruler the centre of gravity is in the middle.
The centre of gravity can also lie outside the body, for example in the middle of a ring.
A body stands steadily as long as its centre of gravity is above its base.
A low centre of gravity makes vehicles and objects more stable.
In a person standing upright the centre of gravity is roughly in the area of the pelvis.
You find the centre of gravity of a flat shape by hanging it up from two points and drawing in the plumb lines.

abschnitte.titel: What is the centre of gravity?
abschnitte.text: Every body is made up of countless small parts, all of which are pulled by the Earth. For many calculations you can pretend that the whole weight is gathered in one single point, the **centre of gravity**. If you lay a ruler on your finger, it balances exactly when your finger is under the centre of gravity. In evenly made objects such as a ruler, a ball or a cube, it lies exactly in the middle. More than 2000 years ago the Greek scholar **Archimedes** was already studying where centres of gravity lie.

It is easy to find the centre of gravity of a flat, irregular piece of card. You hang it up freely from one corner and use a thread with a weight to draw in the vertical **plumb line**. Then you hang it up from another point and draw the second plumb line. Where the two lines cross is the centre of gravity. The centre of gravity does not have to lie in the material: in a ring or a boomerang it lies in the air.

An object stands safely as long as the vertical line through its centre of gravity lies within its **base**. If the centre of gravity moves beyond it, it tips over. The Leaning Tower of Pisa is only still standing because, despite its tilt, its centre of gravity is above its foundations. A **low centre of gravity** makes things more stable: that is why racing cars sit very low on the road and do not tip over so easily in fast bends. A **roly-poly toy** always rights itself again, because its centre of gravity is right at the bottom in its heavy, round base.

abschnitte.titel: The centre of gravity in sport
abschnitte.text: In a person standing upright the centre of gravity is roughly in the area of the pelvis. If you move your arms or legs, it shifts. In the **Fosbury Flop**, with which the American Dick Fosbury became Olympic high jump champion in 1968, the body arches backwards over the bar. In doing so, the centre of gravity can stay outside the body and even below the bar, while the body crosses it bit by bit. Gymnasts on the balance beam and tightrope walkers also constantly keep their centre of gravity above the narrow surface.

abschnitte.titel: Centre of gravity in everyday life
abschnitte.text: When packing a **hiking rucksack**, heavy things belong close to your back. That way the centre of gravity stays close to your body and you are not pulled backwards while walking. Lorries and buses are loaded so that the centre of gravity is not too high. Ships also have heavy ballast at the bottom so that they do not capsize in the waves. Crane operators have to make sure that the load does not make the crane topple over, which is why many cranes carry counterweights.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point where you can imagine the whole weight of a body to be concentrated.
An exactly vertical line shown by a hanging weight.
The surface on which a body rests or stands.
A state in which a body does not tip over and does not move.
A weight that balances a load so that nothing tips over.

gewusst: If you stand with your back and heels against a wall, you cannot bend forward without falling over, because your centre of gravity cannot get above your feet.
A fork and a spoon slotted into each other and joined with a toothpick can balance on the rim of a glass, because their shared centre of gravity lies below the point of support.
The shared centre of gravity of the Earth and the Moon still lies inside the Earth, but not at its centre.

teile.einleitung: A mirror image is the image you see in a mirror or on a smooth surface of water. It looks like an exact copy, but it is swapped: if you raise your right hand, your mirror image seems to raise its left. Mirror images play an important part in physics, in mathematics and even in animal research.
wichtigste: A mirror image in a flat mirror is the same size as the object.
It is upright and seems to be as far behind the mirror as you are in front of it.
If you raise your right hand, your mirror image seems to raise its left.
You cannot touch a mirror image; it is only an image.
To see yourself from head to toe you need a mirror half as tall as you are.
Small children usually recognise themselves in the mirror at about 18 months.
Chimpanzees can also recognise themselves in the mirror.

abschnitte.text: Light from your face falls on the mirror and is sent back. In your mind your eye extends the light rays straight backwards. That is why the image seems to be behind the mirror, even though there is only the wall there. Because no real light comes together there, it is called a **virtual image**: you cannot touch it and cannot catch it on a sheet of paper.

In a flat mirror the mirror image is **the same size** as you and upright. If you stand 1 metre in front of the mirror, your image seems to stand 1 metre behind it, so 2 metres away from you. If you go closer, the image comes closer too. A wall mirror only has to be **half as tall** as you for you to see all of yourself, no matter how far away you stand.

People often say that a mirror swaps left and right. Strictly speaking, though, it swaps **front and back**: what is closer to the mirror is also closer to the mirror in the image. Because your mirror image is looking at you, it seems to raise its left hand when you raise your right. That is why writing appears reversed in the mirror, as **mirror writing**.

Whether a living creature recognises itself in the mirror is tested with the **mirror test**: a spot of colour is secretly put on its face, and you watch whether it touches the spot on its own body. Chimpanzees pass this test, as do other great apes, dolphins, Asian elephants and magpies. Many other animals, on the other hand, think their mirror image is a strange member of their own species. Small children usually recognise themselves at about 18 months.

In geometry, reflecting in a line is called **reflection in an axis**. A shape that looks the same on both sides of a line has **line symmetry**, like a butterfly or a heart. Many letters, such as A, H or M, are also symmetrical and look the same in the mirror. Our face, on the other hand, is never completely symmetrical, which is why you sometimes look a little different in photos than in the mirror.

On the front of some ambulances the word “Ambulance” is written in **mirror writing**, so that drivers can read it the right way round in their rear-view mirror. The artist Leonardo da Vinci wrote many of his notes in mirror writing. If you put two mirrors opposite each other, you get a seemingly endless tunnel of mirror images. And in curved mirrors, for example in a hall of mirrors, you look funny: fat, thin or tall.

begriffe.erklaerung: An image that only seems to lie behind the mirror.
Writing that is written back to front and only looks right in a mirror.
Experiment that tests whether a living creature recognises itself in the mirror.
Exactly the same on both sides of a line.

gewusst: Your mirror image is never exactly how others see you, because they see you without the reflection.
A full-length mirror only has to be half as tall as you, whether you stand close or far away.
Magpies are the first birds for which scientists were able to show that they recognise themselves in the mirror.

teile.einleitung: A zip line is a tightly stretched cable on which you whizz from a higher to a lower point with a pulley and a seat or harness. You find them in playgrounds, rope parks and in the mountains. On one you experience the physics of gravity, energy and inertia with your own body.
wichtigste: The seat of a zip line hangs from a pulley on the cable.
You start moving by yourself, because the start is higher than the finish.
Pulleys run much more easily than a simple hook, because they reduce friction.
The cable is usually made of steel wire.
The cable sags because the weight of the person riding pulls it down.
At the end a spring buffer often brakes, and because of inertia you swing forwards.
Before setting off, you check that the line is clear.

abschnitte.titel: How a zip line is built
abschnitte.text: A zip line consists of a tightly stretched **steel cable** between two posts, trees or rocks. A trolley with one or more **pulleys** runs on the cable. From it hangs a seat, a disc or, on large installations, a climbing harness. At the end a **spring buffer** or a brake makes sure that you stop gently.

At the start you have a lot of **potential energy** because of the height. During the ride gravity pulls downwards, and this energy is turned into kinetic energy. The bigger the difference in height, the faster you go. Part of the energy is lost through friction and air resistance.

A simple hook would rub hard on the cable and soon get stuck. Pulleys turn with the movement and therefore have only a small **rolling friction**. Good pulleys also have ball bearings. This way you can still go a long way with only a small slope.

No cable is completely straight; it sags, especially when someone is riding on it. This **sag** means that towards the end you go a little uphill and slow down. If the trolley suddenly stops at the end, your body swings on forwards because of **inertia**. That is why you hold on tight and sit up straight.

Before starting you check that nobody is standing on the line or in the landing area. Only one person rides at a time, and you wait until the seat has been brought back. In rope parks and on long zip lines in the mountains you are secured with a harness and two karabiners. These large installations are often also called a **zip line** or flying fox.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that a body has because it is high up.
Small friction that occurs when a wheel rolls.
How far a cable hangs down in the middle.
Property of bodies to want to keep their movement.

gewusst: On long zip lines in the mountains you reach speeds like a car on a country road.
Zip lines were originally used in mountain regions to carry goods across gorges.
The English term flying fox is actually the name of a kind of large bat.

teile.einleitung: A cable car is a means of transport in which cabins, chairs or carriages are pulled or carried by a cable. In the mountains it quickly takes people over steep slopes and deep valleys. Switzerland is a real cable car country with several world records.
wichtigste: In an aerial cableway the cabins hang from cables.
In a funicular the carriages run on rails and are pulled by a cable.
The cable is driven by a large electric motor in a station.
Pylons stop the cable from sagging too low.
On a chairlift you sit on open seats.
The Stoos funicular in the canton of Schwyz is considered the steepest funicular in the world.
The cabin of the Titlis Rotair turns during the journey.

abschnitte.text: In an **aerial cableway** the cabins float on cables high above the ground. An **aerial tramway** usually has two large cabins that take turns going up and down. In a **gondola lift** many small cabins run round in a continuous loop. Chairlifts have open seats, and on a ski tow you are pulled up the slope on your skis.

In a **funicular** the carriages run on rails on the slope. Often two carriages are attached to the same cable: when one goes up, the other goes down, and they pass each other in the middle. In this way the heavy carriage going downhill helps to pull the other one up. The **Stoos funicular** in the canton of Schwyz opened in 2017 and, with a gradient of up to 110 per cent, is considered the steepest funicular in the world. Its round cabins turn as it goes, so that the floor always stays level.

In one of the stations there is a large **electric motor**, which moves the haul rope via a huge wheel. The track ropes are twisted from many thin steel wires and are very strong. Between the valley and the mountain there are **pylons**, so that the cable does not hang too low. Several brakes and an emergency drive make sure that the cable car can stop safely even if there is a fault.

There are a great many cable cars in Switzerland, many of them in the ski resorts of the Alps. In 1992 the **Titlis Rotair** near Engelberg was the first revolving aerial cableway cabin in the world. A cable car goes up the Klein Matterhorn near Zermatt to almost 3900 metres above sea level. Some villages, for example in the mountains of Central Switzerland, can even only be reached by cable car.

Cable cars are among the safest means of transport. Cables, pulleys and brakes are checked regularly and replaced after a certain time. In strong **wind** or thunderstorms the service is stopped. If a cable car gets stuck, rescue teams can lower the passengers out of the cabin on ropes.

begriffe.erklaerung: An aerial cableway with two cabins that shuttle back and forth.
A cable car with many small cabins that run round continuously.
The thick steel cable on which the cabin of an aerial cableway rolls.
The cable that is moved by the motor and pulls the cabin.
How steep a route is; 100 per cent equals an angle of 45 degrees.

gewusst: A gradient of 110 per cent is steeper than 45 degrees, so steeper than a normal staircase.
In winter many cable cars have a ski rack on the outside of the cabin.
In cities such as La Paz in Bolivia, cable cars also serve as public transport.

teile.einleitung: Temperature tells you how warm or cold something is. In physics it shows how fast the tiny particles of a substance are moving. In Switzerland it is usually measured in degrees Celsius, and in science also in kelvins.
wichtigste: Temperature describes how warm or cold a body is.
The higher the temperature, the faster the particles of a substance move.
Pure water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at normal air pressure.
In the mountains water boils below 100 °C, because the air pressure is lower there.
Absolute zero is at about minus 273 °C; it cannot get colder.
20 °C is about 293 kelvins.
Most substances expand when warm, which is why bridges have expansion joints.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of tiny **particles** that are constantly moving. Temperature is a measure of how vigorous this movement is. When the temperature rises, the particles vibrate and dart about faster. It is measured with a **thermometer**.

The **Celsius scale** comes from the Swedish scientist Anders Celsius, who proposed it in 1742. Its fixed points are the freezing point and the boiling point of water. In science the **kelvin scale** is used, which starts at 0 at absolute zero. To get from Celsius to kelvin, you add about 273, so 20 °C is about 293 K. In the USA people still measure in degrees Fahrenheit in everyday life.

**Absolute zero** is at minus 273.15 °C or 0 kelvin. There the particles would have the least possible movement. This temperature can never quite be reached, but scientists have come very close to it in laboratories. For comparison: in space between the galaxies it is about minus 270 °C.

At normal air pressure at sea level, water boils at 100 °C. The higher you climb, the lower the **air pressure**, and the sooner water starts to boil. At about 3000 metres above sea level it already boils at about 90 °C. That is why pasta and eggs take longer to cook in a mountain hut.

When a substance gets warmer, its particles need more space and it expands. That is why bridges have **expansion joints**, so that they can expand in summer without breaking. At certain temperatures a substance also changes its state, for example when ice melts. Our body keeps its temperature at about 37 °C; just a few degrees more means a fever.

The highest temperature ever measured in Switzerland is 41.5 °C, recorded in August 2003 in Grono in the canton of the Grisons. The lowest official temperature was measured in January 1987 in La Brévine in the Neuchâtel Jura: minus 41.8 °C. That is why La Brévine is also called the “Siberia of Switzerland”. In Switzerland weather data is collected by the federal office **MeteoSwiss**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The usual unit of temperature in Switzerland; water freezes at 0 °C.
The unit of temperature used in science; it starts at absolute zero.
The lowest possible temperature, about minus 273 °C.
The temperature at which a liquid starts to boil.

gewusst: Anders Celsius originally decided that water freezes at 100 degrees and boils at 0 degrees; the scale was only turned round later.
