On the summit of Mount Everest water boils at about 70 °C.
The surface of the Sun is about 5500 °C hot.

teile.einleitung: SEV 1011 is the Swiss standard for plugs and sockets in the home. It sets out what Swiss plugs look like, so that they fit safely into the matching sockets. That is why people travelling to Switzerland from abroad often need an adapter.
wichtigste: SEV 1011 is the name of the Swiss standard for household plugs and sockets.
Internationally the Swiss plug system is called Type J.
The Type 11 plug has two pins; the three-pin Type 12 plug has three pins and a hexagonal body.
On the three-pin plug, the middle pin, which is slightly offset, is the earth.
Ordinary Type 13 sockets are designed for 10 amperes.
Liechtenstein also uses the Type J plug system.
A German Schuko plug does not fit, because it is too wide and round.

abschnitte.text: SEV 1011 is a **standard**, that is, a binding technical rule. It comes from the former Swiss Electrotechnical Association, which today is called **Electrosuisse**. The standard describes the shape, size and spacing of the pins of plugs and sockets. This way all devices sold in Switzerland fit into every Swiss socket.

**Type 11** is a flat plug with two round pins for devices without an earth. **Type 12** has three pins and a hexagonal body; the middle pin is offset and serves as the earth. The normal socket is called Type 13 and takes both plugs, as well as the flat Europlug. For more powerful devices there is Type 23 for 16 amperes with square pins.

The offset middle pin makes sure that the plug only fits one way round. In this way the **earth** is always connected correctly. The pins are close together, and many newer sockets are slightly recessed so that you cannot touch the pins. Sockets in bathrooms and outdoors are also protected by a residual current device.

Most neighbouring countries use the **Schuko plug**, which is round and wider. It does not fit into a Swiss socket. That is why you need a **travel adapter** when travelling. The flat Europlug of mobile phone chargers, on the other hand, fits in many countries, including Switzerland.

In Swiss homes the socket supplies an alternating voltage of 230 volts at 50 hertz. The ordinary Type 13 socket is designed for 10 amperes. That is enough for most household appliances such as lamps, computers or vacuum cleaners. Large appliances such as cookers, on the other hand, are permanently wired in or have their own sockets.

begriffe.erklaerung: Binding rule for how something must be built technically.
Green and yellow wire that protects against electric shock.
Unit of electric current.
Connector that lets foreign plugs fit into a socket.

gewusst: The Swiss plug system is used almost only in Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
Because Swiss sockets are so narrow, three of them often fit into a single frame on the wall.
The Europlug fits into sockets in many countries of Europe.

teile.einleitung: Sublimation is the name for the direct change of a substance from a solid to a gas, without becoming liquid in between. That sounds strange, but it happens every winter outside your front door. Dry ice, which makes the fog in the theatre, also disappears in this way.
wichtigste: In sublimation a substance changes directly from solid to gas.
The opposite way, from gas directly to solid, is called deposition.
Dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide and sublimates at about minus 78 °C.
Snow and ice can also sublimate in dry, cold air.
Hoar frost and frost patterns form through deposition of water vapour.
For sublimation a substance needs energy in the form of heat.
Freeze-drying of food uses sublimation.

abschnitte.text: Normally a solid substance first melts and then evaporates. In **sublimation** this in-between step is skipped. The particles break free directly from the solid structure and fly off as a gas. Whether this happens depends on temperature and **air pressure**.

The best-known example is **dry ice**, that is, solid carbon dioxide. At normal air pressure it cannot become liquid at all. It turns directly into gas at about minus 78 °C. If you put dry ice into warm water, a thick white fog forms, which is used on stages and at parties.

Water can also sublimate. On very cold, dry and sunny winter days a layer of snow gets thinner even though it never thaws. This is well known in the Alps and in Antarctica. In the past people also hung their washing outside in winter, because the ice in the frozen clothes slowly **evaporates** through sublimation.

When a gas turns directly into a solid, this is called **deposition**. This is how **hoar frost** forms on trees and fences, when damp air freezes on very cold surfaces. Frost patterns on the window and snow crystals in clouds also grow in this way. The substance gives off heat to its surroundings as it does so.

In **freeze-drying**, food is deep-frozen and then put into a room with very low pressure. The ice in it sublimates, and the fruit or coffee becomes dry without losing its shape. This is how instant coffee or astronaut food is made, for example. Mothballs and toilet fresheners also get smaller over time, because they sublimate.

Comets are partly made of frozen water and other kinds of ice. When a comet comes close to the Sun, this ice sublimates. The gas drags dust along with it and forms the glowing **comet's tail**. On Mars, too, part of the carbon dioxide ice at the polar caps sublimates in spring.

begriffe.erklaerung: The form a substance takes: solid, liquid or gas.
The direct change from gas to solid, for example with hoar frost.
Frozen carbon dioxide that turns into gas without melting.
A process in which the water is removed from frozen food by sublimation.

gewusst: Dry ice got its name because it leaves no puddle when it disappears.
Frozen washing on the line can get dry even at temperatures below zero.
The tail of a comet can be many millions of kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: A fountain is a structure from which water spurts upwards and falls back into a basin. Fountains decorate squares, parks and palace gardens all over the world. The most famous in Switzerland is the Jet d'eau in Geneva, whose jet rises about 140 metres.
wichtigste: In a fountain water is sprayed upwards and falls back into the basin.
Modern fountains need a pump.
The water is collected in the basin and pumped up again and again.
Because of gravity the water falls back down.
In the past fountains used water from a higher place instead of a pump.
A fountain without a pump spurts at most almost as high as its source.
The Jet d'eau in Geneva spurts about 140 metres high.
In sunshine you can often see a rainbow in the spray.

abschnitte.text: A fountain consists of a **basin**, one or more nozzles and a water supply. From the **nozzle** the water shoots into the air as a jet, a fan or a bell shape. Then it falls back into the basin. Fountains are mainly for beauty and refreshment, not for supplying water.

Today the water is usually driven by an electric **pump**. It sucks water from the basin and pushes it upwards through the nozzle at high pressure. **Gravity** slows the jet down until it turns round and falls back down again. Because the water goes round in a circle, you only need to top up what evaporates or is splashed out.

In the past there were no motor pumps, so water was led through pipes to the fountain from a higher **spring** or water tank. The water wants to rise as high as the place it came from. But because of friction in the pipes and the air, it never spurts quite as high as the spring. The ancient Romans built splendid fountains in this way, and the **Trevi Fountain** in Rome is still a major attraction today.

The **Jet d'eau** stands in Lake Geneva and is the landmark of Geneva. Originally, in 1886, it was only a pressure relief valve for a hydroelectric plant. Because people found the jet so beautiful, it was given a permanent place on the lake shore. Today powerful pumps push about 500 litres of water per second upwards at about 200 kilometres per hour, so that the jet reaches about 140 metres.

In the palace gardens of **Versailles** near Paris, French kings had hundreds of water features built. In Basel there is the **Tinguely Fountain**, with crazy metal machines that wriggle and splash in the water. Today many cities have fountains with lights and music that put on colourful water shows in the evening. When the sun shines into the fine spray, a **rainbow** often appears.

begriffe.erklaerung: A narrow opening from which the water shoots out under pressure.
A device that sucks in water and pushes it on under pressure.
The force with which the Earth pulls everything down towards itself.
The force with which water presses against walls, and which drives it upwards.

gewusst: In clear weather you can see the jet of the Jet d'eau from the plane as you fly in to Geneva.
In strong wind or frost the Jet d'eau is switched off so that people walking by do not get wet and no ice forms.
Many people throw coins into fountains, because according to an old custom this is supposed to bring luck.

teile.einleitung: A speedometer shows how fast a vehicle is travelling at the moment. In a car it is usually behind the steering wheel, on a bike on the handlebars. The German word Tachometer comes from the Greek word “tachos”, which means speed.
wichtigste: The speedometer shows the speed of a vehicle.
In German it is called Tacho for short.
In a car the speedometer is usually behind the steering wheel.
If the speedometer shows 50, the car is travelling at 50 kilometres per hour.
When the car is standing still, the speedometer shows 0.
A bike speedometer is usually fixed to the handlebars.
The odometer shows how many kilometres a car has travelled in total.

abschnitte.text: The speedometer is a measuring device for **speed**. In a car it is part of the dashboard and sits directly behind the steering wheel, so that the driver can see it easily. The speed is usually given in **kilometres per hour**, km/h for short. If the car goes faster, the number shown gets bigger; if it brakes, it gets smaller.

A speedometer actually measures how fast the wheels are turning. A **sensor** counts the turns, and a small computer works out the speed from them. Older cars had a flexible shaft that led from the gearbox to the display and moved a needle there. Today many cars show the speed as a number on a screen.

Right next to or inside the speedometer there is usually the **odometer**. It counts all the kilometres a car has travelled in its whole life. There is often also a trip meter, which can be reset to zero, for example before a holiday journey. When buying a used car, people look at the mileage to see how far it has already travelled.

Many cyclists have a small bike computer on their handlebars. A magnet on a spoke passes a sensor on the fork with every turn of the wheel. From the circumference of the wheel and the number of turns, the device calculates the speed and the distance travelled. Today many devices and mobile phones also measure speed with **GPS**, that is, using satellites.

The speedometer helps drivers keep to the permitted **speed limit**. In Switzerland the limit is usually 50 in built-up areas, 80 outside them and 120 kilometres per hour on the motorway. By law a car speedometer must never show less than you are really going. That is why it usually shows a little more than the car is actually doing.

begriffe.erklaerung: Device that shows the speed of a vehicle.
Kilometres per hour, the number of kilometres you would travel in one hour.
Counts all the kilometres a vehicle has travelled.
The panel in front of the driver's seat with displays and switches.

gewusst: The word tachometer means roughly “speed measurer”.
A car speedometer usually shows a little too much, but never too little.
Lorries have a tachograph, which records speed and driving times.

teile.einleitung: The particle model is an idea in physics and chemistry: all substances are made of tiny particles that are constantly moving. With this model you can explain why there are solid, liquid and gaseous substances and why things expand when they are heated. The particles are so small that you cannot see them even with an ordinary microscope.
wichtigste: In the particle model all substances are made of tiny particles that are constantly moving.
In a solid the particles are packed closely and regularly and vibrate in place.
In a liquid the particles slide past each other.
In gases the forces of attraction between the particles are smallest.
A gas can easily be squeezed together, because there is a lot of empty space between the particles.
At absolute zero, minus 273.15 °C, the particles would have the least possible movement.
When ink spreads out in water by itself, this is called diffusion.

abschnitte.text: Imagine you could magnify a drop of water more and more. At some point you would see that it is made of countless tiny **particles** that dart about. This is exactly how the **particle model** describes all substances. A model is a simplified picture that helps to explain things, even if reality is more complicated still.

In a **solid** such as ice, the particles lie closely and regularly side by side and only vibrate in place, which is why it keeps its shape. In a **liquid** such as water, the particles hold together but slide past each other, which is why it flows. In a **gas** such as water vapour, the particles fly around freely and the forces of attraction are smallest. Because there is a lot of empty space between them, you can easily squeeze a gas together, for example in a bicycle pump.

The warmer a substance is, the faster its particles move. So they need more space, and most substances **expand when heated**. That is why bridges and railway lines have small gaps, the expansion joints. If you cool a substance down further and further, the particles get slower and slower, down to **absolute zero** at minus 273.15 °C, the lowest possible temperature.

If you put a drop of ink into water, after a while it spreads out by itself, even without stirring. This is called **diffusion**: the particles keep bumping into each other and mix as they do so. In warm water this happens faster than in cold water, because the particles move faster. The fact that you can smell fresh bread all over the house is also due to diffusion.

In 1827 the Scottish botanist Robert Brown saw under the microscope that tiny grains in water were constantly jiggling. He could not explain this **Brownian motion**. Only in 1905 did Albert Einstein, who was then working at the patent office in **Bern**, show that the grains are being pushed by invisible water particles. This was important proof that atoms and molecules really exist.

Around 400 BC the Greek thinker **Democritus** already suspected that everything is made of particles that cannot be divided, which he called “atomos”. For a long time this was only an idea that nobody could prove. Around 1800 the Englishman John Dalton used the idea of atoms to explain chemical reactions. Today special microscopes can even make individual atoms visible.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny building block of a substance, for example an atom or molecule.
The form a substance takes: solid, liquid or gas.
The mixing of substances by themselves through the movement of their particles.
Jiggling movement of small grains that are pushed by particles.
The lowest possible temperature, minus 273.15 °C.

gewusst: A single drop of water contains more particles than there are stars in our Milky Way.
Albert Einstein wrote his famous paper on Brownian motion while he was living in Bern.
Water is an exception: it expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats.

teile.einleitung: Inertia is the tendency of a body to keep its state of motion. What is at rest wants to stay at rest, and what is rolling wants to keep rolling. You notice it every time a bus suddenly brakes.
wichtigste: Inertia means that a body keeps its speed and direction as long as no force acts on it.
The greater the mass of a body, the greater its inertia.
If a bus brakes suddenly, standing passengers tip forwards.
If a bus jerks into motion, the passengers tip backwards.
Galileo Galilei described inertia even before Isaac Newton.
Newton turned it into his first law, the law of inertia.
Seat belts protect us from the effects of inertia.

abschnitte.text: Every body has the property of carrying on as before. A ball at rest stays where it is until someone pushes it. A rolling ball would roll on in a straight line for ever if **friction** and air resistance did not slow it down. This property is called **inertia**.

In the past people believed that every movement stops by itself. Around 1600 the Italian scientist **Galileo Galilei** realised, with balls on inclined planes, that movements only end because of friction. In 1687 Isaac Newton summed this up in his first law, the **law of inertia**. It says: without a force a body stays at rest or moves steadily in a straight line.

Inertia depends on **mass**. You can easily push and stop an empty shopping trolley, but a fully loaded one is much harder. A long goods train often needs more than a kilometre to stop. Huge tankers even have to slow their engines many kilometres before the harbour.

When the bus brakes, your body wants to keep going, so you tip forwards. When the bus jerks into motion, your body stays behind and you tip backwards. In a fast bend you are pushed towards the **outside of the bend**, because your body wants to go straight on. If you pull a tablecloth away very fast, the crockery stays where it is because of its inertia.

If a hammer head is loose, you bang the bottom of the handle hard on the floor. The handle stops, but the heavy head keeps moving and slides firmly onto the handle. You can get ketchup out of the bottle in the same way: you move it quickly and stop it suddenly. When you shake water out of a cloth, you are also using inertia.

In an emergency stop, objects that are not secured fly forwards with great force. That is why luggage in the car should be well secured. People, too, would keep flying forwards without a **seat belt** and crash into the windscreen. That is why in Switzerland everyone in the car must wear a seat belt, and small children need a child seat.

begriffe.erklaerung: The property of a body to stay at rest or in motion.
Newton's first law: without a force, motion does not change.
Measure of how sluggish and how heavy a body is.
A force that slows down movements when surfaces rub against each other.

gewusst: A space probe such as Voyager 1 has been flying for decades almost without propulsion, because there is hardly any friction in space.
Astronauts measure their mass in space with a swinging seat, because ordinary scales do not work there, but inertia does.
A dog shakes its wet coat back and forth so fast that the water flies off because of inertia.

teile.einleitung: A mirror is a very smooth, shiny surface that sends light back in such a way that you see an image in it. Mirrors hang in the bathroom, are fitted in cars and telescopes and help in traffic to see round corners. Thousands of years ago people were already making mirrors from stone and metal.
wichtigste: A mirror sends light back; this is called reflection.
Smooth and shiny surfaces reflect best.
An ordinary bathroom mirror is made of glass with a thin layer of metal.
A ray of light that comes in at a slant is sent back at a slant to the other side.
Without light you see nothing in a mirror.
Before glass mirrors, mirrors were made of polished metal.
Curved mirrors at exits help you to see round corners.

abschnitte.text: A mirror does not shine by itself; it only sends back light that falls on it. That is why you see nothing in a mirror in a completely dark room. For **reflection** there is a simple rule: the **angle of incidence** is the same as the angle of reflection. So a ray of light that falls on the mirror at a slant is sent back at the same angle to the other side.

For a clear image to form, the surface must be very **smooth**. Rough surfaces such as paper or a wall scatter light in all directions, so you see no image in them. In nature a calm lake can act like a mirror, in which mountains and trees are reflected. As soon as the wind makes waves, the reflection disappears.

An ordinary mirror consists of a sheet of glass with a wafer-thin **layer of metal**, silver or aluminium, on the back. A layer of paint protects the metal from scratches and damp. The glass itself provides a smooth surface and protects the metal layer from the front. In 1835 the German chemist Justus von Liebig invented a process for silvering glass chemically.

The oldest known mirrors are about 8000 years old and were made of polished **obsidian**, a black volcanic glass; they were found in Anatolia in today's Turkey. Later bronze, copper and silver were polished into mirrors, for example in ancient Egypt and the Roman Empire. On the island of Murano near Venice craftsmen made famous glass mirrors from the 16th century onwards. For a long time they were so expensive that only rich people could afford one.

A **concave mirror**, which curves inwards, magnifies; it is used as a make-up mirror and in large telescopes. A **convex mirror**, which curves outwards, shows everything smaller, but a larger area. That is why such round mirrors hang at exits and bends where you cannot see well. The wing mirrors of cars are also often slightly curved.

abschnitte.titel: Mirrors in everyday life and technology
abschnitte.text: With a small mirror you can direct sunlight onto the wall as a bright spot of light. In a submarine's **periscope**, two mirrors redirect the light so that you can look over obstacles. Solar power stations use many mirrors to focus sunlight in order to heat water. And since 1969 there have been special mirrors on the Moon, which scientists use with a laser to measure the distance to the Earth.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sending back of light at a surface.
The angle at which light hits a surface.
A mirror that curves inwards and magnifies.
A mirror that curves outwards and shows a large area.
Black, shiny glass that forms in volcanic eruptions.

gewusst: The largest telescope mirrors in the world are several metres across.
In the Palace of Versailles near Paris there is a famous Hall of Mirrors with 357 mirrors.
With the mirrors that astronauts set up on the Moon in 1969, the Moon's distance is measured to within a few centimetres.

teile.einleitung: A trampoline is a piece of sports equipment on which you can jump high into the air. An elastic mat is fixed to a frame with many springs. It stretches when you land and flings you back up.
wichtigste: A trampoline consists of a frame, springs and an elastic jumping mat.
When you land, the mat stretches and springs you back up.
A material is called elastic if it goes back to its shape after being stretched.
Padding covers the springs, and a net stops you falling out.
It is safest to jump in the middle, without shoes and preferably alone.
Trampolining has been an Olympic sport since 2000.

abschnitte.text: A trampoline has a sturdy **frame** made of steel tubes. All around it hang many steel springs, which keep the **jumping mat** taut. The mat is made of a tear-resistant woven plastic. Soft **padding** covers the springs and frame, and on garden trampolines a net often makes sure that nobody falls out.

When you land, you push the mat down and stretch the springs. Your kinetic energy is turned into **elastic energy**, as in a stretched rubber band. Then the springs pull together again and give the energy back, so that you fly up. Because the springs and mat are **elastic**, they always go back to their shape.

If you bend your knees strongly when pushing off and straighten your legs, you add extra energy. In this way each jump gets a little higher until you reach the height you want. To slow down, you bend your knees when you land and absorb the bounce. A small part of the energy is lost as heat with every jump.

If many children jump at the same time, they can collide or unexpectedly fling each other up. That is why, if possible, only one person should jump at a time. The middle of the mat is safest, because at the edge you risk falling onto the frame or the ground. It is better to jump without shoes, because shoes can damage the mat, and somersaults should only be practised with a coach.

The modern trampoline was developed in the 1930s by the American **George Nissen**. The word comes from the Spanish “trampolín”, which means springboard. In Olympic **trampolining** athletes perform somersaults and twists several metres up in the air. Trampolining is also trained in many Swiss gymnastics clubs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material that takes on its old shape again after being stretched.
A coiled metal wire that can be stretched and snaps back.
Energy stored in a stretched spring or rubber band.
A flip in the air in which you turn right over once.

gewusst: Astronauts have also practised on trampolines how to find their orientation in the air.
In competitions trampolinists fly up to about eight metres high.
The first ideas for trampolines came from circus acrobats who wanted to keep bouncing after dropping into the safety net.

teile.einleitung: Ski wax is a care product that you put on the underside of a ski, the base. Glide wax makes skis glide faster over the snow, and grip wax gives cross-country skis hold when you push off. Behind this is some exciting physics of friction.
wichtigste: Glide wax makes skis faster because it reduces sliding friction.
In classic cross-country skiing, grip wax stops the ski from slipping backwards when you push off.
You choose the wax to suit the temperature of the snow.
Glide wax is often ironed in with a hot waxing iron.
The ski base is usually made of the plastic polyethylene.
Waxes containing fluorine have been banned in international ski racing since the 2023/24 season.
Some cross-country skis have scales or skins under the binding instead of grip wax.

abschnitte.text: When a ski glides over the snow, **friction** develops, which slows it down. Glide wax makes the base smooth and water-repellent, so the sliding friction becomes smaller. A freshly waxed ski is therefore faster than an unwaxed one. The wax also protects the base from drying out and from scratches.

When gliding, friction produces a little heat. This melts a wafer-thin **layer of water** under the ski, on which it glides. Cold snow has sharp crystals and rubs differently from warm, wet snow. That is why there are waxes for different **snow temperatures**, often marked with colours.

Glide wax is melted with a **waxing iron** and ironed into the base. Once it has cooled, the extra wax is scraped off with a plastic scraper. Then the base is brushed out so that only a thin layer remains. Fine grooves, the **structure**, are also ground into the base so that wet snow does not create a suction effect.

In classic cross-country skiing the ski needs grip under the binding, otherwise it slips back when you push off. That is what **grip wax** is for: when the ski stands still, the snow crystals grip into the wax, but when gliding it still slides. For wet or icy snow, sticky klister is used. Skis with **scales** or skins that do not need waxing are simpler.

For a long time **fluoro waxes** were considered especially fast, above all on wet snow. But the substances they contain hardly break down in nature and can get into soil, water and living things. That is why waxes containing fluorine have been banned in international ski racing since the 2023/24 season. Checks are made with measuring devices directly on the ski.

Centuries ago people in Scandinavia were already coating their wooden skis with **tar** so that they would run better and not soak up water. Modern skis have a base made of polyethylene, which takes up wax well. A well-known ski wax brand, Toko, comes from Altstätten in the canton of St Gallen. Before races, service technicians in the World Cup often test many waxes to find the fastest.

begriffe.erklaerung: Wax that makes skis glide faster.
Wax for cross-country skis that gives hold when pushing off.
The underside of the ski, which glides on the snow.
A tough plastic that ski bases are made of.
Very sticky grip wax for wet or icy snow.

gewusst: In big races the right wax can decide between victory and defeat, because often only hundredths of a second count.
A ski actually glides on a wafer-thin film of water that it creates itself through the heat of friction.
Before cross-country races, teams sometimes test dozens of waxes on the course.

teile.einleitung: Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor and businessman who lived from 1847 to 1931. He improved the light bulb, invented the phonograph and built one of the first electricity networks. Hardly anyone else has had so many inventions protected as he did.
wichtigste: Thomas Alva Edison was a famous American inventor.
He improved the light bulb so that it could shine in many homes.
With his phonograph it was possible for the first time to record sounds and play them back.
Edison had more than 1000 inventions protected by patents.
He was called the Wizard of Menlo Park.
He also worked on the film camera and on devices for moving pictures.
Edison wanted to supply homes with direct current.
Edison was hard of hearing and almost deaf in old age.

abschnitte.text: Edison was born on 11 February 1847 in Milan in the US state of Ohio. He only went to school for a short time and was mainly taught at home by his mother. As a teenager he was already selling newspapers on the train and experimenting in a small laboratory. Later he worked as a **telegraph operator** and improved early telegraph equipment. He was hard of hearing from an early age, but this hardly stopped him working.

In 1876 Edison founded a large research laboratory in **Menlo Park** in the state of New Jersey. There many experts worked together on new inventions, which was something completely new at the time. Because so many astonishing devices were created there, Edison was called the **Wizard of Menlo Park**. Later he moved his laboratory to West Orange, also in New Jersey.

In 1877 Edison invented the **phonograph**, the first device that could record sounds and play them back. A needle scratched the sound vibrations into a cylinder that was covered first with tin foil and later with wax. On playback the needle followed the grooves and made the sound audible again. The first thing Edison recorded was a nursery rhyme.

There were light bulbs before Edison, but they only lasted a short time or were too expensive. In 1879 Edison and his team made a **light bulb** with a carbon filament that shone for a long time. For lamps to burn in homes, power stations, cables and meters were also needed. In 1882 Edison opened one of the first public **power stations** in New York.

Edison backed **direct current**, in which the current always flows in the same direction. His rival George Westinghouse and the inventor Nikola Tesla backed **alternating current**. Alternating current can be carried over long distances more easily with transformers. In the end alternating current won, and today it also flows in Swiss sockets.

Together with Edison, his employee William Dickson developed a **film camera** and the kinetoscope, a peep box for moving pictures. Altogether Edison had more than 1000 inventions protected by **patents**. He died on 18 October 1931 in West Orange. Among other things, the large company General Electric grew out of his businesses.

begriffe.erklaerung: A protection that gives a person the sole right to their invention for a certain time.
An early device for recording and playing back sounds on a cylinder.
Electric current that always flows in the same direction.
Electric current that keeps changing its direction.
A device that sends messages along wires with electrical signals.

gewusst: For the filament Edison's team tested thousands of materials, and later it used carbonised bamboo.
Edison is said to have said that genius is one per cent inspiration and ninety-nine per cent perspiration.
Edison gave his first two children the nicknames Dot and Dash, like the dot and dash in Morse code.

teile.einleitung: A black hole is a place in space where so much mass is squeezed into such a small space that nothing can escape any more, not even light. That is why it is invisible and black itself. But you can recognise black holes by their enormous effect on stars, gas and light around them.
wichtigste: Nothing can escape from a black hole, not even light.
The boundary beyond which there is no way back is called the event horizon.
Stellar black holes form when a very massive star collapses at the end of its life.
At the centre of the Milky Way sits the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*.
In 1916 Karl Schwarzschild found a solution to Einstein's field equations that sets the radius of a non-rotating black hole.
In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope published the first image of a black hole.
According to the no-hair theorem, a black hole is completely described by its mass, angular momentum and electric charge.

abschnitte.text: A **black hole** is not really a hole, but mass that has been squeezed together extremely tightly. Its gravity is so strong that nothing near it can escape any more. The boundary from which there is no way back is called the **event horizon**. If you squeezed the Earth so hard that it became a black hole, it would only be about the size of a marble. The name black hole became well known from 1967 through the American physicist John Wheeler.

In 1915 Albert Einstein published his general theory of relativity, which describes gravity as a curving of space and time. As early as 1916 the German astrophysicist **Karl Schwarzschild** found a solution to these field equations. From it comes the **Schwarzschild radius**, the size of the event horizon of a non-rotating black hole. In 1963 the New Zealand mathematician Roy Kerr found the solution for rotating black holes. In 1974 Stephen Hawking predicted that, because of quantum effects, black holes give off a weak **Hawking radiation**.

**Stellar black holes** form when a very massive star has used up its fuel. Its core then collapses under its own gravity, often together with a huge explosion, a supernova. Such black holes have a few to a few dozen solar masses. At the centre of almost all large galaxies, on the other hand, there are **supermassive black holes** with millions to billions of solar masses. Astronomers are still researching today how these giants came about.

Gas and dust falling into a black hole form a fast-spinning **accretion disc**. In it, friction heats the matter to millions of degrees and it glows brightly before it disappears. If an object comes too close to a black hole, it is stretched out because the pull on its front and back is so different in strength. Experts jokingly call this process **spaghettification**. But the Earth is in no danger, because the nearest black hole is very far away.

In 2019 the **Event Horizon Telescope**, a network of radio telescopes all over the world, published the first image of a black hole. It shows the shadow of the black hole in the galaxy Messier 87, surrounded by a glowing ring. In 2022 an image followed of **Sagittarius A***, the black hole at the centre of our Milky Way, with about four million solar masses. Back in 2015, instruments had picked up gravitational waves from two merging black holes for the first time. In 2020 Roger Penrose, Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez received the Nobel Prize in Physics for their research on black holes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can escape any more.
A spinning disc of gas and dust that spirals into a black hole.
The mass of our Sun, used as a measure for comparing stars.
The stretching of an object by extreme tidal forces near a black hole.
A weak radiation that, according to Stephen Hawking, black holes should give off.

gewusst: Close to a black hole, time passes more slowly than far away from it.
A black hole does not suck everything in like a vacuum cleaner: at a safe distance you can orbit it, just as the Earth orbits the Sun.
The black hole in Messier 87 is several billion times as heavy as our Sun.

teile.einleitung: SI base units are the seven basic units of the International System of Units, SI for short. All other units in physics can be built from them, from the newton to the volt. Thanks to them, a metre in Switzerland means exactly the same as in Japan or Brazil.
wichtigste: The International System of Units has exactly 7 base units.
The seven are the second, metre, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela.
The kilogram is the only base unit with a prefix in its name, namely “kilo”.
All other units, for example the newton, joule or volt, are derived units.
Since 2019 all base units have been defined by unchangeable constants of nature.
A temperature difference of 1 kelvin is exactly the same size as 1 degree Celsius.
The SI was introduced in 1960 and is used almost all over the world today.

abschnitte.text: Each **base unit** belongs to a basic quantity. Time is measured in seconds (s), length in metres (m) and mass in kilograms (kg). Electric current has the ampere (A), thermodynamic temperature the kelvin (K). The amount of substance is counted in moles (mol) and luminous intensity in candelas (cd).

Many well-known units are made up of base units; they are called **derived units**. The newton for force, for example, is kg·m/s², so it is not a base unit. The volt can also be broken down: it equals kg·m²/(s³·A). In this way the whole of physics fits together like a construction kit.

The **kelvin** scale starts at absolute zero, the coldest possible temperature of minus 273.15 °C. But the steps are the same size as on the Celsius scale. So if water warms up from 20 °C to 35 °C, the temperature rises by 15 K. Scientists like to calculate in kelvins, because there are no minus numbers.

A **mole** is a number, like a dozen, only huge: it is exactly 602,214,076,000,000,000,000,000 particles. Chemists need the mole to count atoms and molecules. The **candela** measures how brightly a light source shines in a certain direction. An ordinary candle has about one candela, which is also where the name comes from.

In the past a kilogram was exactly as heavy as a metal cylinder, the **international prototype kilogram** in Sèvres near Paris. Since 20 May 2019 the kilogram, like all the other base units, has been defined by fixed constants of nature. The metre, for example, is the distance that light travels in a vacuum in one 299,792,458th of a second. The second is defined by the oscillations of caesium atoms in atomic clocks.

In 1875 Switzerland was one of the first countries to sign the **Metre Convention**. Today the Federal Institute of Metrology, METAS for short, in Bern-Wabern makes sure that measurements in Switzerland are correct. It checks, for example, scales, petrol pumps and clocks. So you can rely on a kilogram of apples in the shop really being a kilogram.

begriffe.erklaerung: Abbreviation for the International System of Units, in French “Système international d'unités”.
A basic unit from which other units are built.
A unit made up of base units, for example the newton or volt.
A number in nature that never changes, for example the speed of light.
The science of precise measurement.

gewusst: For over 100 years the prototype kilogram was the most important lump of metal in the world, because all kilogram weights were compared with it.
The kilogram is the only base unit that already has a prefix in its name.
An atomic clock is so precise that it is not even one second wrong in many millions of years.

teile.einleitung: Steiner's theorem, also called the parallel axis theorem, is a rule in physics for calculating the moment of inertia of a body about a shifted axis of rotation. It tells you how hard it is to make a body turn when the axis does not pass through its centre of mass. It is named after the Swiss mathematician Jakob Steiner from what is today the canton of Bern.
wichtigste: Steiner's theorem is J = J_S + m · d².
J_S is the moment of inertia about the axis through the centre of mass, m the mass and d the distance of the parallel axis.
One of the two axes must pass through the centre of mass.
Of all parallel axes, the moment of inertia is smallest about the axis through the centre of mass.
The moment of inertia tells you how strongly a body resists a change in its rotation.
The theorem is named after Jakob Steiner, who came from what is today the canton of Bern.
It is also called the Huygens-Steiner theorem or the parallel axis theorem.

abschnitte.titel: What is a moment of inertia?
abschnitte.text: A body that is not turning does not want to start turning by itself. How strongly it resists this is described by the **moment of inertia**. It depends on the mass and on how far this mass is from the **axis of rotation**. The further the mass is from the axis, the greater the moment of inertia. It is measured in kilograms times square metres, kg·m² for short.

**Steiner's theorem** is J = J_S + m · d². Here J_S is the moment of inertia about an axis through the **centre of mass**. If you shift the axis parallel by the distance d, the part m · d² is added. That is why the moment of inertia about the axis through the centre of mass is always the smallest. It is important that the two axes are parallel and that one of them passes through the centre of mass.

A body of 2 kg has 0.1 kg·m² about its axis through the centre of mass. About a parallel axis 0.3 m away it has 0.1 + 2 · 0.09 = 0.28 kg·m². A thin rod of 3 kg and 2 m length has 1 kg·m² about its middle, so about one end it has 1 + 3 · 1 = 4 kg·m². For a solid cylinder of 2 kg and radius 0.1 m that turns about a line on its curved surface, the result is 0.03 kg·m². A solid sphere of 1 kg and radius 0.1 m has 0.014 kg·m² about a tangent.

**Jakob Steiner** was born in 1796 in Utzenstorf in what is today the canton of Bern and grew up on a farm. He did not learn to write properly until he was a teenager. Later he went to the school of the famous educator **Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi** in Yverdon and discovered his talent for mathematics there. He became a professor in Berlin and is regarded as one of the greatest geometers of his time; he died in Bern in 1863.

A figure skater spins faster when she pulls her arms in to her body, because her moment of inertia becomes smaller. A door can easily be turned on its hinges, but its moment of inertia about them is greater than about its middle. A **pendulum** or a swinging swing can also be calculated with Steiner's theorem. Engineers need it for flywheels, rotors and machine parts.

The Dutch scientist **Christiaan Huygens** already knew the idea of the theorem in the 17th century. That is why it is also called the Huygens-Steiner theorem. In English it is simply called the parallel axis theorem. Today it is taught in physics and engineering lessons at grammar schools, universities of applied sciences and universities.

begriffe.erklaerung: Measure of how hard it is to set a body turning.
Point where you can imagine the whole mass of a body to be gathered.
Imaginary line around which a body turns.
Two lines that are the same distance apart everywhere and never meet.

gewusst: At 14 Jakob Steiner could still hardly write, and yet he became a famous mathematician.
Jakob Steiner is regarded as one of the most important figures of synthetic geometry, which works entirely without coordinates.
A long rod is four times easier to set turning about its middle than about one end.

teile.einleitung: Radiant energy is energy that travels through space as radiation, for example as light, heat radiation or ultraviolet radiation. Our most important source is the Sun, whose radiation warms the Earth and makes plants grow. Radiation does not need air, so it even reaches us through empty space.
wichtigste: Radiant energy is carried by electromagnetic radiation such as light.
Outside the Earth's atmosphere about 1360 watts of solar radiation fall on one square metre.
When a body takes in radiation and turns it into heat, this is called absorption.
Ultraviolet radiation from the Sun causes sunburn.
Blue light carries more energy per particle of light than red light.
Fresh snow reflects sunlight especially strongly.
The greenhouse effect holds back part of the Earth's heat radiation.

abschnitte.text: **Radiant energy** is the energy of electromagnetic radiation. This includes radio waves, microwaves, **infrared radiation**, visible light, ultraviolet radiation and X-rays. All these rays travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres per second. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to get to the Earth.

Light is made of tiny packets of energy, the **photons**. How much energy a photon carries depends on its colour or wavelength. Blue light carries more energy per photon than red light. Ultraviolet radiation has even more energy, which is why it can damage the skin and cause **sunburn**.

abschnitte.titel: The Sun as a source of energy
abschnitte.text: Outside the atmosphere about 1360 watts of solar power fall on one square metre; this value is called the **solar constant**. Part of the radiation is reflected or swallowed by clouds and air. Plants use sunlight for **photosynthesis** and make sugar from it. In this way almost all living things on Earth depend on the Sun's radiant energy.

When radiation hits a body, it can be **absorbed**, that is taken in, or **reflected**, that is sent back. Dark surfaces absorb a lot and get hot, which is why a black T-shirt gets warmer in the sun than a white one. Fresh snow reflects most of the sunlight, which is why you need sunglasses in the mountains. Emergency blankets are silvery so that they reflect the body's heat radiation back.

A thermal **solar collector** on a house roof uses solar radiation to heat water for showers and heating. A solar cell or **photovoltaic system** turns light directly into electricity. In Switzerland many new solar systems are built on roofs every year. A microwave oven also uses radiation to heat food.

The Earth gives off the energy it has taken in again as heat radiation. Gases in the atmosphere such as carbon dioxide and water vapour hold back part of this radiation; this is called the **greenhouse effect**. Without it the Earth would be icy cold. But when people release more and more greenhouse gases, the Earth gets warmer, and this leads to **climate change**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny packet of energy of light, also called a particle of light.
Taking in radiation, which is often turned into heat in the process.
Sending radiation back at a surface.
Power of the Sun's radiation per square metre outside the Earth's atmosphere.

gewusst: The sunlight you see today left the Sun about 8 minutes ago.
Your body also gives off heat radiation all the time; thermal imaging cameras can make it visible.
In the mountains UV radiation is stronger than in the lowlands, because the layer of air above is thinner.

teile.einleitung: A spectrometer is a measuring device that splits light into its individual colours and measures how bright each colour is. From this, scientists can tell what substances something is made of, whether in the laboratory or in a distant star. In 1995 two astronomers from Geneva used a spectrometer to find the first planet around a Sun-like star.
wichtigste: An optical spectrometer measures the intensity of light depending on its wavelength.
A prism or a grating splits the light into its colours.
A narrow entrance slit lets only a thin beam of light in.
Modern compact spectrometers measure the whole spectrum at once with a CCD or CMOS line sensor.
The scale is calibrated with a lamp with known lines, such as a mercury vapour lamp.
The spectral resolution shows how close two wavelengths can be and still appear separate.
In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz from Geneva found an exoplanet with the radial velocity method.

abschnitte.text: Light is a mixture of many colours, and each colour has a certain **wavelength**. A spectrometer fans the light out, as a rainbow does. Then it measures how much light arrives at each wavelength. The result is a **spectrum**, a kind of fingerprint of the light.

At the entrance a narrow **entrance slit** lets only a thin beam of light in. A **prism** or a diffraction grating bends the colours by different amounts. With a prism this works because the refractive index of the glass depends on the wavelength: blue light is refracted more strongly than red. In the past people looked in with their eyes; today a **detector** such as a CCD or CMOS line sensor records the whole spectrum at once.

So that the measurement is correct, the device is lit with a lamp whose lines are known exactly, for example a **mercury vapour lamp**. This tells you which point of the detector belongs to which wavelength. Good devices have a high **spectral resolution** and separate even very close lines. For ultraviolet light, optics made of quartz glass are used, because ordinary glass swallows a large part of the UV light.

In the 17th century Isaac Newton was already splitting sunlight with a prism. In 1814 the Munich optician **Joseph von Fraunhofer** discovered dark lines in the Sun's spectrum. Around 1860 Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen realised that every chemical element has its own lines. With this **spectral analysis** they discovered new elements such as caesium and rubidium.

A planet pulls its star very slightly back and forth. This shifts the lines in the star's spectrum a tiny bit towards the blue and the red side. With this **radial velocity method**, **Michel Mayor** and **Didier Queloz** of the University of Geneva found the planet 51 Pegasi b in 1995. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019.

In laboratories, spectrometers check the purity of medicines and food. Environmental agencies use them to measure pollutants in water and air. Space probes use spectrometers to study the rocks on Mars and the atmospheres of other planets. In factories, the colour of car paint is also checked with spectrometers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fanned-out band of all the colours or wavelengths of a light.
The distance between two wave crests; it determines the colour of the light.
To set a measuring device with known values so that it measures correctly.
A planet that circles a star other than our Sun.

gewusst: The element helium was first discovered in the spectrum of the Sun and only found on Earth later.
If you hold a CD up to the light you see rainbow colours, because its fine grooves act like a diffraction grating.
With spectrometers you can even tell whether a star is moving towards us or away from us.

teile.einleitung: The tonne is a unit of mass for heavy things. One tonne is exactly 1000 kilograms, written “t” for short. A small car weighs about one tonne, a large bull elephant about six.
wichtigste: One tonne (t) is exactly 1000 kilograms.
Half a tonne is 500 kg, three tonnes are 3000 kg.
A small car weighs about one tonne.
One cubic metre of water has a mass of about one tonne.
The tonne is not one of the SI units, but it is allowed to be used alongside them.
Loads of ships, lorries and trains are usually given in tonnes.

abschnitte.text: The tonne is a unit of **mass**, just like the gram and the kilogram. One tonne equals 1000 kilograms or one million grams. To be scientifically correct, you could also say **megagram** (Mg), but almost nobody uses this word in everyday life. For even larger amounts there are the kilotonne (1000 t) and the megatonne (one million t).

To convert tonnes into kilograms, you multiply by 1000. So 3 tonnes are 3000 kg and half a tonne is 500 kg. The other way round, you divide by 1000: so 2000 kg are 2 tonnes. The decimal point simply moves three places, which makes the **conversion** easy.

A tonne is about as heavy as a **small car**. A fully grown bull elephant can weigh about six tonnes. A blue whale, the heaviest animal on Earth, even weighs well over a hundred tonnes. A cube full of water with sides of one metre also weighs about one tonne.

In front of some bridges there is a sign with a number such as “3.5 t”. It means that heavier vehicles may not drive over it, because otherwise the bridge could be overloaded. In Switzerland lorries with trailers may weigh at most 40 tonnes in total. With an ordinary category B **driving licence** you may drive vehicles with a total weight of up to 3.5 tonnes.

The load of a ship, a goods train or an aeroplane needs big numbers, so it is calculated in tonnes. Harvests, amounts of rubbish or steel production are also measured in tonnes. In climate protection people talk about tonnes of **CO2** being released. A large container ship can carry more than a hundred thousand tonnes of cargo.

In the USA and Great Britain there are old units that are also called “ton”. The American “short ton” is about 907 kg, the British “long ton” about 1016 kg. For ships there used to be the **register ton**, which does not describe a mass at all, but a volume. In Switzerland and in Europe, tonne always means 1000 kg.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much matter a body has, measured in grams, kilograms or tonnes.
The basic unit of mass; 1000 kg are one tonne.
Weight of a vehicle including its load and passengers.
The scientific name for a tonne, that is one million grams.

gewusst: A cubic metre of water weighs almost exactly one tonne, but a cubic metre of air only just over one kilogram.
The tongue of a blue whale alone can be as heavy as an elephant.
The word tonne comes from the barrel: in the past ships' cargoes were measured by how many large barrels would fit in.

teile.einleitung: A low-pressure area, or low for short, is an area where the air pressure is lower than in its surroundings. Lows often bring clouds, rain, wind and sometimes storms. On weather maps they appear as swirls around which the air turns.
wichtigste: In a low the air pressure is lower than all around.
The technical term for a low-pressure area is cyclone.
On German weather maps a low is marked with a T, on English-language maps with an L for “low”.
In a strong low it is stormy, because the air pressure changes a lot over a short distance.
When a low passes over a place, the barometer first falls and then rises again.
When a low approaches from the west, the Föhn often blows in Swiss Alpine valleys.
The storm Lothar caused huge damage to forests in Switzerland on 26 December 1999.
A heat low forms through strong warming of the ground.

abschnitte.text: The air above us presses on the ground with its weight; this is **air pressure**. At sea level it averages about 1013 **hectopascals** (hPa). In a low the pressure is lower, for example 980 hPa. Because air always flows from high to low pressure, it flows into the low from all sides. There it rises and cools, and clouds and rain form.

Because of the Earth's rotation the air does not flow straight into the low, but is deflected. That is why in the northern hemisphere a low turns anticlockwise, and in the southern hemisphere clockwise. This deflection is called the **Coriolis force**. That is why a low is called a **cyclone** in technical language, from the Greek word for circle. On weather maps lines called **isobars** join places with the same air pressure, and where they are close together there are strong winds.

The lows that move to Europe usually form over the Atlantic. There cold air from the north and warm air from the south meet. At the **warm front** warm air slides over cold air and brings long, steady rain. At the cold front cold air pushes under the warm air, and then there are often heavy showers, thunderstorms and gusts of wind. When a low passes over a place, the barometer first falls and then rises again.

When a low approaches from the west, warm air often flows from the south over the Alps. On the north side it falls into the valleys as the warm, dry **Föhn** wind, for example into the Reuss valley or the Rhine valley. On 26 December 1999 the storm **Lothar** swept across Switzerland and snapped millions of trees. On the Jungfraujoch gusts of almost 250 kilometres per hour were measured, and there were hurricane-force gusts in the lowlands too.

In summer a **heat low** can form over strongly warmed land, because hot air rises. Over warm tropical seas the most dangerous lows form: tropical storms, which are called hurricanes, typhoons or cyclones depending on the region. The lowest air pressure ever measured in such a storm was about 870 hPa, measured in 1979 in Typhoon Tip over the Pacific. The opposite of a low is a high-pressure area, which usually brings fine, calm weather.

begriffe.erklaerung: The weight of the air pressing on the ground.
Unit of air pressure, hPa for short.
Lines on the weather map that join places with the same air pressure.
Boundary between warm and cold air.
Instrument for measuring air pressure.

gewusst: In Europe high and low-pressure areas are given names, which can even be bought; in one year the lows get women's names, in the next men's names.
A low can travel thousands of kilometres in a day.
Lothar was one of the worst storms in Switzerland since weather records began.

teile.einleitung: A shooting star is a short streak of light in the night sky. But it has nothing to do with a star: it is a small piece of rock from space that burns up in the Earth's atmosphere. On some nights, for example in August, you can see especially many of them.
wichtigste: A shooting star is a small piece of rock that burns up in the air.
Experts call the streak of light a meteor and the particle in space a meteoroid.
Shooting stars glow because they get very hot when they enter the air.
They travel at many kilometres per second.
Most of them burn up at a height of about 100 kilometres.
A stone from space that reaches the ground is called a meteorite.
The Perseids in August are a meteor shower whose particles come from a comet.

abschnitte.text: Countless small lumps of rock and metal fly around in space; they are called **meteoroids**. Most are no bigger than a grain of sand. When such a particle hits the Earth's atmosphere, a streak of light appears, a **meteor**. In everyday language it is called a shooting star. It has nothing to do with real stars, which are huge suns far away.

Meteoroids race into the **atmosphere** at about 11 to over 70 kilometres per second. As they do, they crash into the air, which is squeezed strongly in front of them and gets very hot. The particle melts and evaporates, and the air along its path begins to glow. This usually happens at a height of about 80 to 120 kilometres. After less than a second it is all over.

On their path around the Sun, comets lose dust and small lumps. When the Earth crosses this trail of dust every year, you see especially many shooting stars, a **meteor shower**. The **Perseids** are strongest around 12 August and come from the comet Swift-Tuttle. In December there are the **Geminids**, in November the Leonids. The showers are named after the constellation from which the shooting stars seem to come.

If a lump is big enough, it does not burn up completely and falls to the ground. Then it is called a **meteorite**. Most meteorites are made of rock, some of iron and nickel. In Switzerland, for example, many pieces of an iron meteorite were found on the Twannberg in the canton of Bern. Very large impacts are rare, but can leave craters.

Shooting stars are best seen on a clear night, far from the lights of the city. You do not need a telescope, because they streak quickly across the whole sky. After midnight you usually see more, because the Earth is then flying towards the particles. During the Perseids you can sometimes count several dozen an hour in dark areas. A warm blanket and some patience are part of it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small lump of rock or metal flying through space.
The streak of light in the sky when a meteoroid burns up.
A stone from space that reaches the ground.
A body made of ice and dust that forms a tail when it flies close to the Sun.
The layer of air that surrounds the Earth.

gewusst: Every day many tonnes of tiny dust particles from space fall onto the Earth.
Especially bright shooting stars are called fireballs or bolides.
An old custom says that when you see a shooting star you may silently make a wish.

teile.einleitung: Fluid mechanics studies how liquids and gases move and what forces act as they do. It explains why aeroplanes fly, how water flows through pipes and why a cyclist in someone's slipstream has to pedal less. Important foundations come from the Basel scholars Daniel Bernoulli and Leonhard Euler.
wichtigste: Fluid mechanics describes the movement of liquids and gases, the fluids.
Aerodynamics mainly studies how air flows around bodies.
An ideal fluid is frictionless and incompressible.
The Euler equations describe frictionless flows, the Navier-Stokes equations viscous flows.
A streamline points in the direction of the velocity everywhere.
Up to about Mach 0.3 air can usually be treated as incompressible.
Ludwig Prandtl founded boundary layer theory in 1904.

abschnitte.text: Physicists group liquids and gases together under the term **fluid**, because both can flow. Fluid mechanics studies how fluids move and what forces they exert on bodies. **Aerodynamics** deals mainly with air flowing around aeroplanes, cars or buildings. **Hydrodynamics** studies flowing water, for example in rivers, pipes or around ships.

A **streamline** is an imaginary line that points in the direction of the velocity everywhere; in a wind tunnel it can be made visible with smoke. In a **steady flow** the velocity at each place stays the same over time. If the layers flow calmly side by side, it is called laminar flow. If the flow becomes swirling and chaotic, like smoke rising from a candle and suddenly swirling, it is called **turbulent**.

An **ideal fluid** is frictionless and cannot be squeezed, that is, it is incompressible. Its motion is described by the **Euler equations**, named after the Basel mathematician Leonhard Euler. Real fluids have inner friction, **viscosity**; honey, for example, has much more than water. For these you need the Navier-Stokes equations, which are so difficult that a prize of one million dollars has been offered for their complete mathematical solution.

In 1738 **Daniel Bernoulli** from Basel published his book “Hydrodynamica”. It contains the idea that in faster-flowing fluids the pressure is lower, which among other things helps us understand how a wing gets lift. In 1904 the German Ludwig Prandtl founded **boundary layer theory**, which explains what happens in the thin layer directly next to a surface. Osborne Reynolds studied when a flow changes from laminar to turbulent.

Because real aeroplanes and ships are huge, small **models** are often tested in a wind tunnel or a towing tank. So that the results can be transferred, dimensionless numbers are used. The Reynolds number describes the ratio of inertia to friction, and the **Froude number** is especially important for ships that make waves. The Mach number compares the speed with the speed of sound; up to about 0.3, air can usually be treated as incompressible.

Fluid mechanics is found in aeroplane wings, racing cars, wind turbines and ski suits. Weather services use it to calculate how air masses move, and doctors study the flow of blood in veins and arteries. The Swiss yacht Alinghi, which won the America's Cup in 2003, was also developed with a lot of flow research. Today engineers often simulate flows on a computer before they build anything.

begriffe.erklaerung: Collective term for liquids and gases.
The study of how air flows around bodies.
The thickness or inner friction of a fluid.
Swirling, disorderly flow.
Thin layer of fluid directly next to a surface, in which the flow is slowed down.

gewusst: The Navier-Stokes equations are one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, each with a prize of one million dollars for its solution.
Daniel Bernoulli and Leonhard Euler both came from Basel and knew each other well.
Golf balls have dimples, because these give them less air resistance and make them fly further.

teile.einleitung: A thermometer is a measuring device used to find out the temperature. It shows whether it is freezing outside, whether the bath water is pleasant or whether someone has a temperature. Thermometers come in many forms, from a glass tube to a digital sensor in a mobile phone.
wichtigste: A thermometer measures temperature.
The word comes from Greek and means something like “heat measurer”.
Many thermometers use the fact that liquids expand when they get warm.
Digital thermometers measure with electronic sensors.
Infrared thermometers measure temperature without touching.
In a healthy person a clinical thermometer shows about 37 °C.
Mercury thermometers are hardly used any more because the metal is poisonous.

abschnitte.text: A thermometer shows how warm or cold something is. The reading is usually in **degrees Celsius**. There are thermometers for the air, for water, for the oven, for the body and for many machines. It is important that the thermometer takes on the same temperature as the thing being measured.

In a classic **liquid thermometer** there is a liquid, often coloured alcohol, in a thin glass tube. When it gets warmer, the liquid expands and rises up the tube. You can read off the temperature on a scale. A **bimetallic thermometer**, on the other hand, uses two different metals that expand by different amounts when warm and so bend.

**Digital thermometers** have an electronic sensor whose electrical resistance changes with temperature. Infrared thermometers measure the invisible heat radiation that every body gives off. With them you can measure the temperature on the forehead or in the ear in a second without touching anything. Such devices were often used at entrances during the coronavirus pandemic.

Around 1600 the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei built a simple **thermoscope**, which showed differences in temperature but had no scale yet. In 1714 Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit built one of the first accurate mercury thermometers. In 1742 Anders Celsius proposed his scale with 100 steps between the freezing and boiling points of water. Since then thermometers have become more and more accurate.

With a **clinical thermometer** you measure body temperature, which is normally about 37 °C. From about 38 °C it is called a fever. Outdoor thermometers show whether you need a jacket or whether the roads might be icy. In the kitchen a meat thermometer helps to make sure meat is properly cooked.

In the past many clinical thermometers contained **mercury**, a silvery liquid metal. But mercury vapour is poisonous if a thermometer breaks. That is why mercury clinical thermometers are banned in many countries today. Old devices do not belong in the rubbish, but at a collection point or the chemist's.

begriffe.erklaerung: The division with numbers and lines on which you read a measurement.
Two metal strips firmly joined together that bend when warm.
An electronic part that measures something, for example temperature.
Invisible heat radiation that every warm body gives off.

gewusst: The Galileo thermometer with floating coloured glass balls is named after Galileo, but was only developed by other scientists after his death.
In Fahrenheit, normal body temperature is about 98.6 degrees.
Some thermometers for research can measure temperatures a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero.

teile.einleitung: An electric shock happens when electric current flows through the body of a person or animal. It can be very painful and even life-threatening, because electricity can throw the heart out of rhythm. If you know the most important rules, you can protect yourself and others well.
wichtigste: An electric shock happens when current flows through the body.
You must never climb on electricity pylons or railway wagons, because there is a risk of death from electricity.
The SBB overhead line carries 15,000 volts, and the electricity can jump across even without contact.
A yellow warning sign with a black lightning arrow warns of danger from electricity.
If someone is still touching a live appliance, you first switch off the electricity.
In Switzerland the emergency number for the ambulance is 144.
A residual current device switches off the electricity if it flows through a person.

abschnitte.text: Our body is made largely of salty water and therefore conducts electricity. If you touch a live part and at the same time the ground or another part, current can flow through your body. This is called an **electric shock**. Even a small current can make muscles cramp so that you cannot let go any more.

Our heart is controlled by tiny electrical signals. If current from outside flows through the chest, the heart can get out of rhythm; this is called **ventricular fibrillation**. Then it no longer pumps blood, and life is in danger. Electricity can also cause inner and outer **burns**.

Above the SBB tracks hangs the **overhead line** with 15,000 volts. With such a high voltage the electricity can jump across in an **electric arc**, even if you do not touch the line at all. That is why you must never climb on railway wagons, pylons or bridges over tracks. Sadly, every year young people who underestimate this have accidents.

A bird on a power line does not get an electric shock, because it is touching only one wire. There is hardly any difference in voltage between its feet, so no current flows through it. It only becomes dangerous if it touches two lines at the same time, or a line and the pylon. This does not apply to people, because you are almost always connected to the ground as well.

In houses the **residual current device** protects people. It notices when current takes the wrong path, for example through a person, and switches off in a fraction of a second. In Switzerland such switches are required in new installations. Broken cables and appliances, water near sockets and tinkering with the mains are dangerous and off limits.

If someone is still touching a live appliance or cable, you first switch off the electricity, for example at the plug or the fuse. Only then may you touch the person, otherwise you get a shock yourself. Then you call the **ambulance** on 144. With high voltage you always keep a long way away, wait for experts and alert the emergency centre.

begriffe.erklaerung: What drives the electric current, measured in volts.
Switch that turns off the electricity immediately if it takes the wrong path.
Bright spark with which electricity jumps through the air.
Dangerous disorder in which the heart only quivers and no longer pumps blood.

gewusst: The SBB overhead line carries 15,000 volts, about 65 times more than the socket at home.
Lightning is a giant electric shock from the clouds.
A defibrillator gives the heart a targeted electric shock to bring it back into the right rhythm.

teile.einleitung: The floating needle is an astonishing experiment: a steel sewing needle stays lying on the water, even though steel is much heavier than water. The reason is surface tension, which makes the water act like a thin skin. You can try the experiment quite easily at home.
wichtigste: A steel sewing needle can stay lying on the water because the water surface carries it like a skin.
This property of water is called surface tension.
To get the needle onto the water, you lay it on a piece of kitchen paper.
The paper soaks up water and sinks, while the needle stays on top.
Around the needle you can see a small dent in the water surface.
A drop of washing-up liquid next to the needle makes it sink.
If you put the needle into the water point first, it sinks at once.

abschnitte.text: You fill a bowl with water and wait until the surface is completely still. Then you lay a dry **sewing needle** on a small piece of **kitchen paper** and carefully place both on the water. After a short time the paper soaks up water and sinks to the bottom. But the needle stays on top and floats. If you have very steady hands, you can also lay the needle flat on the water with a fork.

Water is made of tiny particles, the **molecules**, which attract each other. Inside the water they are pulled equally strongly from all sides. At the surface, however, there are no neighbours above, so the top particles pull together especially strongly sideways and downwards. This creates a kind of stretched skin: **surface tension**. This skin is strong enough to carry a light needle lying flat.

If you look closely, you can see a small **dent** in the water surface around the needle. The needle pushes the water down a little, like a person standing on a trampoline. The stretched surface pushes back diagonally upwards from both sides. Held against the light, the dent even casts a visible shadow on the bottom of the bowl. If the needle becomes too heavy or breaks through the surface, it sinks.

If you put a drop of **washing-up liquid** next to the needle, it sinks after a short time. Washing-up liquid contains substances that greatly reduce surface tension; they are called **surfactants**. If you put the needle into the water point first, it also sinks at once. Then the point pierces the water skin instead of just pressing it in. Greasy fingers or dirty water can also spoil the experiment.

Animals use surface tension too. **Pond skaters** are insects that dart across ponds and streams on their long, water-repellent legs without sinking. Some spiders can also walk on water. Drops of water are round because of surface tension. When washing, on the other hand, you need soap, which lowers the surface tension so that the water gets into the fabric better.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force that holds the water surface together like a thin, stretched skin.
A tiny particle that a substance such as water is made of.
Substances in soap and washing-up liquid that reduce surface tension.
An insect that can walk on the surface of the water.

gewusst: Steel is about eight times as heavy as the same amount of water and still floats as long as the water skin does not tear.
Instead of a needle you can also make a paper clip or a light aluminium coin float on the water.
A magnetised floating needle turns towards the north, so you can build a simple compass with it.

teile.einleitung: A power line carries electricity from the power station to our homes. It can be stretched high across the landscape as a thick cable or lie under the ground. In the room it finally ends in the socket.
wichtigste: Electricity comes to our homes from the power station through power lines.
Thick lines that carry electricity over long distances are called high-voltage lines.
In towns many power lines run under the ground.
The wires in cables in the house are often made of copper.
A plastic covering protects against electric shock.
If a storm brings a line down, the power can go off.
If a power line is lying on the ground, you stay well away and fetch adults.

abschnitte.text: A **power line** is a wire or cable through which electric current flows. Electricity needs a path made of a material that conducts it well, a **conductor**. Metals such as copper and aluminium conduct especially well. So that the current does not flow away in the wrong place, lines are protected by **insulation** made of plastic, glass or porcelain.

abschnitte.titel: From the power station to the house
abschnitte.text: Electricity is produced in power stations, in Switzerland mainly in hydroelectric and nuclear power stations, and more and more with solar systems too. Over long distances it flows in **high-voltage lines** with up to 380,000 volts. In substations, transformers lower the voltage step by step. In the house the electricity finally comes out of the **socket** at 230 volts.

In the countryside power lines usually hang on tall pylons as **overhead lines**. The cables there have no covering; instead the air acts as insulation, which is why they hang so high. In towns many lines lie under the ground as **underground cables**, where they are protected and do not get in the way. But underground cables are more expensive and harder to repair than overhead lines.

Switzerland's extra-high-voltage grid is run by the company **Swissgrid**. It is connected to the grids of neighbouring countries, so that electricity can flow across borders. From there, smaller networks run by the electricity companies lead to every village. In this way electricity from reservoirs in the Alps and electricity from solar roofs on the Swiss Plateau come together.

If a storm throws trees onto a line or heavy snow damages the cables, the **power can go off**. Then the lights, fridge and heating stop working. Experts from the electricity company repair the line as quickly as possible. Large grids are built so that the electricity can often take another route.

A power line lying on the ground may still be live and is life-threatening. So you stay well away, touch nothing and fetch adults at once. Damaged cables in the house must not be used any more. Only trained **electricians** are allowed to work on power lines.

begriffe.erklaerung: Material through which electricity can flow well, for example copper.
Protective layer that does not let electricity through.
Very high electrical voltage used to carry electricity over long distances.
Device that raises or lowers the voltage of the electricity.

gewusst: With high voltage, less energy is lost when electricity is carried over long distances.
Through cables on the seabed, electricity is even carried between countries and islands.
The cables of an overhead line sag lower in summer, because the metal expands in the heat.

teile.einleitung: A sundial shows the time with the help of the shadow cast by the Sun. A rod casts its shadow onto a dial, and because the Sun moves across the sky, the shadow moves too. Sundials are among humanity's oldest timekeepers.
wichtigste: On a sundial a rod casts a shadow onto a dial.
Because the Sun moves across the sky, the shadow moves during the day.
On a flat sundial in our part of the world, the shadow turns clockwise.
In Switzerland sundials are often found on the walls of houses and churches.
A sundial that lies flat on the ground is called a ground sundial.
You cannot put a sundial forward to summer time.
You can build a simple sundial yourself with a stick and stones.

abschnitte.text: The Earth turns once a day, so to us the Sun seems to move across the sky from east to west. A rod, the **shadow caster** or **gnomon**, casts a shadow that slowly moves on. Lines for the hours are drawn on the **dial**. At midday, when the Sun is highest in the south, the shadow is shortest. On a flat sundial in our part of the world, the shadow turns clockwise, and that is exactly why clock hands go round that way.

On an accurate sundial the rod does not point straight up, but slants towards the north. It is parallel to the Earth's axis and points roughly towards the **Pole Star**. That is why it is also called a **polar style**. In Switzerland it is tilted at about 46 to 47 degrees to the ground, which matches the latitude. This way the sundial shows the right hours all year round.

In Switzerland there are many sundials on the walls of houses and churches, especially in the mountain valleys of Valais, the Grisons and Ticino.
