A sundial on a south-facing wall is called a **vertical sundial**. Many are beautifully painted and carry sayings about how time passes, often in Latin. A **ground sundial** lies flat on the ground; sometimes a person is the shadow caster. Such sundials you can walk on are found, for example, in squares and parks.

A sundial shows **local apparent time**, that is, the time according to the position of the Sun at exactly that place. Our watches, on the other hand, show Central European Time, which is the same for a whole region. That is why a sundial in Switzerland usually shows a slightly different time from a watch. In spring watches are put forward to **summer time**, but a sundial cannot be changed. So in summer in Switzerland it usually shows more than an hour less than a watch.

More than 3000 years ago in ancient Egypt people were already using shadows to tell the time of day. The Greeks and Romans also built sundials before there were mechanical clocks. You can build a simple sundial in the garden with a **stick** and a few **stones**. You push the stick into the ground and at every full hour put a stone at the end of the shadow. On the next sunny day you can read the time, but in the following weeks the clock becomes less accurate, because the Sun's position changes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rod of a sundial that casts the shadow.
The surface with the hour lines or numbers on which you read the time.
A slanting shadow rod lined up parallel to the Earth's axis.
The time that follows exactly the position of the Sun at a place.

gewusst: Clock hands turn in the same direction as the shadow of a flat sundial in the northern hemisphere.
A sundial only works when the sun is shining; at night and when it is cloudy it is useless.
There are sundials that work with a hole instead of a rod and make a spot of light move.

teile.einleitung: Spin is a property of elementary particles such as the electron, like their mass or their charge. It behaves a little like angular momentum and turns particles into tiny magnets. Spin is purely quantum mechanical and cannot be fully compared with anything in our everyday life.
wichtigste: Spin is an internal property of particles, like mass and charge.
An electron has the spin quantum number 1/2.
Along an axis, the spin of an electron can only take the values +ħ/2 or -ħ/2.
You must not imagine spin as the turning of a small ball.
In the Stern-Gerlach experiment of 1922 a beam of silver atoms split into two beams.
George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit proposed electron spin in 1925.
The magnetism of iron is based on electron spins that are lined up the same way.
The Higgs boson has spin 0.

abschnitte.text: Every elementary particle has a fixed **spin**, just as it has a fixed charge. The English word spin means turning, and mathematically spin behaves like **angular momentum**. Even so, the electron does not really spin like a top, because according to what we know today it is point-like. Spin is a purely **quantum mechanical** property with no exact counterpart in everyday life.

If you measure the spin of an electron along any axis, you always find only two values: **+ħ/2** or **-ħ/2**. In simple terms these are often called “spin up” and “spin down”. The symbol ħ stands for the reduced Planck constant, a very small constant of nature. Because the electron is charged, its spin turns it into a tiny **magnet**.

In 1922 **Otto Stern** and **Walther Gerlach** in Frankfurt sent a beam of silver atoms through an uneven magnetic field. The beam split into exactly two beams, which could not be explained by the old physics. In 1925 the young Dutchmen George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit proposed that the electron has its own angular momentum. After that the physicist **Wolfgang Pauli**, who taught for a long time at ETH Zurich, built spin into quantum theory.

Particles with half-integer spin such as 1/2 are called **fermions**; they include electrons, protons and neutrons. The Pauli principle applies to them: two electrons in an atom may never be the same in all their properties. That is why electrons arrange themselves in shells, and why the variety of chemical elements exists at all. Particles with whole-number spin are called **bosons**, for example the photon with spin 1 and the Higgs boson with spin 0.

In **iron** the spins of many electrons line up the same way, which is why it is ferromagnetic and can be made into a magnet. **Giant magnetoresistance**, for which Albert Fert and Peter Grünberg received the Nobel Prize in 2007, uses spin in thin layers. It made hard disks with much greater storage possible. MRI scanners in hospitals are also based on spin, namely the spin of the hydrogen nuclei in the body.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle that, according to what we know today, cannot be split further, such as the electron.
A physical quantity that describes how strongly something is turning.
A particle with half-integer spin, for example an electron.
A particle with whole-number spin, for example a particle of light.
The ability of substances such as iron to become magnets themselves.

gewusst: In the calculations, a particle with spin 1/2 has to be turned right round twice before it is back in the same state.
Wolfgang Pauli received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1945 for the exclusion principle named after him.
Scientists are trying to use the spin of electrons as memory for quantum computers.

teile.einleitung: A wheelbarrow is a cart, usually with just one wheel, that you lift by two handles and push. It is indispensable on building sites, farms and in the garden. Its secret is a simple physical tool: the lever.
wichtigste: An ordinary wheelbarrow has one wheel, a tray, two handles and two legs at the back.
It is used to carry heavy things such as soil, sand or stones.
The wheelbarrow works on the principle of the lever.
The wheel carries a large part of the weight.
A heavy load should be put as close to the wheel as possible.
Its German name, “Schubkarre”, comes from pushing (“schieben”).

abschnitte.text: A wheelbarrow consists of a **tray**, usually made of sheet steel or plastic, and a frame with two long handles. At the front there is a **wheel**, often with a pneumatic tyre, so that it rolls over uneven ground. At the back it has two **legs**, on which it stands securely. There are also models with two wheels, which are more stable but go round corners less well.

The wheelbarrow is a **second-class lever**. The pivot is the axle of the wheel, the load lies in the tray, and the force acts on the handles. Because the handles are much further from the wheel than the load, you need much less force to lift it than the load weighs. The wheel carries a large part of the weight.

The closer the load is to the wheel, the easier it is to lift the handles. That is why heavy stones or sacks are put as far forward as possible. The load should be spread evenly, otherwise the barrow easily tips over sideways. When lifting, bend your knees and lift with a straight back to protect your **spine**.

Wheelbarrows with one wheel already existed in **China** almost 2,000 years ago. Some large models were built there with the wheel in the middle, which could carry a lot of luggage or even people. In Europe, the wheelbarrow appeared in the **Middle Ages** and helped with building castles and cathedrals. Its German name comes from pushing, and in Switzerland people also call it “Garette”.

On building sites, wheelbarrows are used to carry concrete, sand and gravel. In the garden, you use one to move soil, leaves or compost around. On a farm, it helps with mucking out the stable. It is especially handy on narrow paths where there is no room for a larger vehicle.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bar that moves about a pivot and saves force.
The point about which a lever turns; for the wheelbarrow, the wheel axle.
The tub of the wheelbarrow in which the load is placed.
A lever in which the load and the force are on the same side of the pivot.

gewusst: In old Chinese texts, the wheelbarrow was sometimes called the wooden ox.
With a wheelbarrow, a person can easily move a load of 100 kilograms.
There are races in which one person pushes another in a wheelbarrow to the finish.

teile.einleitung: A tuning fork is a small metal device that looks like a fork with two prongs and makes a very pure note when it is struck. Musicians use it to tune instruments. Usually the note A sounds, known as concert pitch.
wichtigste: A tuning fork is used to tune instruments.
It has 2 prongs and a stem by which you hold it.
A standard tuning fork gives the note A with 440 vibrations per second.
You make it sound by striking it lightly.
If you hold a sounding tuning fork in water, the water splashes.
If you stand it on a table by its stem, the note gets louder.
If you touch the prongs, the note stops.

abschnitte.text: A **tuning fork** is usually made of steel and has the shape of a U with a stem. The two arms are called **prongs**. If you strike it lightly, for example on your knee or on a rubber block, the prongs start to vibrate quickly back and forth. This produces a very pure note without many overtones.

The prongs move outwards and back inwards at the same time. As they do, they push the air, and **sound waves** form that reach our ear. The number of vibrations per second is called the **frequency** and is measured in hertz. An A tuning fork vibrates 440 times a second, which is why this note is also called 440 hertz. Shorter and thicker prongs vibrate faster and give a higher note.

On its own a tuning fork is rather quiet, because the thin prongs move only a little air. If you stand it on a table by its stem, the whole tabletop vibrates along with it and the note gets louder. This is called **resonance**. That is why some tuning forks stand on a small wooden box, the resonance box. If you touch the prongs with your hand, the vibration is slowed down and the note falls silent.

If you carefully hold a sounding tuning fork in water, it splashes away in fine drops. This shows you that the note really comes from a fast movement. If you touch a table tennis ball hanging on a thread with the prongs, it is flung away. With two identical tuning forks you can show that one makes the other vibrate along with it.

Musicians use the tuning fork to tune their violins, guitars or pianos. Choir leaders also use it to give the right starting note. The note A at 440 hertz is called **concert pitch** and is the standard in most countries today. Today many people also use electronic tuners or apps on their mobile phone.

The tuning fork was invented in 1711 by the English trumpeter **John Shore**. Since then it has been an important tool in music and physics. Doctors also use tuning forks to test hearing or the sense of vibration in the feet. In the past, tiny vibrating parts working on the same principle were even fitted in some electric clocks.

begriffe.erklaerung: The two arms of the tuning fork, which vibrate.
Number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
The note A at 440 hertz, to which instruments are tuned.
A body vibrating along, which makes a note louder.

gewusst: The inventor of the tuning fork was a trumpeter himself and played for famous composers such as George Frideric Handel.
A tuning fork sounds exactly the same for years, because its size hardly changes.
The prongs of a sounding tuning fork move so fast that you only see them blurred.

teile.einleitung: The Schwyzerörgeli is a small accordion and one of the best-known instruments of Swiss folk music. It sounds because air flows through small metal reeds and makes them vibrate. That also makes it an exciting example of the physics of sound.
wichtigste: The Schwyzerörgeli is a small accordion.
You pull and push the bellows so that air flows through the instrument.
Inside, small metal reeds vibrate and produce the note.
With the melody buttons, a different note sounds when you pull than when you push.
You play the bass notes with your left hand.
Its forerunner from the Emmental is called the Langnauerli.
Robert Iten was already building Schwyzerörgeli early on in Pfäffikon in the canton of Schwyz.

abschnitte.text: The Schwyzerörgeli consists of two wooden boxes joined by folding **bellows**. On the right-hand side are the melody buttons, on the left-hand side the bass buttons. With your left hand you move the bellows and at the same time play the bass notes and accompanying chords. Many Örgeli are beautifully decorated with wood inlays, flower patterns or edelweiss.

Inside there are many small metal **free reeds** on reed plates. When air flows through, the reed vibrates back and forth and produces a note. Short, thin reeds vibrate quickly and sound high; long, heavy reeds vibrate slowly and sound low. Because each reed only responds to one direction of air, a different note sounds when pulling than when pushing; this is called **bisonoric**.

The accordion was patented in Vienna in 1829 by Cyrill Demian. In Switzerland an early form developed in the Emmental, the **Langnauerli**. Towards the end of the 19th century Robert Iten built instruments in Pfäffikon in the canton of Schwyz that became the model for today's Schwyzerörgeli. The name refers to the canton of Schwyz.

The Schwyzerörgeli belongs to **Ländler music**, the typical dance music of Swiss folk music. It often plays together with clarinet, double bass and piano in a Ländler band. Typical pieces are Ländler, schottische, waltz and polka. Many children and young people learn the Örgeli at music schools or with private teachers.

Schwyzerörgeli are still built by hand today in small workshops in Switzerland. A single instrument takes many hours of work and hundreds of individual parts. The reeds have to be **tuned** precisely so that all the notes fit together cleanly. The sound of the Örgeli can often be heard at folk music festivals and wrestling festivals.

begriffe.erklaerung: Folding part of the accordion that sucks air in and pushes it out.
Thin metal strip that vibrates and sounds in the air flow.
A button gives different notes when pulling and when pushing.
Traditional dance music of Swiss folk music.

gewusst: You can change the pitch of a reed by scraping a tiny bit of metal off its tip or its base.
The harmonica also works with free reeds, just like the Örgeli.
In everyday speech the instrument is often simply called Örgeli.

teile.einleitung: A vacuum cleaner is an electrical appliance that sucks dust and dirt off the floor with a stream of air. Today almost every household has one. In the past people had to beat carpets outside with a carpet beater, which was hard work.
wichtigste: A vacuum cleaner sucks in air and drags dust along with it.
An electric motor drives a fast fan.
A filter or bag holds back the dust.
If the bag is full, air can hardly flow through any more, and it sucks less well.
You use a narrow crevice tool to vacuum in tight corners.
Cordless vacuum cleaners and robot vacuums are widespread today.
Before the vacuum cleaner, carpets were cleaned with a carpet beater.

abschnitte.text: Inside a vacuum cleaner an **electric motor** drives a fan that turns very fast. The fan blows air out of the back of the appliance. This creates **low pressure** inside, and air flows in at the front through the nozzle and tube. This stream of air drags dust, crumbs and hairs along with it.

The air that is sucked in flows through a **dust bag** or into a container. Fine **filters** hold back even tiny dust so that it is not blown back into the room air. If the bag is completely full, air can hardly flow through any more, and the vacuum cleaner sucks less well. Bagless appliances separate out the dust with a whirl of air, as in a small tornado.

For carpets and hard floors there is a wide floor nozzle, often with bristles that can be switched in or out. With the narrow **crevice tool** you vacuum in tight corners and between cushions. A brush nozzle is good for bookshelves and lampshades. Some appliances have a rotating brush that combs hairs out of the carpet.

Before there were vacuum cleaners, carpets were hung over a pole outside and beaten with a **carpet beater**. Around 1901 the Englishman Hubert Cecil Booth built one of the first motor-driven suction machines in London. It was so big that it was pulled through the streets by horses. A few years later handy appliances for the home appeared in the USA and were soon sold in Europe too.

Today there are cordless vacuum cleaners that run on a **rechargeable battery**. Robot vacuums drive through the flat on their own and use sensors to find their way back to the charging station. Industrial vacuum cleaners even suck up water and rubble on building sites. In the European Union, new household vacuum cleaners have been allowed a maximum of 900 watts since 2017, so that they use less electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: When there is less air pressure in one place than in the surroundings, air flows there.
A wheel with blades that moves air.
A fine material that lets air through but holds back dust.
A battery that can be charged again.

gewusst: The first suction machines around 1900 stood in the street, and long hoses led through the window into the house.
A robot vacuum uses sensors to notice when it comes to a staircase, so it does not fall down.
House dust is partly made of tiny flakes of skin and fibres from fabrics.

teile.einleitung: A torch is a small, portable lamp that shines using batteries or a rechargeable battery. With it you can find your way in the dark, look for things under the bed or read secretly under the duvet. In physics it nicely shows how electricity becomes light and how light can be directed.
wichtigste: Most new torches have LED bulbs.
A battery or rechargeable battery supplies the electricity.
A shiny funnel behind the bulb directs the light forwards.
A wind-up torch shines without a battery when you turn the handle.
The distress signal SOS is flashed as three short, three long, three short.
After use you should switch the torch off so that the battery does not run flat.
You should not shine a torch into anyone's eyes, because it dazzles and can harm the eyes.

abschnitte.text: A torch consists of a casing, a **battery** or rechargeable battery, a switch and a bulb. When you switch it on, the **circuit** closes and current flows through the bulb. Behind the bulb there is a shiny funnel, the **reflector**. At the front a clear lens protects the inside.

In the past torches had small **light bulbs**, in which a thin wire glowed. A lot of electricity was turned into heat instead of light. Today most torches have **LEDs**, that is, light-emitting diodes. They are much brighter, use less electricity and hardly ever break. That is why the batteries last much longer.

A bulb gives off light in all directions. The curved **reflector** sends the sideways light forwards, creating a bright beam. On some torches you can turn the head and make the beam wide or narrow. How brightly a torch shines is given in **lumens**.

A **wind-up torch** has a small generator built in. When you turn the handle, it produces electricity and charges a rechargeable battery. There are also shake torches and torches with small solar cells. Such torches are handy for an emergency kit, because you do not need batteries.

You can also send signals with a torch. The distress signal **SOS** is flashed in Morse code as three short, three long and three short. In the mountains there is the alpine distress signal: six signals a minute, then a minute's break. But anyone in an emergency should always first call for help on a mobile phone, for example on the emergency number 112 or Rega on 1414.

The first torches appeared around 1900, after small dry batteries had been invented. Because the batteries were weak, you could only shine them briefly in flashes, which is why in American English they are called a **flashlight**. Today many adults carry a mobile phone that can also be used as a torch. For hikes and camps a **head torch** is handy, because it leaves your hands free.

begriffe.erklaerung: Light-emitting diode, a small electronic part that produces light very economically.
A shiny, curved mirror that directs light in one direction.
A closed path along which electric current can flow.
The unit used to give how much light a lamp gives off.
A code made of short and long signals.

gewusst: If you hold a torch against your fingertip, it glows red, because red light passes through skin best.
In Great Britain the word is torch, which originally meant a flaming stick.
An LED can shine for tens of thousands of hours before it gets weaker.

teile.einleitung: Solar Impulse is a Swiss project for aircraft that fly on solar energy alone. In 2016, with Solar Impulse 2, the pilots Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg became the first to fly around the Earth in a solar aircraft. The project was meant to show what clean technology can already do today.
wichtigste: Solar Impulse is a solar aircraft project by the Swiss Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg.
In 2016 Solar Impulse 2 completed the first round-the-world flight by a solar aircraft.
The start and finish of the round-the-world flight was Abu Dhabi.
The wingspan was about 72 metres.
More than 17,000 solar cells supplied the electricity.
At night the aircraft flew on electricity from batteries that were charged during the day.
There was only room for one person in the cockpit.

abschnitte.text: Behind Solar Impulse are the doctor and adventurer **Bertrand Piccard** and the engineer and pilot **André Borschberg**. In 1999 Piccard had already travelled non-stop around the Earth in a balloon. He comes from a famous family of explorers: his grandfather Auguste rose into the stratosphere in a balloon, and his father Jacques dived into the deep sea. The project started in the early 2000s.

In 2010 the first aircraft, **Solar Impulse 1**, became the first manned solar aircraft to fly right through a night. After that the larger **Solar Impulse 2** was built. At about 72 metres, its wings were wider than those of a jumbo jet, yet it weighed only about as much as a car with a trailer. The aircraft were tested at Payerne airfield in the canton of Vaud.

There were more than 17,000 **solar cells** on the wings and the body. They drove four electric motors with propellers. During the day, spare electricity charged large **batteries**, which let the aircraft keep flying at night. Because the power was small, Solar Impulse flew at a leisurely pace, about as fast as a car on a country road.

In March 2015 Solar Impulse 2 took off in **Abu Dhabi**. The journey went in stages across Asia, the Pacific, the USA, the Atlantic, Europe and North Africa. Because of damaged batteries the aircraft had to pause in Hawaii for several months. In July 2016 it landed back in Abu Dhabi, after more than 40,000 kilometres.

André Borschberg flew the longest stage in 2015, from Japan to **Hawaii**. He spent almost five days and nights alone in the cramped cockpit. He could only sleep in short naps of about 20 minutes. At the time this flight was the longest solo flight without a stop that any pilot had ever managed.

Solar Impulse was not meant to replace air travel, but to show how much is possible with renewable energy. After the round-the-world flight Piccard founded the **Solar Impulse Foundation**. It collects clean and affordable solutions to environmental problems. The aircraft itself was later sold and used for test flights without a pilot.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin plate that turns sunlight into electricity.
The width of an aircraft from one wing tip to the other.
One part of a long journey between two landings.
A rechargeable battery that stores electricity.

gewusst: Solar Impulse 2 was wider than a jumbo jet, but weighed only about 2.3 tonnes.
The pilots had to put up with big differences in temperature in the cockpit, because there was no heating and no pressurised cabin.
With this, Bertrand Piccard's family has produced three generations of record-breaking adventurers.
